There might be hope for Arkane after all: A new report says multiple companies have made offers for it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new report from Bloomberg says Dishonored developer Arkane might not be as doomed as it appeared last month, as multiple companies have made offers to acquire the studio.

Citing "people familiar with the negotiations," the Bloomberg report says Ubisoft is among Arkane's suitors, as are at least two other unnamed gaming companies. Xbox has also considered selling the studio to its own management, effectively making it independent, although whether that option is still on the table isn't clear.

Despite producing an enviable slate of acclaimed immersive sims over the years (until it was compelled by senior leadership to do otherwise), Arkane fell victim to the Xbox "reset" in July that saw thousands of employees laid off (with more still awaiting their fates) and four studios cast adrift. Arkane avoided being the fifth, reportedly thanks to France's "Florange Law" that compelled Xbox to search for a buyer before pulling the plug.

The deadline for that search was November 13, after which Arkane would be shuttered—but a few weeks ahead of that date, Microsoft extended it by a month, to "explore options, including finding a partner to support the studio through the development work still ahead," a reference to the Marvel's Blade game Arkane currently has in development. That extension suggested there was at least some hope that Arkane might find a new home, instead of being closed.

Going from Xbox to Ubisoft could be viewed as a "frying pan to fire" move, given Ubisoft's own ongoing financial struggles, layoffs, and closures. But Arkane's immersive sim expertise could be a good fit for some of Ubisoft's biggest properties, including Assassin's Creed, Far Cry, and—yes, I'm just going to say it—Splinter Cell, which would be magnificent in the style of Dishonored. Arkane and Ubisoft both being French companies can't hurt, either.

I've reached out to Xbox and Ubisoft for comment on the report, and will update if I receive a reply.

Dancing with the Stars will be without one of its pros on Disney Night, but there's no drama involving Carrie Ann Inaba. Adele Zaikman is going to sit out this episode on the 2026 TV schedule, and she's really bummed about it. As viewers wait to see their favorite Disney songs and who gets sent home, Zaikman will be watching at home with the rest of us. While it's not due to a suspension like what happened with Val Chmerkovskiy, it is because of an illness.

Adele Zaikman will miss Dancing with the Stars because she's feeling "unwell." The dancer revealed this on her Instagram Stories and sent the following message to the rest of the cast ahead of the episode:

I'm sadly feeling unwell and won't be performing in the opening number on Dancing With The Stars tomorrow. I'm so sad to miss a show day, but I'll be taking this time to take care of myself. Sending so much love to everyone on that ballroom floor. I'll be cheering you on from home.

As mentioned, Zaikman was scheduled to be a part of the opening dance number, which, based on rehearsals posted by Bach Scoop, will be a number from The Greatest Showman. I'm once again baffled by Disney Night featuring a musical that is not explicitly a Disney movie, but I digress.

While the pros participating on Dancing with the Stars often get the spotlight, those eliminated still have plenty to do. Adele Zaikman and others usually help prepare the opening dance numbers or transition pieces while the competitors prepare for their routines.

Witney Carson (Who Is Pregnant) Absolutely Crushed Her ‘Fat Thor’ Halloween Costume

In addition to that, the DWTS pros often help out with the TikTok Live show and can even help those still in the competition with their routines. Brandon Armstrong's wife even joked once that pro dancers would get busier when they're eliminated, which might explain why Adele Zaikman is so apologetic. Her absence could make for some last-minute changes, but I imagine the show will come together all the same.

Disney Night is a beloved episode each season on Dancing with the Stars, and it just got a bit bigger in Season 35. The show will welcome Cynthia Erivo as a guest star, and she'll be giving her input on the dance routines. I'll be curious to see how she scores competitors, and if we'll see any more 10s handed out.

Another way this night stands out is that there's an emphasis of Disney on Broadway. As such, we have the aforementioned nods to The Greatest Showman and Hamilton. I'm sure there will also be a nod or two at Wicked, given Erivo sitting in on all of the performances. All that aside, though, let's just hope Adele Zaikman gets well soon (and not just for the sake of the show, of course).

Catch Dancing with the Stars on ABC tonight, Monday, November 2nd, at 8 p.m. ET, and the show also streams live on Disney+. Take note of the start time, as Tuesday will be Election Day, which means people won't be able to vote ten times per candidate!

#3714. Tatyana Ali Hints at How She Chose Her 'DWTS' Group Dance Team

Tatyana Ali is explaining her thought process behind selecting her group dance members on Dancing With the Stars’ Disney Night.

“Tatyana… as the lowest scored person why wouldn’t you choose at least ONE of the stars with a dance background for your team ? 😭,” one user wrote via Threads, while another added, “Maybe I’m reading too much into it but she strikes me as someone who is very intentional about who she shares space with. And I think who she picked was a reflection of that 🤷🏽‍♀️.”

The former Fresh Prince of Bel-Air star, 47, then chimed in to agree with the user’s assessment, writing, “Very much so.”

Ali and fellow season 35 contestant Connor Wood were crowned the team captains of the two group dances for the Monday, November 2, episode due to having the lowest combined total of judges scores.

Ali first selected Maura Higgins before then picking Amber Glenn and Julia Stiles to join her team. The group then performed a freestyle to Zootopia 2’s “Zoo” with cohost Alfonso Ribeiro.

Wood, meanwhile, chose Ezra Frech, Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Dewan for his group dance freestyle to High School Musical’s “We Are All In This Together” with cohost Julianne Hough. Team Wildcats earned a perfect 40 out of 40 from the judges.

“This is the most amazing team,” Ali said in the package of the Monday episode, adding in a confessional, “Being captain is a lot of responsibility.”

In keeping with their “Slaytopia” team name, Ali and her group ultimately slayed their performance and earned a 36 out of 40 from judges Carrie Ann Inaba, Derek Hough, Bruno Tonioli and guest judge Cynthia Erivo.

The score was then added to each pair’s individual tally from the first round of the episode. Ali and partner Jan Ravnik had previously performed a contemporary to “Easy As Life” from Aida and earned a 33 out of 40.

“Jan had me do things that when I first came here I couldn’t have done. And I just wanted to do his work justice because it’s so beautiful,” Ali said in the skybox after the performance, to which Ravnik replied, “And she did.”

The pair were ultimately safe from elimination, with Stiles and partner Ezra Sosa saying goodbye to the ballroom. Ali and Ravnik’s dance style and song have yet to be revealed for next week’s Grammy Night.

Dancing With the Stars airs on ABC and Disney+ Tuesdays at 8 p.m. ET.

#3713. Sir Patrick Stewart, Theater Titan and ‘Star Trek’ Captain, Dies at 86

Sir Patrick Stewart, the beloved actor of stage, screen, and television, died Wednesday following “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia,” according to his representative, Kelly Bush Novak. The performer, best known in this and every other star system as Captain Jean-Luc Picard of the USS Enterprise, first appeared in the legendary role in September 1987. After seven seasons of television, four feature films, several video games, and site-specific interactive experiences, he returned to the character in the age of streaming, finally warping to retirement and surrounded by his crew, in January of 2020. He was 79 years old.

Stewart began his long and prosperous life in Yorkshire, England, as the youngest of three boys. His father was a World War II veteran, and, as Stewart discussed, suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder. Witnessing violence against his mother as a child, he said, led to Stewart’s later charity work for causes surrounding domestic violence.

He took theater classes in his youth and befriended a slightly older local lad, the actor-mountaineer Brian Blessed. He went on to study at the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, a small, competitive conservatory that began with support from Sir Laurence Olivier, and boasts Daniel Day-Lewis, Olivia Colman, Jeremy Irons, Miranda Richardson, and many others as alumni.

In 1966, at age 26, Stewart joined the Royal Shakespeare Company, one of the most prestigious theater companies in Britain. During his time there, he appeared as the lead in The Life and Death of King John, as Oberon in A Midsummer Night’s Dream, and as Shylock in The Merchant of Venice, as well as more than 80 other roles, at the RSC’s main home in Stratford-upon-Avon, in London, and on tour. During this part of his career, he also appeared in supporting roles on television. The two most notable were the BBC production of I, Claudius, in which he played Emperor Tiberius’s double-crossing Praetorian guard Sejanus opposite a who’s who of British thespians (Derek Jacobi, John Hurt, Siân Phillips, Bernard Hill, John Rhys-Davies, Stewart’s old chum Brian Blessed, just to name a few), and as the evil mastermind Karla opposite Sir Alec Guinness in the adaptation of John Le Carré’s Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy and Smiley’s People.

As the 1970s turned to the 1980s, there were some film roles of note, including the part of Leodegrance in John Boorman’s Excalibur and Gurney Halleck in David Lynch’s version of Frank Herbert’s Dune. At one moment in the film, he leads a charge into battle clutching a cute li’l pug. (This same character, without the use of domesticated pets, was played by Josh Brolin in the more recent iteration.)

In 1986, with the original Star Trek still drawing good numbers in reruns and on videocassette, and with the feature films starring William Shatner and Leonard Nimoy doing well at the box office, Paramount thought it wise to update the series for television. Franchise creator Gene Roddenberry, who had worked on a “Phase II” Star Trek project in the late 1970s (which led, eventually, to the 1979 film) soon found himself at the drafting board for Star Trek: The Next Generation.

With a bridge crew of several writers and producers from what we now call The Original Series, the new version, set a little less than 100 years down the timeline, differentiated itself in a number of ways. The most notable change was reversing many of the attributes between the Captain and his first officer. Whereas Captain Kirk was a man of action, Captain Jean-Luc Picard was more cerebral, calculating, and cultured, sharing many characteristics with TOS’s half-Vulcan second-in-command, Mr. Spock. (TNG’s Commander Riker, played by Jonathan Frakes, was a bit more rough-and-tumble, and also likelier to woo interplanetary women.)

Patrick Stewart was not Roddenberry’s first choice (Belgian actor Patrick Bauchau, Yaphet Kotto, Roy Thinnes, and Dark Shadows’s Mitch Ryan were also in the mix). But in time, the not-too-well-known Shakespearean won out. When the casting was announced, a reporter suggested to Roddenberry that by the 24th century, in a time of faster-than-light starships, surely humankind would have found a cure for male pattern baldness, no? “No, by the 24th century, no one will care,” Roddenberry retorted, to the delight of bald guys everywhere.

As Stewart has repeated time and again, he took the gig thinking it was a doomed project, as no one would want to watch a retread of a classic. He figured he’d make a few quick bucks, secure some contacts, then head back to his real job on the British stage. He later called the decision to join Starfleet “the most important thing” in his career and his life.

But the first season of Star Trek: The Next Generation did not sail out of spacedock without some bumps. (Please don’t rewatch episode four, “Code of Honor,” if you know what’s good for you.) Though wanting to differentiate itself from TOS was the right move, some of the scripts could have used a little more derring-do, and the Picard character comes off at times as a little too cold. This unease was mirrored a bit behind the scenes, where Stewart experienced a little bit of culture clash.

Most of his fellow cast members were Americans who had worked in TV, like Night Court alum Brent Spiner. They were prone to goofing around in between takes, to the point that Stewart actually called a company meeting to scold them. It did not go over too well, but in time, Stewart began to loosen up. (This has now become a favorite thing for the gang to reminisce about during panels at Star Trek conventions, as everyone quickly became, and remained, good pals.)

The chemistry on the USS Enterprise (the Enterprise-D, if we’re getting specific) synched, and the show was a massive hit, making television history as a model for a successful first-run syndication. (If you happened to be a budding sci-fi nerd in central New Jersey that got both New York and Philly stations, it meant you could watch the show twice in the same weekend—not that I would know anything about that.)

From the first episode of TNG in late 1987, through a crossover to Star Trek: Deep Space Nine, and then feature films ending with 2002’s Star Trek: Nemesis, Stewart’s Picard saved the galaxy countless times with class, strength, and poise. Now is not the time to ask, “Who was the best captain?” But one can say, unequivocally, that Picard was the most quotable.

As TNG transitioned from television series to movies, Stewart, with more time on his hands, saw to it that his first role out of the gate would prove his range as an actor. As such, he costarred in the LGBTQ classic Jeffrey, based on Paul Rudnick’s play, as the flamboyant interior decorator Sterling. It may seem like nothing now, but, in 1995, to see a science fiction hero embracing a gay role was a bold move for progressivism.

In the 1990s, between Trek movies, Stewart played Captain Ahab in a USA Network adaptation of Moby Dick, led a one-man show version of A Christmas Carol, and played Prospero in The Tempest for the New York Shakespeare Festival. Then, in 2000, Stewart took on another clutch role in science fiction, Professor Charles Xavier in Bryan Singer’s version of X-Men.

As the schoolmaster/spiritual leader of Marvel’s mutant population, Stewart has played Professor X in eight features, most recently in Sam Raimi’s Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness. It was through the X-Men universe that he and Sir Ian McKellen forged their delightful and public friendship, which led to the two performing in Waiting for Godot together, and McKellen officiating at Stewart’s wedding to jazz singer Sunny Ozell in 2013.

In 2006, Stewart made the first of several returns to the Royal Shakespeare Company to play Mark Antony in Antony and Cleopatra. His most recent turn on the boards at his old haunt was 2011’s The Merchant of Venice, once again playing Shylock, for director Rupert Goold.

But after a slew of television guest spots (from Frasier to Extras) and lending his voice to various projects including several led by Seth MacFarlane, an album with classical pianist Emanuel Ax, and a profitable Pontiac campaign, he found himself going back to the future. Star Trek: Picard launched in 2020 with a rocky first two seasons before the ship righted itself for a final, triumphant season in 2023, shepherded by Terry Matalas, that reunited Stewart with the cast (and the more than 35-year-old ship) from The Next Generation.

Patrick Stewart was not Captain Jean-Luc Picard, but he brought him to life. Over 178 episodes of TNG (and countless novels and comic books that you can pretend are episodes in your head, not to mention daydreams) the French space explorer with the English accent was a beacon of righteousness and leadership. He accepted input and analysis from anyone in his crew, but felt no obligation to consensus when his mind was made up. He was bookish but also sexy and liked to keep his tunic straight.

As Stewart aged, he increasingly recognized the degree to which Star Trek meant something to millions (and would defend those hardcore fans when needed!) In 2010 he was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II. He won a Grammy in 1996 for best spoken word album for children (a recording of Peter and the Wolf) and in 2008 was nominated for a Tony for a production of Macbeth. He was nominated for four Emmys, though none of them for Star Trek.

During the coronavirus pandemic, he initiated a series on social media in which he read a new Shakespeare sonnet each day. We’ll conclude here with the final one.

Mamdani and others have called out Google's decision to disable search functionality for schools who opt out of its AI tools.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Saying that it believes "schools should have control over AI in their classrooms," Google announced today that it will turn off access to its AI tools for K-12 student accounts. But there's a catch: Along with those AI tools, it will also disable Google search functionality.

In a blog post entitled "Designing responsible AI for learning," Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager of education, extolled the virtues of AI tools in "productive struggle," which he described as "enabling students to be actively challenged without getting so overwhelmed that they give up."

"That's the philosophy behind Guided Learning," Philips wrote. "In Gemini, Guided Learning acts as an interactive study tool that coaches students through the process of problem solving through open-ended questions and step-by-step breakdowns. Our research shows that Guided Learning leads to measurable learning gains for students, and we're now bringing Guided Learning to more products." Those products include Google Search and Google Classroom.

"After listening to schools, teachers, leading researchers, and policymakers, we are now updating our approach to controls for Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search," Phillips continued. "Access to these products will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on."

It sounds like Google Search on student accounts can be re-enabled separately, but that also ushers AI back into the equation: Google said in the update that it is "building Guided Learning capabilities into Search for student accounts to help them work through problems without skipping straight to answers." In other words, there is no search functionality on these accounts without AI intrusion.

Speaking to the New York Times, Phillips said "search and AI are deeply integrated," and confirmed that schools can't have one without the other: Students at schools that have turned off Google's AI tools "will not have access to search, and they'll see a message from their school that indicates it's not available."

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Fairplay, a non-profit that aims to protect children from "the exploitative and harmful business practices of marketers and Big Tech," was somewhat harsher in its assessment. "Google's attempt to strong-arm schools into using its AI products is likely to backfire," Fairplay executive director Josh Golin said in a statement. "Schools should use this opportunity not only to turn off AI, but to teach students that 'Google' isn't a verb, but the name of a surveillance and advertising company whose presence in schools has nothing to do with learning and everything to do with developing lifetime brand loyalty.

Former FTC chair Lina Khan, who was right about Microsoft's acquisition of Activision Blizzard, also weighed in, accusing Google of "using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI."

"Multiple courts have found Google liable for violating antitrust laws, and this latest move shows it remains unchastened," Khan wrote on X. "As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools, Google is making clear it will punish those who don't fall in line."

New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani, a longstanding critic of oligopolies and corporate greed, said that "Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools."

Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools. No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children.  Our public schools exist to serve students, not to grow the profit margins of Big Tech.

As NBC noted, research on the impact of AI in education is still quite limited, and some studies purporting to show meaningful benefits have been found to be flawed. That makes the headlong rush into AI integration, championed by massive AI companies and pretty much no one else, so controversial and potentially dangerous. Trying to force AI into classrooms while the technology's impact on mental health is an increasingly serious concern is audacious, and promises of more rigorous safety standards tend to ring hollow anyway: In October, the attorneys general for eight US states accused competing product OpenAI of ignoring its own safety warnings in pursuit of profit.

Google's new policy on AI in schools comes just days after shares in Google parent company Alphabet took a hammering as the company's AI Mode cut deep into its search business and revenue. I've reached out to Google for more information about the new educational policy and will update if I receive a reply.

The 2026 movie schedule has marked the releases of plenty of high-profile titles, but it could be argued that few have sparked as many discussions as Digger has. Directed by Alejandro Iñárritu, the Tom Cruise-fronted film mixes satire with a significant helping of social commentary to create a bold swing. Early reactions to Cruise and Iñárritu’s film were tepid, and it eventually flopped at the box office as well. Now, one of the film’s cast members, John Goodman, is opening up about the film being “killed” before it could even reach theaters.

Digger was released in early October, and the first reactions began to hit social media after its UK premiere in late October. Goodman sat down for an interview on the Happy Sad Confused podcast, which was recorded on October 5th (right after the movie’s opening weekend). Both Goodman and host Josh Horowitz got real about the reception to the Iñárritu flick, with Horowitz emphasizing how the film really has people “talking.” The Argo alum didn’t disagree but also got candid about how the reception was affecting him:

People are talking…. Yeah, it hurt. They kind of killed us before we opened. ‘This will only make $5,’ and it's a good reason for people to avoid it.

Digger heavily focuses on the story of oil tycoon Digger Rockwell (Cruise), who finds himself in the position of having to save the planet from an environmental catastrophe he caused. Ultimately, it’s a comedy of errors that has a lot to say about the state of the world, particularly our feelings towards climate change. There’s also a big twist in the film, which is so massive that I’m still not keen on spoiling it for readers here.

Ultimately, the full reviews of the black comedy weren’t strong, and they earned Cruise his worst Rotten Tomatoes score for a film in nearly a decade. (As of this writing, the film has a critics rating of 53% on RT and an audience rating of 77%.) The reception actually became so hard to ignore that the marketing team even addressed the polarizing reviews head on in a TV spot. From a financial perspective, the film has reportedly earned $49 million worldwide against a reported production budget between $125 and $180 million.

With all that said, Digger does have its share of defenders, with filmmaker Guillermo del Toro emerging as a champion for it along with the likes of Ben Affleck, Anna Hathaway, Glen Powell and Bill Burr. Tom Cruise himself has also expressed his appreciation for the cast and crew amid the tepid responses. Likewise, John Goodman – who broke his hip amid production – feels fortunate to have been a part of the massive movie:

I'm proud of it, and I had a ball doing it. It was a good six months out of my life. It is a huge swing…. It’s gonna be around for a long time.

To that point, there are indeed films that prove to have staying power if they’re initially polarizing or not well received upon their releases. Goodman even made a good point in that a number of his collaborations with the Coen brothers initially generated lukewarm receptions before finding major followings later. (And, believe it or not, that includes The Big Lebowski.) So, while Goodman may have been “hurt” by responses to his latest movie, he’s still of the belief that it’ll have quite the shelf life.

Digger is still playing in some theaters, meaning anyone who wants to see it for themselves still has the time to do so.

#3710. Kristen Bell and Dax Shepard's Most Polarizing Comments Over the Years

Kristen Bell and Dax Shepard have become some people’s favorite couple in Hollywood, but others scrutinize their every move.

Bell started dating Shepard in 2007. The couple got engaged in 2009, eventually tying the knot in 2013. Bell and Shepard went on to welcome daughters Lincoln (born in March 2013) and Delta (born in December 2014).

While their relationship has made headlines since the start, Shepard’s popular podcast, “Armchair Expert,” and Bell’s success on Netflix’s Nobody Wants has put even more attention on the pair.

“Having someone I feel that is very opposite from me is certainly something that I feel. I feel like my real-life husband and I are ‘opposites attract,'” she told People while comparing her onscreen romance with Adam Brody to her real-like marriage ahead of the release of season 2 in October 2025. “But that doesn’t mean we couldn’t make it work, or didn’t want to make it work.”

Keep scrolling for a full breakdown on why people can’t stop talking about Bell and Shepard:

In 2021, Shepard and Bell made major headlines for sharing their showering habits.

The couple admitted to only giving their daughters showers when they start to “stink” during an interview on The View at the time. Shepard and Bell said they used to give their girls a bath “every single night before bed,” but things changed as they got older.

“Once you catch a whiff, that’s biology’s way of letting you know you need to clean it up,” Bell said, noting that they sometimes would go “five or six days” without washing the girls. “There’s a red flag, because honestly, it’s just bacteria. And once you get the bacteria, you gotta be like, ‘Get in the tub or the shower.’”

Months after the shower admission, Bell and Shepard got real about how they speak with their daughters about sex.

“The woman takes the man’s penis and puts it in her vagina,” he said during a 2021 “Armchair Expert” episode. “Right away it’s like, you’re in charge of this and you will decide to put this in your vagina. Not the man puts his penis in your vagina.”

He said it was a “nice little adjustment” they made to discuss consent with their kids.

Bell made headlines in September 2024 when she admitted to letting her daughters roam free during a family trip to Denmark.

“The hack is when we went to Copenhagen, we stayed at this hotel that was right at Tivoli Gardens, which is like a 7-acre theme park. It’s an old one,” she said on Jimmy Kimmel Live!. “The hotel opens up into the theme park and so we just were kind of like, ‘Are we going to free-range parenting and roll the die here?’ They woke up at, like, 6 every morning. They scanned their bracelets to go outside. [We] didn’t see them for seven hours. Just running around Copenhagen.”

She said it was “heaven” for her and Shepard.

“We just had coffee. We played Spades, and then around 3, we’d be like, ‘Anybody see them?’” she recalled. “And then one of them would run up and need a Band-Aid or whatever.”

Over the years, Shepard has not been shy when it comes to showing off his wife.

In May 2021, he made headlines for sharing a photo of Bell doing naked yoga to celebrate Mother’s Day.

“Mom’ing has changed since I was a kid … and I’m here for it. Look at this specimen: kind, patient, nurturing, hilarious, Uber talented, generous, hard AND soft,” he captioned the since-deleted Instagram post. “My girls and I hit the MegaMom Lottery. We are so grateful and so in love with you.”

Years later, he gave social media followers more than they bargained for after Bell was nominated for a 2025 Emmy Award. He posted a photo of Bell’s butt up in the air — but it was blurred out for the folks at home.

“People might not know everything that happens behind the scenes in order to create an Emmy nominated performance like Kristen’s,” he captioned the photo. “This may or may not have been a part of her training, but it felt right. CONGRATULATIONS!!!!!”

Bell shared a controversial post when celebrating her and Shepard’s 12th anniversary in October 2025.

“Happy 12th wedding anniversary to the man who once said to me: ‘I would never kill you,” she captioned the post. “A lot of men have killed their wives at a certain point. Even though I’m heavily incentivized to kill you, I never would.’”

Instagram users called out Bell for writing that caption during Domestic Violence Awareness. The National Network to End Domestic Violence shared a statement to Page Six amid the controversy.

“There’s nothing funny about domestic violence ‘jokes’ that trivialize the very real fear, trauma and pain that millions of victims and survivors face each day,” they shared. “Especially during Domestic Violence Awareness Month, we all have a responsibility to support victims and survivors, to invest in proven solutions and to speak about this issue with the seriousness it deserves.”

After the anniversary post, a video of them from 2012 resurfaced where Shepard made an off-color joke about “hitting” Bell. The two were discussing riding in a car he worked on with Bell in the passenger seat.

“He was so excited. We drove to brunch and the first thing I said, five minutes into the ride, I said, ‘This sounds like it’s gonna break,’” she said, recalling that Shepard was “very offended” by her reaction.

“And then I hit her several times,” Shepard replied, joking. Bell responded, “And then I got beat up, and guess what — I never opened my mouth again.”

During an October 2026 episode of Shepard’s “Armchair Expert” podcast featuring guests Bell, Justine Lupe, Timothy Simons and Adam Brody, the Frozen star revealed that her husband flirts with her by complimenting other people.

“If we go to a dinner or something, like, there’s a couple things Dax does where he doesn’t have to look up and wink at me, but I know that he’s just being the best boy,” she said. “We’ll be at dinner, and, like, he’ll say to the waiter or waitress, he’ll go, ‘Wow, you have incredible eyelashes, gorgeous eyes, great job.'”

When Shepard’s cohost, Monica Padman, pointed out that this is a form of flirting with other women, Bell responded, “But that’s flirting with me, because he just made someone else feel good.”

“‘Cause he’s gonna have zero interaction with — let’s say it is a girl. He’s gonna have zero interaction with this girl for the rest of his life. The chances of him ever having another conversation with her are so microscopic,” she continued. “But to me, to know that my partner actively smiles at people and gives them compliments [makes me feel good].”

Bell also said that Shepard has never crossed the line and gone too far with his compliments.

“You’ve never done anything that’s felt even borderline … you, like, you’ll point out someone has great eyebrows, or great cheekbones,” she said.

“That’s why it makes me fluttery inside. That’s why it gives me butterflies,” Bell noted. “Because everyone saw it, he’s the only one that said it, maybe she hadn’t had a compliment today. And I’m with the guy that’s pouring compliments on people? Making people feel good?”

The revelation stirred up controversy as fans questioned whether this is respectful behavior in a relationship.

#3709. Inside Airbnb.org’s Gala With Jimmy Kimmel, Charli xcx, and Brian Chesky

Nothing says billionaire-hosted gala quite like an olive sphere. What’s an olive sphere, you ask? Imagine a bite-sized gelatinous membrane filled with olive juice that is served on a tiny silver platter, and requires two servers—two!—to pass out: one to offer guests the savory blobs, and another to collect the discarded platters.

Before taking the stage at Milk Studios in Los Angeles on Wednesday night, Jimmy Kimmel walked past two olive sphere servers and a third handing out caviar. He told me he’d been listening to The Howard Stern Show on the drive over, and something so X-rated came on that he had to quickly turn down the volume when he pulled up alongside another car. Evidently, it put him in a silly mood by the time he welcomed guests to the first ever gala for Airbnb’s independent nonprofit—or “gay-la,” as he put it, “depending on your sexual orientation.”

Kimmel had been tapped to serve as master of ceremonies at the fundraiser for the home-sharing behemoth’s nonprofit, which was created in 2020 to provide free temporary housing to people displaced by disasters and other crises. Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky announced a $500 million funding commitment over the next five years, allowing the organization to expand its services to families traveling for medical treatment and survivors of domestic violence.

Among the guests were people who had lost their homes in the devastating Eaton Fire in 2025. They shared a room with a group of people who presumably have little need for emergency housing: Charlize Theron, Serena Williams, Matthew McConaughey, Katie Couric, Joaquin Phoenix, Rooney Mara, Cynthia Erivo, and Demi Lovato, among others. It was a collision of two Los Angeleses: People who had lost everything, and people who wore bling worth as much as a house in Altadena.

Most of the men were dressed in tuxedos. Williams shined in a sparkly animal-print gown. Paul Bettany wore a black Chairman Mao-style shirt. Jaden Smith wore jeans, apparently missing the black-tie memo.

Kimmel, decked out in a perfectly tailored black tuxedo, had some ground rules as the emcee. Guests were expected to wash their dishes. No pets, except service animals, “which we know none of them really are.” “And absolutely no sitting naked on the furniture or on chef José Andrés.”

Chesky, who hard-launched his relationship with girlfriend designer Carly Helfrich on the red carpet, delivered his remarks with the cadence of Vanessa Bayer’s Jacob the Bar Mitzvah Boy Saturday Night Live character, staring down at the teleprompter positioned on the floor. “People are fundamentally good,” he declared, explaining that Airbnb’s business would have never worked otherwise.

On the red carpet, I asked Chesky whether the Trump administration had made it harder for his nonprofit to house people fleeing tragedy. “No, absolutely not,” he insisted, describing emergency housing as a cause that transcends partisan politics. This was a rather diplomatic answer from a man whose company once ran advertisements welcoming refugees in pointed opposition to Trump’s 2017 Muslim travel ban. But Chesky wasn’t taking the bait. “This is a very united kind of issue,” he said.

The night took an emotional turn when Kimmel talked about his son Billy’s three open-heart surgeries before introducing a video of a young boy receiving cancer treatments who was the beneficiary of the charity’s efforts. At that moment, the child, who was in attendance with his mom and grandma, stood on his chair and made a heart symbol using his two hands. The crowd went wild.

José Andrés, whose name appeared on the menu but who was rather noncommittal when asked whether he had actually designed it, insisted that the evening’s charitable mission was more than an excuse for Hollywood to get dressed up.

By dessert, Kimmel was shaking down the wealthy guests. “Don’t cheap out,” he warned, noting that anyone who could afford the new folding iPhone (which retails at roughly $2,000) could surely spare $110 to provide a family with a night of emergency housing. He also accidentally revealed the evening’s secret musical guest: Charli xcx.

“Oh shit!” he exclaimed, realizing his mistake. “Okay, it’s not a surprise anymore.”

Charli eventually took the stage, with will.i.am and Greta Lee dancing from the front row. “That was soooooo good,” Lee said to me on the way out.

And although the set wasn’t particularly long, Charli rocked it, sending heads banging everywhere. She got the Hollywood room doing what it does best: partying for a cause.

#3708. How To Share Story Tips With Kotaku

Here at Kotaku, we strive to cut through the noise and nonsense and tell you real, interesting, and thought-provoking stories about the world of video games. In order to help us do that, we want people who know things about those video games and everything surrounding them to be able to talk to us securely and anonymously.

So weâve created a guide for anyone who wants to tip or share information with Kotaku, whether youâre a game developer, a customer service representative, a community leader, a PR representative, or a video game fan with a story to tell. The video game industry is shrouded in a culture of corporate silence that we do our best to penetrate every day, because we believe that people should have as much information as possible. So if you see or experience something that you think is important for people to know, or maybe just interesting, we want to hear from you, including in cases when you want your identity to be protected.

If you want to reach all of us, send your tips to: [email protected]

And if you want to send an e-mail to an individual Kotaku writer, find your favorite one on our masthead and shoot them a note.

Our tips inbox is only read by full-time staffers, and we check it every hour of every day. If you donât get a response, donât worry, weâve definitely seen it. And if you read this entire page and still arenât sure if you should send your tip, send it anyway. At worst, everyone at Kotaku will learn something new about the world of video games, and weâll be grateful for it.

But please do read the rest of the page first:

Weâre interested in news involving any aspect of gaming: game development, publishing, sales, things going on within games, things people are doing with games, all of it. Sometimes that means reporting on big cancelled projects or doing in-depth looks at chunks of video game history. Sometimes it means exposing malfeasanceâsharing stories about horrible work conditions at a game studio or reporting on a multinational company that isnât paying its staff on time. Sometimes it means answering big questions that everyoneâs asking, like why a game really keeps getting delayed over and over, or the events that led to a studio closure. We care about things that you yourself find interesting or surprising, and we want to help people know whatâs cool to play and what to avoid.

We primarily want gaming news, of course, and we care about it whether it comes from a gamer, a game-maker, or anyone else who gives a damn about video games. And if you have pictures, screenshots, video, or other first-hand evidence of whatever you want us to know about, thatâs a huge bonus.

We also, obviously, accept press releases, news about your cool indie game thatâs about to come out, pitches from PR to interview developers or preview or review games, and all the usual stuff. We recommend sending those to individual writers you have relationships with if possible, especially if you already know someone on staff is familiar with your game/genre/franchise. But if youâre just trying to reach us for the first time, the tips email is fine for that too.

Sometimes, you might want to share something with us, but want to remain anonymous because having your name attached to that information could come with consequences of some kind. Thatâs totally okay. In most cases, the journalist you speak to will still need to verify your identity (to prove youâd be in a position to know what youâre claiming to know), but will keep that information entirely to themselves if you prefer. We strictly do not share any information about anonymous sources with anyone for any reason.

In stories where we refer to sources who spoke to us anonymously, we will generally refer to those sources with as few details as possible. Often, that will just mean writing, âa source familiar with the matterâ or âan employee of [company]â or similar. Sometimes, some context clues will be necessary: for instance, if weâre writing about sexism at a studio, it may be important to identify the gender of our sources. We will always check with you first to make sure youâre comfortable with how youâre being referred to in the piece.

While we strictly do not share full articles with anyone outside of Kotaku prior to publication, we can on request go over your quotes with you after we speak to remind you of what was said and confirm there are no identifying details being used. We can also provide some general context about how the quotes are being used in the story, so you can help us confirm that our reporting is accurate to your understanding.

As a rule of thumb, you may not want to tell anyone that youâre talking to usâthe fewer people who know about any correspondence you may have with Kotaku, the more protected youâll be. Donât use your company e-mail account, any company-connected phone, work computer, or work WiFi network to contact us as an anonymous source. Instead, use a personal account or phone from home, or a public Wi-Fi network if you can do so safely. You can also reach most of our writers via Signal. Several of us have our Signal information in our social media bio pages, but if youâre looking for a specific writer, you can just email us directly and ask for our Signal name, no further context needed.

If the story youâd like to share with us would be improved by photos, screenshots, or other documentation, such records are often extremely helpful for us in corroborating a story and protecting your identity. If you can, itâs best to take pictures of photos or documents with a personal phone and send those, rather than the documents themselves. And when you send them to us, remove the metadata first. We do our own metadata scrubbing before we post leaked photos on Kotaku, but itâs best to be as safe as possible.

Similar to news tips, but different. While a lot of our stories are about game companies and creators, we also love writing about what gamers do.

Did you just play through Call of Duty without firing a shot? Are you one of the last dozen people playing the multiplayer in a game thatâs long since faded in popularity? Did you see someone pull off a crazy move in a Street Fighter tournament and happen to get video of it? Have you found a glitch no one knows about? Were you the person who figured out how to game the Steam summer sale? Did you make an incredible mod for your kids?

Maybe itâs not just you. Maybe youâve got a big Discord community dedicated to a game thatâs doing something neat. Or maybe youâre part of a subreddit thatâs very worked up about a niche update in the latest patch of your favorite game. Perhaps youâve got a local community putting on an in-person event surrounding something in a video game. Might be your guild in an MMO, your group chat, or maybe youâre still on forums.

We want to hear about all that stuff. Send it to tips. Send it to the staff. Just send it!

As wishlisted games miss their release dates, Valve creates a new checklist to help devs get it right the first time.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new kind of Steam problem has emerged: Games keep missing their release dates because Valve can't keep up with approving them.

Several frustrated indie devs have publicly posted about the limbo status of their finished games in the past week—including the developers of Food Devils, Wheel Make It, and Cubic Earth—saying that their applications have gone unanswered after up to 20 days, despite Valve's listed review window of three to five business days.

In the case of Cubic Earth, developer structmira hasn't been able to contact Valve and has no choice but to wait. "Our game's trailer amassed more than 60,000 views on YouTube, and we had more than 6,000 wishlists," the developer told PC Gamer over email. "Now, our Steam Community page is rapidly filling with player complaints, and we've lost all momentum."

Valve commented on the backlog today in the form of a Steamworks update aimed at helping developers pass the preview process. In it, the company admitted that it's "running a little behind" with wait times that are up to double the usual.

"We aim to test every game build in a timely manner, typically within 3-5 days. However, we're running a little behind right now and taking up to 12 business days," Valve's FAQ reads. "Much of that delay is due to having to re-review games, which isn't great for you or for us."

The update itself is, primarily, a new series of checklists that places the onus on developers to submit better applications that "pass review quickly the first time." The most significant new requirement is to have "run your game through Steam for at least five minutes" to make sure it functions correctly, which you'd think wouldn't need to be said. The tone of Valve's request suggests that it's also surprised by the state of some of the games it's being asked to approve..

"Believe it or not, sometimes we review builds that have not ever been played through Steam," the update reads. "This means that even if a game runs smoothly when a dev launches their executable directly, they might have missed basic steps that would impact a user installing and playing via Steam."

From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews

Other checks include confirming which of those "common redistributables" a game needs before submission, confirming cloud saves and achievements are in order, and adding a minimum of five screenshots to the store page that depict gameplay (another obvious, but apparently necessary standard).

Though Valve did not comment on why a logjam in its processes has developed only recently, despite the number of new Steam games rising rapidly every year, the elephant in the room is AI.

New language models capable of whipping up functioning games very quickly, and Valve's laissez-faire curation, has prompted an explosion of AI slop games on Steam in the past few months—most of which don't receive much visibility, unless you're unlucky enough to browse Steam Next Fest without the "personalized" mode on. A Valve developer recently acknowledged that there's a slop problem on Steam, but said that they don't want to "be gatekeepers telling developers which tools they should or shouldn't use."

If you look at today's update through that lens, perhaps Valve isn't so much speaking to experienced developers with these obvious-sounding guidelines, but vibe coders who lack basic game dev understanding. Also today, Itch.io announced that it deleted "a couple terabytes of AI slop" from its videogame storefront to combat the wave of low-quality games appearing online.

Whatever the cause of the holdup, Valve said more changes are coming to the build review process, but this is a "great starting point."

I'm a hardcore reality TV fan, who regularly watches drama-filled shows like The Real Housewives, Survivor (which is streaming with a Paramount+ subscription) and The Traitors. For some lighter fare (pun intended) I decided to watch the new season of Great British Baking Show with my Netflix subscription, and I've found the series endlessly charming. I'm not one who typically gets hungry watching bakes, but Pastry Week had me drooling.

There's been a ton of discourse about the new season of Bake Off. Some fans are upset about the twists, while others can't get over judge Nigella Lawson's way of eating. Regarding the actual bakes of the show, I think that Pastry Week by far had the most mouthwatering choices. Let me explain.

I like the occasional sweet treat on special occasions, but I'm not necessarily a dessert person. Instead of ordering one after dinner I'd usually opt for another appetizer instead. Even when snacking at home I prefer savory treats like pretzels and popcorn over baked goods. Perhaps this means I'm not the choice demographic to watch Bake Off, but I'm largely watching the competition series for the low-stakes drama and British charm.

Aside from Bread Week (which was chock full of epic fails) most of the bakes this season have been sweet treats. That switched up during Pastry Week, with the remaining bakers making a number of savory treats that I wish I could have reached into the TV and tried. Seriously, why haven't they made the Wonkavision technology from Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory yet?

The Signature Challenge immediately had my stomach growling, so much so that I ordered Chinese Food to my house so I could properly enjoy the latest episode of The Great British Baking Show. Tom's Banh Mi pies looked incredible, as did Moyin's take on a Nigerian meat pie and Connie's jerk chicken pies.

While we went back into dessert land for Nigella's technical, the Showstopper Challenge once again brought savory goodness Bake Off. It was once again Connie, and Tom who created pies that I was dying to try. The latter ended up winning Star Baker for the third time as a result of his work, and it certainly seemed like he deserved it.

I traveled to Ireland and Northern Island last year, and I found myself obsessed with some of the savory baked goods during that time. Seriously, why aren't sausage rolls a thing in the United States? While I ponder this question I might just re-watch the latest episode of Bake Off. Although I won't be doing it on an empty stomach.

New episodes of The Great British Baking Show air Fridays on Netflix as part of the 2026 TV schedule. I assume the remaining episodes will mostly be about sweet treats, but who knows? Maybe the savory lovers like me will be treated to one or more of these bakes. Fingers crossed.

#3705. Parents Convicted After They Withheld Food and Beat Their Adopted Kids

A couple in Michigan have been convicted of abusing their adopted and fostered children by withholding food and beating them.

A Clinton County jury found Tamal Flore guilty of six counts of first-degree child abuse, two counts of second-degree child abuse and three counts of third-degree child abuse, while Jerry Flore was found guilty on one count of second-degree child abuse.

Jerry, 61, was acquitted on seven counts of first-degree abuse, as well as two additional counts of second-degree abuse.

Each first-degree count is punishable by up to life in prison, while Tamal, 59, and Jerry could face up to 10 years in prison for the second-degree child abuse charge.

The Michigan Attorney General announced the couple’s convictions in a Friday, October 30, following a six-week trial at the state’s 29th Circuit Court.

The pair were arrested after authorities learned of their mistreatment of children, whom they adopted or fostered beginning in 2007. During the trial, prosecutors argued that Tamal and Jerry took the children in “for financial gain and subjected the children to abuse under the guise of discipline.”

“Tamal and Jerry Flore subjected their foster and adopted children to prolonged, routine and systemic mental and physical abuse all for personal financial gain,” Attorney General Dana Nessel said. “Children who become wards of the state are some of the most vulnerable and they must be protected. Today’s conviction ensures that no other children will be subjected to the Flores’ abuse again. I want to offer my heartfelt thanks to Clinton County Sheriff Sean Dush and the prosecutors in my office for their years of effort towards justice.”

They were accused of abusing seven out of 16 children that they fostered or adopted, according to The Detroit News. The children spoke to investigators and reportedly claimed they had been whipped by belts, beaten with spoons and locked in rooms or the garage for days at a time.

The children also claimed they were occasionally forced to sit and sleep in an area of the kitchen, which was known as “the square,” for several weeks and the couple had them do “strong sitting” exercises as a form of punishment.

Following the trial, Jerry’s attorney David Carter said he and his client were “deeply grateful” for the jury’s time after he was only charged with the lone second-degree child abuse conviction.

“They sat through weeks of highly charged, emotional allegations and did exactly what the law required: they looked for independent, verified proof,” Carter said in a statement to the Lansing State Journal. “By returning ‘not guilty’ verdicts on nearly every single count in this indictment, the jury completely rejected the state’s overreached narrative and the deeply flawed, unverified investigation that built it.”

Tamal and Jerry were initially arrested in 2021 and charged with multiple counts of child abuse. Prosecutors dismissed the case in 2023, citing the need for additional investigation. The couple was charged again in December 2025.

“This has been a long and in-depth investigation and without the help of the Michigan Attorney General’s Office we would not have been able to bring this case to a successful completion,” Clinton County Sheriff Sean Dush said following the verdict.

Tamal and Jerry will be sentenced during a hearing on January 11.

If you or someone you know is experiencing child abuse, call or text Child Help Hotline at 1-800-422-4453.

#3704. Actor Keith McDermott on Robert Wilson’s Legacy and Ghostwriting His Memoir: “I Saw a Robert Wilson Play and It Changed My Life”

Over the more than 50-year period of his career, Wilson was arguably the most produced American theater director in Europe, if not the world. His aesthetic style has permeated European theater and opera culture to the extent that few directors have remained uninfluenced by what is commonly referred to as the “Wilsonian” use of lighting, set design, and performance style. However, he is not well-known in his own country.

The Robert Wilson productions that have reached the United States are some of the most iconic stage works of the 20th and 21st century: Einstein on the Beach and Lohengrin at the Metropolitan Opera House and at least 10 full productions at Brooklyn Academy of Music. Even in New York, Wilson’s artistic home, and even among artists, a not uncommon response at the mention of his name is “Should I know who that is?”

However, there is another response from New Yorkers of my generation, those of us living here when the city was at the artistic peak of the ’60s and ’70s, when Balanchine oversaw the New York City Ballet, Joe Papp headed the Public Theater, Andy Warhol ran The Factory, and apartments were affordable. That response, my response, is “I saw a Robert Wilson play and it changed my life.”

In 1975, a friend offered me a free ticket to a Broadway play. The title was A Letter for Queen Victoria, and I assumed I was in for a fusty historical drama, but as a young actor pursuing a commercial career, I never passed up an opportunity to see a play, especially if it was free.

Robert Wilson's A Letter for Queen Victoria.

The play began before the houselights went down as a young man and woman in ordinary dress stood in front of the curtain on opposite sides of the stage slowly turning in place. Nothing about their slow, hypnotic movement suggested “performance” until the houselights began to dim. Still turning, they raised their hands from their sides. Their palms, pressed in turmeric, became a blur of orange as their revolutions increased in speed and the curtain rose. The cast included the director’s grandmother as Queen Victoria, and a neurodivergent teenager, Christopher Knowles, whose nonacting presence broke the fourth wall, as he shielded his eyes from the stage lights to gaze into the house.

Audience members left in droves. A woman shouted something about child abuse on her way to the exit. But I sat mesmerized as the play evolved through a series of scenes unconnected by narrative or plot, fantastic in design, exquisitely lit, and often extraordinarily slow. Those of us who stayed until the end leapt to our feet, applauding and cheering for the actors, call after call. I stumbled from the theater into the city night feeling as if I had fallen in love.

My enthusiasm for that play led to both a professional and personal involvement with Bob (as anyone who knows him calls him). As a performer, I have appeared in five Wilson productions in various parts of the world and understudied him in a one‐man show. As a writer, I published an article about his chair collection and a roman à clef in which a character based on Bob pretty much takes over the book. In addition to our working relationship, Bob, a fellow Texan, has been my friend for over 50 years, and early in 2023 he asked me to ghostwrite his memoir.

Our sessions began formally at the Watermill Center, “a laboratory for the arts and humanities” on the South Fork of Long Island, founded by Bob in 1992. He had an apartment there where he stayed when he was in town. Assuming we’d work through his life chronologically, I came armed with questions about his childhood in Waco, Texas, his parents, and his schooling. But later, transcribing our recorded sessions, I cringed at my attempts to get Bob back on topic as he segued into a tale about absentmindedly depositing his airline ticket into a mailbox, then trying to board the plane with the postcards he had meant to mail, or a harrowing memory of six weeks spent in a Greek prison for a bit of hash discovered by airport security. My interruptions only spoiled the spontaneous flow of Bob’s thoughts.

Bob was a storyteller. Everyone who knew and worked with him was familiar with his stories, often told in a regional Texas twang and often more than once – and occasionally with a remarkable addendum. For instance, I knew that in his 20s, while working as a recreational therapist at the Goldwater Memorial Hospital for the terminally ill, Bob had choreographed a “dance” for quadriplegic patients in iron lungs, tying Day-Glo strings to mouth sticks they used to turn book pages that connected to mobiles hung from the ceiling. But in the retelling, I learned that Bob, after attending an Otis Redding concert, had persuaded the singer to come to the ward to accompany his quadriplegic dancers.

Once we gave up the chronological approach and Bob, unburdened by the need to deliver “The Story of My Life,” began to think in terms of “Life Stories,” our process relaxed and stories flowed. In addition to scheduled sessions, I could collect them everywhere, because Bob told them everywhere: at dinner parties, in the car, over the coffee and English muffins I began to deliver early each morning, or on our daily golf cart trips around the Watermill grounds. I always met him armed with my tape recorder.

A story he told frequently, both publicly, in interviews, and privately, was about seeing a policeman about to strike a young boy and intervening. From the sounds the boy made, Bob realized he was deaf. The boy, Raymond Andrews, was diagnosed as ineducable, but Bob realized he simply relied on visual cues not words. At 27 Bob became Raymond’s legal guardian and enrolled him in a school for the deaf. Raymond flourished in the creative community Bob created at his Spring Street loft (in SoHo before it was SoHo). Using Raymond’s drawings and his own observations of the boy, Bob created Deafman Glance, a seven-hour silent opera that signaled his European renown.

Bob told many stories about Jessye Norman, but the one that always brought him and his listeners to tears was of the great singer attempting to get through a Winterreise concert just after 9/11. During the third song, Norman began to cry and had to stop singing. When she regained control, she stood for 10 minutes, motionless, in silence, while the audience wept.

Bob’s vast social network also included socialites and celebrities, and those stories are filled with irresistible gossip: Marlene Dietrich divulged the name of the only contemporary American performer she completely admired (spoiler alert: it was Tina Turner); Diana Vreeland swallowed vials of cod liver oil to act as a buffer for vodka before an evening out; Samuel Beckett claimed that his lead actress in Happy Days was so brilliant because she didn’t understand a word she said.

In June of 2025, Bob went to Lithuania to stage rehearsals of a new production and then to Ljubljana, Slovenia, to direct Tristan and Isolde. When he was away, he sent me emails with story topics for our next session: “Ask me about my boat trip in the Middle East with Helen de Rothschild,” “Ask me about Louis Malle offering me the lead in Pretty Baby.”

When Bob returned to Watermill in July, we were to meet for final interviews, although by that time, I had all the material needed for the book. Shortly before my travels, I received a message that Bob’s health had declined, and he would be unable to see me. He died a week later on July 31 in his Watermill apartment.

Months after Bob’s death, I was still listening to and transcribing our taped conversations. In one conversation, recorded when we were having dinner at an Indian restaurant, Bob was telling me a story about being dressed as Santa Claus and handing out presents in Bali, where he spent every Christmas. Suddenly, he stopped mid-sentence and after a short silence, said, “I love you, Keith.”

I love you too, Bob, you changed my life.

THE SPACE BEHIND THE FACE, a memoir by the visionary theater director and visual artist, Robert Wilson, is published by Penguin Press and arrives on November 3.

#3703. Fan Who Went Viral Wishing To Stay Alive Long Enough To Play GTA 6 Has Passed Away

Jerry Fort, the GTA VI fan who went viral on TikTok for expressing his hope to live long enough to play the game, has passed away. As reported by Dexerto, his family confirmed the sad news, announcing that he passed on October 29th after complications following lung transplant surgery.

Earlier this year, Fort posted a video from his hospital bed titled “I just want to play GTA VI” in which he detailed his situation and prognosis. The video quickly went viral, garnering millions of views and tens of thousands of comments wishing him a speedy recovery and urging Rockstar Games to get in touch to make his wish come true. His family put up a Gofundme to raise money for a lung transplant and it quickly blew through its original $15,000 goal to reach over $100,000.

Fort and occasionally his sister posted regular updates to his account informing his followers of his progress, and it generally seemed like he was improving. In September, Fort went in for lung transplant surgery. After the surgery he developed an infection and after fighting the infection for several weeks, declining to go into hospice care, he finally succumbed.

After his plea to make it to GTA VI went viral, he put out a video thanking people for their support, promising to stream the game when he fully recovered. “That’s gonna be our goal as a community.”

Johnny Depp is an accomplished character actor with a long and wildly successful career. Arguably one of Depp's best roles is as Captain Jack Sparrow in the Pirates of the Caribbean movies, which are streaming in their entirety with a Disney+ subscription. I didn't expect the 63 year-old to have jokes when talking about possibly returning to the franchise alongside Orlando Bloom's Will Turner.

While Depp will return to theaters in Ebenezer this month, some moviegoers are hoping to see him return in a future Pirates of the Caribbean movie. During a recent interview with People, the Edward Scissorhands actor was asked about possibly returning to the beloved franchise, and responded with:

Well, I think we should have a contest of who can grow the fastest non-beard. Because neither of us can grow a beard, I don’t think. I can’t, for sure, but maybe he can. I don’t know.

Shots fired. Despite having facial hair in the Pirates of the Caribbean films, it turns out that neither Johnny Depp nor Orlando Bloom can actually grow a beard. While sidestepping whether or not he'd be down to return as Jack Sparrow, the Sweeney Todd actor was sure to poke fun at both himself, and his famous co-star.

Ebenezer marks Depp's first real return to a big Hollywood movie since the verdict of his defamation trial with Amber Heard was revealed. He spent a few years living abroad and getting out of the spotlight, but he's back playing the title role of Ti West's forthcoming holiday movie. Only time will tell if the upcoming book to screen adaptation ends up being considered one of the best Christmas movies of all time, but it seems like a game changer for the actor.

There's been chatter about more Pirates movies for a few years. At one point multiple movies were in development, including one that would star Margot Robbie. Unfortunately, there hasn't been any concrete updates about one of these projects moving forward in the development process. Although with Johnny Depp returning to the big screen, I have to assume that the chatter surrounding the franchise, and his possible return as Captain Jack Sparrow, will get louder.

Depp starred as the protagonist in all five of the Pirates of the Caribbean movies, which ran in theaters from 2003 to 2017. The same can't be said for Orlando Bloom, who was absent for On Stranger Tides. He ended up returning in Dead Men Tell No Tales, which is the most recent installment in the action/adventure property.

All five of the Pirates of the Caribbean movies are streaming now on Disney+. Only time will tell if a sixth movie ends up being green lit by the powers that be at Disney, but there does seem to be a ton of chatter about that possibility online.

"See that mountain? You can overanalyze it."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When the Greybeards invite you to High Hrothgar in Skyrim, you have to climb a mountain to reach them. There's a messenger called Klimmek waiting in the village of Ivarstead at the bottom to warn you what an arduous journey this is going to be. To get to the top of the Throat of the World, he says, you have to work your way up The 7,000 Steps.

It's well-documented that there aren't actually 7,000 steps carved into the side of the mountain. Some of them are buried under the snow, making an exact count impossible, but the actual number is closer to 700. And even if you argue that The 7,000 Steps refers to the number of footsteps it takes to ascend the mountain, according to the dedicated researchers at the Ultimate Elder Scrolls Portal it only takes "approximately 2,400 footsteps" to get there.

As part of Bethesda's 40th anniversary, which included the reveal of The Elder Scrolls 6's subtitle, the studio reminisced about their previous work, which is how we know they really did try to get 7,000 steps into the side of the mountain.

While not responsible for the rough layout of Skyrim's terrain, I was responsible for refining the shapes of High Hrothgar. I would look at the mountain from various viewpoints and tried to keep the shape interesting. My work on the "Throat of the World" was not limited to sculpting the mountain, but also included cluttering and dressing the mountain with visual effects, plants, and objects. This of course, included the infamous 7,000 steps. Now, I love trying to be as faithful to lore or real-life as possible and I did my darndest to find a way to fit all 7,000 steps into the storied path. However, my best attempt to do so included extending far past Ivartstead, wrapping around the mountain and ending near Whiterun in the frozen tundra. It turns out, 7,000 is quite a lot! By the way, my work did NOT include enemy encounters, so I take no responsibility for the Frost Troll that was the woe of many players.

Of course, like most open world games, Skyrim isn't designed to scale—otherwise the capital city of Solitude would have a population of less than 100 people. But in the same way that for every named NPC we should assume there are a bunch of people off-camera, distances are compressed so that it doesn't take a week to get anywhere. For every step we watched the Dragonborn climb there are another nine implied steps we don't see, and even more frost trolls.
