#3689. Xbox Game Pass Is Losing 14 Games In November

It's the start of a new month, which means new additions and departures on Xbox Game Pass. To kick off November, 14 games are being removed from the Game Pass library soon, including several simulators, one longrunning Dragon Ball game, and one of the greatest James Bond adventures of all time--at least until that upstart 007 First Light popped up earlier this year.

Simulator fans can say goodbye to Football Manager 26, Firefighting Simulator, Pigeon Simulator, and Police Simulator this month. Believe it or not, those games all come from different developers, as it feels like there's a simulator for every category and hobby out there. Another noteworthy departure is Dragon Ball Xenoverse 2, the action-RPG that was recently upgraded for current-gen consoles. The game has been around for several years and has grown with updates that add new characters and adventures, but with Dragon Ball Xenoverse 3 launching in the second half of 2027, it might be time to wave goodbye to the Time Patrol.

Also on the way are the first Moonlighter, the adorably cozy Winter Burrow, and Barbie Horse Trails. As a reminder, you can save 20% on these games if you decide to buy them before they leave Game Pass.

Leaving Xbox Game Pass on November 15

  • Football Manager 26
  • Barbie Horse Trails
  • Great God Grove
  • GoldenEye 007
  • Firefighting Simulator: The Squad
  • Winter Burrow
  • Wreckfest
  • 1000xResist
  • Pigeon Simulator
  • Police Simulator: Patrol Officers
  • Relic Hunter Legends
  • Moonlighter
  • Total Chaos
  • Dragon Ball Xenoverse 2

This wave of games leaving Game Pass will be followed by a second batch of exits on November 30. Last month saw quite a few titles rotated out of Game Pass, including Expedition 33: Clair Obscur, The Casting of Frank Stone, A Plague Tale: Requiem, Donut County, and several Double Fine classics. At least some new games are filling that void, as Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade, Plants vs. Zombies: Replanted, and The Séance of Blake Manor were all added at the end of October.

It gets to a point where I need to say something.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Warning! The following contains spoilers for the Dexter: Resurrection episode "Risky Business." Stream the episode with a Paramount+ subscription, and read at your own risk!

Dexter Morgan is back on the prowl in the Season 2 premiere of Dexter: Resurrection, and I saw my favorite character again from last season! Eric Stonestreet returned once again as the Rapunzel Killer, but unfortunately, the return was short-lived.

Al Walker was tracked down by Dexter while on vacation with his family, as he was "working" while traveling to parks with his wife and kids. Dex was able to "do what he does," as Harrison puts it, and now no pony-tailed women have to worry about Rapunzel anymore. As satisfying as it was, I'm upset that Dexter: Resurrection is once again killing off fun guest stars.

Last season, Dexter: Resurrection gave us a great plot twist with the Serial Killers Club, which was quickly decimated by the Bay Harbor Butcher. There was a stacked cast of great guest stars, but by the end of the season, they were all dead except for Eric Stonestreet's character.

I had high hopes he'd be a big bad in Season 2, but that hope was squashed pretty quickly. I kind of guessed that would be the case given how many new guest stars were a part of this season, but it's disappointing the show didn't hold off and do a season dedicated to Rapunzel where Dex was on the road.

Dexter: Resurrection has two major guest stars this season, with Dan Stevens playing the Five Boroughs Killer and Brian Cox playing the New York Ripper. Both are big names tied to the Season 2 plot, and with Dexter being so concerned about legacy, it feels as though he's going to try to take out both of them.

I Have A Theory About Dexter: Resurrection And His Downfall. Why I Think Season 2 Could Address It

That's kind of the point of Dexter, to be fair. He's a serial killer who hunts other killers, so I can't sit here and act like Resurrection is going against what this series is about. I just feel as though he's felt very untouchable thus far, and maybe that these serial killers aren't as crafty as the ones from the original series?

I guess I fear that Dexter is becoming an Avengers-level type of anti-hero, and it feels like we haven't seen him face any real adversity. I know that's funny to say with him having been shot by his own son, but he and Harrison were able to put that aside really quickly. I'm just hoping we see Dex face a little more adversity in these upcoming episodes on the 2026 TV schedule, because I fear he's untouchable.

Catch new episodes of Dexter: Resurrection on Paramount+ on Fridays. I'm eager to see how the rest of this season plays out, and if Dexter and Harrison end the season in some trouble with the law.

#3687. Dave Bautista Is Looking More Like Kratos After Packing On 20 Pounds Of Muscle

With filming set to resume soon on Prime Video's God of War series, 55-year-old actor Dave Bautista revealed in an Instagram Story that he's packed on a beefy 20 pounds of muscle for the role of Kratos, bringing his weight to 250 pounds. While it's not the first time Bautista has bulked up for a role, he'd noticeably slimmed down in recent months, and he'd previously said he needed two months to get ready to play Kratos on TV.

While 250 pounds is an impressive weight, it's not the heaviest that Bautista has been during his career. At the peak of his WWE run, when he performed under the ring name Batista, the actor said he started at 325 pounds (as Deacon Batista) and once weighed 370 pounds. Over the years, Bautista usually hovered at around 290 pounds during his WWE runs, which is still massive. For 2023's Knock at the Cabin, Bautista increased his mass to 315 pounds to play the sinister character of Leonard, then began to slim down.

Bautista is stepping in to replace the original Kratos actor, Ryan Hurst, who also became absolutely shredded for the role. Sadly, a devastating bicep tear injury forced him to vacate the role, as he'd have needed months of downtime and rehabilitation to resume filming. Not wanting to wait that long, Amazon quickly began scouting for a replacement and chose Bautista for the series, of which two seasons have been ordered.

Based on the game series' soft reboot that began in 2018, God of War will follow Kratos and his son Atreus (Callum Vinson) as they journey across the nine realms. More games in the series are also on the way, starting with God of War Laufey on February 18, 2027, and a new Kratos-led adventure.

#3686. 31 Moments That Made The Dragon Age Series Unforgettable

BioWare’s closure last month has put a lot of focus on the Mass Effect series, as the shutdown also coincided with the cancelation of the fifth game in the studio’s sci-fi series. But the company’s fantasy series,Â Dragon Age, also deserves some eulogizing. All fourÂ Dragon Age games are vastly different, spanning different RPG frameworks, fantasy subgenres, and corners of the world of Thedas. Though BioWare left some dangling threads at the end ofÂ Dragon Age: The Veilguard, it also seemed like the studio was focusing on narrative closure, just in case this was the last time anyone in the studio would get to go back to the universe it had created over four games and 15 years. With BioWare gone, let’s look back at some of the best moments from all four games.

Dragon Age: Origins begins with one of six playable opening chapters, the one you play based on the race and class of character you choose, providing a unique background for your character before they head out into the main story.

The Hero of Ferelden can be part of human nobility facing a tragic series of losses, a castless dwarf struggling to make it in the city of Orzamar, or a mage evicted from the magic school theyâve known their entire life, and those starkly different origin points are only half of the options. These origins define how your hero will be viewed in the dozens of hours that follow, and also function as a starting point for how a new player will view the franchise. I started as a Mage when I first played Dragon Age: Origins in 2009, and have always felt like a veteran of the Circle at heart. Future Dragon Age games would implement this concept of different player backgrounds with Inquisition and The Veilguard, but none would do it as thoroughlyâOrigins was the only time I got to see that history play out in real-time.

No character in Origins is as impactful as Morrigan, the enigmatic Witch of the Wilds. The apostate carries a sense of superiority toward the rest of the party, as well as the trials and tribulations of Thedas. When you meet her in the early hours of Origins, you still donât know much about the world, but her commanding presence elevated by Claudia Blackâs excellent voice performance tells you that she is unlike anyone or anything youâve met so far. Morrigan is one of the few characters in Dragon Age who watches nearly every important moment in Thedasâ history unfold, so seeing her here, both enigmatic but still so young and naive, is chilling to look back on.

After youâve picked your background and lived out whatever trauma is associated with it, Dragon Age: Origins puts you at the center of a battle with a darkspawn horde. Your job is to signal for reinforcements to help defeat an army of bloodthirsty monsters, but before the battle starts, the vibes seem off. The golden retriever King Cailain is jazzed about the incoming battle, though his father-in-law Loghain Mac Tir seems less enthusiastic. The tension between the two is tangible, but who are you to get involved in royal family affairs? However, when you signal for reinforcements, Loghain instead commands his forces to retreat, leaving everyone, including you and his own son-in-law, for dead at the hands of the Blight. Most of the preceding origin stories are full of some kind of betrayal. You might think you would get some respite from it at some point, but Origins doubles down, reminding you that you know nothing of this world and the lengths people will go to get what they want.

Origins is not an entirely grimdark fantasy dramaâsome of the best character interactions come from your party members hanging out with your dog companion. Though Mabari dogs are trained to be vicious combatants, your canine companion is a sweetheart. Many interactions between the party and dog give him a hard time for being a mangy mutt, only for him to be revealed as a sensitive soul who just wants to play. Examine your preconceived notions, Origins crew. The sharp fangs mask that the Mabari is actually a good boy.

There are several points in the Dragon Age series in which a party member can turn on you, but none have ever been quite as shocking as when the religious bard Leliana, and otherwise kind-hearted Wynne, turn on you if you taint the Urn of Sacred Ashes. This is a crime against one of the most prominent doctrines in all of Thedas, and bringing two of the most devout members of the party to watch is bound to cause drama, but Origins takes it a step further by having both of your teammates take up arms against you.

It doesnât matter how far youâve progressed through their personal stories, or even if youâre involved in a romance with Leliana; faith trumps all other emotions here, and you will have to strike down your allies. Youâll face plenty more betrayals during the Dragon Age series, but Leliana and Wynneâs heel turn is still one of the most sudden and violent.

Much like killing Leliana, Origins has a few choices whose ramifications were so earth-shattering that BioWare later had to write themselves out of the box theyâd created so they could re-use characters that could be dead. One of those was the option to kill Flemeth, Morriganâs even more enigmatic mother who allegedly wanted to steal her daughterâs body as a vessel to live longer, though the reality is a bit more nuanced than that. When Morrigan finds out about this plan, she begs you to slay the old woman in her hut in the woods. You can choose to do so or strike a deal with her to spare her in exchange for her grimoire of old spells, but choosing to slay her means fighting her in a powerful dragon form. Itâs a tough fight, but doing so leaves you not with a rewarding cutscene and major story revelation, but instead an unsettling and anticlimactic quiet. Youâre left with more mysteries than you had when you arrived, and the unshakable feeling that you might have killed something far beyond your understanding. Flemethâs place in the Dragon Age universe was too significant to be silenced by something as trivial as death, but for a moment, you feel like you have driven a stake through the heart of something you cannot comprehend.

Dragon Age: Originsâ big moment where all your choices culminate is The Landsmeet, a political meeting where you can finally unmask Loghain for all his crimes and essentially set up the country of Fereldenâs future. Your relationships and understandings formed over the past 50+ hours of video game are put to the test, and things can change drastically depending on how the battles of wits and blades pan out. To this day, The Landsmeet is one of BioWareâs most effective showcases of its ability to sew hours of choices into a final consequence. In just one quest you solidify the future for Ferelden in a way that sends most players down the same path, but colors that result so differently that many players, especially those who donât know every secret the game has to offer, will see something that diverges significantly from what the next player might see.

One of the last major choices youâll make in Dragon Age: Origins comes back to Morrigan. The witch has had more than enough reasons to leave the party considering she doesnât really get along with anyone on the team, but she sticks around long enough to give you a final choice: ending the Blight will cost you your lifeâunless you or Alistair undergoes a blood magic ritual that will transfer the Archdemonâs soul into an unborn child. It sounds like a get-out-of-jail-free card, all you have to do is lay with her for one night or convince Alistair to do it. But Morrigan is cagey with her intentions and says that whether you agree or not, she will leave the party after the final battle. This is why sheâs been here this whole time, but does that mean any connection youâve formed with her was all an act? What will become of this child? Is it going to be like any other child or will it be some darkspawn demon that could bring about just as much pain in the world as the archdemon would? Morrigan gives you nothing to go on, but makes her terms clear. Dragon Age: Origins would go on to have three sequels that would wipe away the ambiguity of this decision, but at the time, all you had to go on here was your trust of Morrigan, or lack thereof. Everything youâve ever been told about blood magic and interrupting the natural order of the Blight should tell you to say âno,â but are you willing to risk it to save your own life? Itâs a fascinating choice. Did Dragon Age do right by it? Your mileage may vary.

With Dragon Age II, BioWare started earnestly looking for a way to franchise the series. It had built itself a new cage as the âchoice and consequenceâ studio thanks to the Mass Effect series, and Dragon Age followed suit by importing your Origins save to pepper in cameos and references to your past deeds. That includes whether or not you killed Flemeth, but since BioWare still wanted to use the mysterious witch either way, it had new hero Hawke unwittingly carry her to safety through an enchanted amulet even as she fought for her life against the Hero of Ferelden. Reviving Flemeth is one of the most effective moments in all of Dragon Age in showing how playing as different protagonists in each game could create satisfying meta moments. As she rises from the ashes, you watch the impact of one of your heroâs actions be undermined by the one youâre playing as now. Dragon Age takes place over decades, and a big part of its appeal is watching different stories youâve helped write weave in and out of one another. Itâs a course correction, but one that is still bone-chilling to watch unfold.

The second Dragon Age differs from the first in several ways, from taking place almost entirely in one city to swapping the tactical RPG battle system for more action-oriented combat. But one of the most notable and interesting changes it made was to the approval system, which integrated a Friendship and Rivalry mechanic so you didnât have to kiss a party memberâs ass to progress their relationship storyline. The difference between Friendship and Rivalry is all about how you challenge their preconceived notions. Each party member has a pretty defined view of the world; the radical mage Anders, for instance, is all about freeing magic users from the Circle at any cost, while the elven slave Fenris has an aversion to magic. Uncritically enabling them will give you Friendship points, and going against the grain will net you Rivalry points. This changes the tone of your relationships significantly, and even someone youâre in a romantic relationship with may greet you with a thorny disposition. Watching those connections gradually change is one of the most compelling parts of Dragon Age IIâs writing. Romancing Fenris as a mage while being rivals was one of the most interesting, angsty relationships Iâve ever experienced in a BioWare game. Itâs a shame the studio didnât keep the system around.

Dragon Age II is all about years of civil unrest bubbling to the surface of one city, and between the conflict with the stranded Qunari and the Mage/Templar War, the former is certainly handled with more care than the latter. While early Dragon Age games had multiple crisis points in which party members can leave the party or betray you, one of the most memorable is when one party member makes a decision not to leave, but to return. Isabela is the cause of the Qunariâs extended stay in Kirkwall, and when sheâs given the chance to run off with a tome they have been searching for, she takes it. If youâve not established a solid enough friendship or rivalry with her, she will never return. If you have, she makes a big heroâs entrance just as the Qunari are about to strike down what remains of the city. She attempts to make amends, showing the growth sheâs been trying her damnedest to avoid since arriving in the city. But then the Qunari leader says she still must answer for her crimes. You can give her up and betray her, or you can fight for her instead, and seeing her be big enough to not sell you and the rest of Kirkwall out for once in her life is one of Dragon Age IIâs most memorable companion moments.

Choosing to fight for Isabelaâs freedom results in a somewhat silly but exceptionally satisfying fight. Dragon Age IIâs action-based combat isnât quite as snappy and tight as The Veilguardâs, but it has some spectacle that can keep it interesting in fights that donât just pit you against waves of enemies being thrown at you. The Arishok fight can go a few ways depending on if he respects Hawke or not, but fighting the giant Qunari in a one-on-one duel is still one of the best combat sequences in the game. You may be in for a tough time if you havenât specâd into a class and build that can handle a solo fight, but in any case, taking down the Arishok and being crowned the Champion of Kirkwall is one of the defining moments of Dragon Age II

One bright spot in Dragon Age IIâs extremely uneven final act is the conclusion to Merrillâs story. The elven blood mage has gone against the wishes of everyone around her in a tunnel-visioned need to bring back a part of her clanâs history, even seeking out the help of a demon. Dragon Age II takes place across a decade, with Merrill at odds with her clan leader Marethari all the while, and yet the leader sacrifices herself to âsaveâ Merrill by allowing the demon she had been working with to possess her instead. Merrill can insist this was meddling and you can be supportive of her or not, but the real people she has to answer to are the clanâs remaining members. Depending on whether you advocate for her or throw her under the bus, you may have to fight the entire clan on your way out. Itâs a brutal mess thatâs tied to the character with perhaps the most emotional range of any party member in the franchise. Itâs such a terrifying, saddening web of contradicting feelings and subverted expectations, all leading to a stunning payoff.

I have a lot of issues with the handling of the Mage/Templar War in Dragon Age II. It creates this complicated political and religious conflict around an oppressed group of people and a tyrannical religious organization but insists that both sides are equally bad, actually. Donât even get me started on how you can convince Anders, the radical mage who is the face of this conflict, to kill the mages he tried to save. But the moment in which Anders, worn down by a lifetime of captivity and oppression, blows up the Kirkwall Chantry is one of the few unambiguous statements the game makes in its final hours. The scene itself is dramatic and shocking and kickstarts a war that would (in theory) shake the foundations of Thedas. It requires everyone in your party to make a stand. There will be no more fence-sitting in this fight, and all your relationships will be tested as your team decides whether or not to follow you into battle. Sadly, the reveals that follow undermine any choice you make, but as a spark that ignites a flame, Andersâ act of terrorism is a statement in a game that otherwise seems unwilling to make one.

A lot of the highlights weâve talked about are big story moments or reactions to your decisions, but one of the coolest things Inquisition does happens literally the moment the game starts. The main menu shows rows of mages and templars marching toward a building off in the distance. Despite where we left them in Dragon Age II, these two opposing sides donât seem to be fighting, so perhaps theyâre making their way to peace talks? Could the future of Dragon Age be written not in blood, but in signed treaties? Letâs press ânew gameâ and find o-

I have heard some fans say the moment in which members of the Inquisition start singing âThe Dawn Will Come,â a hymn of the Chantry, to your main character in a moment of religious fervor is cheesy and cringe, to which I say, fuck you, itâs one of the most incredible moments in the game. Inquisitionâs themes can be radically different depending on how you play the Herald of Andraste. This hero has been unwillingly made a religious figure, with hundreds of people expecting you to live as a symbol for a god you might not even believe in. If you take this approach, playing as a non-believer who actively shouts down the claims of the faithful, âThe Dawn Will Comeâ can be an unnerving, haunting reminder of how much unwavering belief can compel groups of people even as you insist on a different, provable truth. If, on the other hand, youâre undecided or playing as a believer, it can read like a beautiful moment of hope and community. Inquisition allows you to define so many shades of who your character is and see them reflected in a world that struggles with your very existence. And sometimes, no matter how hard you kick and scream, you cannot stop the world from believing what it does. Instead, you can just awkwardly stand there while people sing to you and then complain about it later.

With each subsequent game, Dragon Age has gotten better at illustrating the closeness (or lack thereof) of your companions. Banter in the overworld is good, but seeing the crew actually get together is better. The Wicked Grace scene, in which the party gets together to play a card game, is one of BioWareâs best scenes that make use of a gameâs entire core ensemble. Everyoneâs personality gets a chance to shine, whether theyâre playful, stuffy, horny, or just trying to wrangle all these weirdos together. Itâs delightful, succinct, and has stayed in the hearts of many Dragon Age fans.

The Dragon Age series has always been explicitly queer. For all the diaper-shitting about The Veilguardâs queer themes, Inquisition was examining the life and times of a Thedas gay long before Taash learned the term ânon-binary.â Dorian Pavusâ personal quest remains one of the most memorable in all of BioWareâs canon. It drops combat for one incredibly well-acted cutscene between the Tevinter mage and his estranged father, where itâs revealed that, to continue their bloodline and climb his way up the Tevinter political ladder, Dorianâs father planned to use a blood magic equivalent to conversion therapy in order to force his son into an arranged marriage. Iâve spoken to many Dragon Age fans over the years about what decision they made here, as youâre able to help the two reconcile, or to get Dorian out of there. Iâve never once considered telling Dorian to hear his father out. Itâs one of the best examples Iâve seen of a game adapting the queer struggle to a fictional culture. Dorian becomes a radical because he has seen how low even those he loves will go to maintain power in Tevinter, and it all ties into his identity as a gay man. Itâs a stunning scene that tells you so much about Dorian and where he came from, and lets you gently nudge history as you stand beside him.

Blackwall goes under the radar for a lot of players. Heâs quiet, keeps to himself, and is even in a pretty out-of-the-way spot in your base in Skyhold. A lot of people think the Grey Warden warrior is boring, but theyâre wrong; the big reveals you experience in his companion missions are outstanding. Blackwall tells you heâs a Warden but is secretive about the organization which, if you played Origins, may nudge you to think back to your own experience playing as one. You know why theyâre all tight-lipped on the inner machinations of the faction, so you donât question it. But it turns out, heâs actually not a Warden at all, and is instead an imposter on the run for war crimes he committed years ago. Eventually, the guilt eats at him and he turns himself in to save others from answering for his orders with a hangmanâs noose. This man duped you for dozens of hours, and youâre left with the power to decide his fate. Blackwallâs quest can go one of several ways, whether you leave him to rot, pardon him, or send him to the Wardens to let them decide what happens to an imposter. Whatever you choose, Blackwallâs quest leaves an impression as one of BioWareâs most surprising and subversive. Yâall need to quit calling characters you donât even talk to boring. This shit rips.

Even as someone who likes Mass Effect more than Dragon Age, I have a hard time thinking of a singular quest in the sci-fi series that matches up to Inquisitionâs Wicked Eyes and Wicked Hearts. While you will unsheathe your weapons a few times, this mission is all about politics, charming the worst people youâve ever met, and working the crowd. Running around the Winter Palace, meeting the most powerful players in Orlais, and manipulating the politics of an entire country to your whims is more intriguing than anything you do with a sword or staff. Mechanically, the mission is surprisingly elegant as it codifies social status and attention into something that can be measured by a video game, and itâs intriguing learning more about the figureheads you can rally to your cause. There are several outcomes at the end of this mission, and getting what you want might come down to blackmail, reuniting long-lost lovers, or a betrayal of your own. Itâs unlike anything else in the Dragon Age series, and I havenât seen many studios pull off something like it since.

At one point, it seemed as if Flemeth might be the throughline connecting all of Dragon Age. For two games, she was presented as a manipulator, lurking in the shadows and moving the pieces of Thedasâ chess board to her liking. Then all her machinations finally came to a head in Inquisition when she, Morrigan, and perhaps the child the player helped conceive two games prior, all gather in the Fade. Flemeth seemingly has control of the situation, appearing to hold her grandson Kieran hostage and using him as leverage against her daughter who has been on the run since Origins. But as anger gives way to truth-telling and the moment softens, the two find not total reconciliation, but at least an understanding that neither is in danger from the other. It is a series-best performance from Black and Flemeth actor Kate Mulgrew, bringing together three games of choices and history into one incredible confrontation. Iâm still unsure how I feel about the final echoes of this moment in The Veilguard, but Flemeth and her family reuniting and acknowledging the struggle of love and fear for one another that theyâre caught in remains one of the most memorable interactions in all of Dragon Age

I could just throw the entirety of the Trespasser DLC in here and it would be in the running for best âmomentsâ in the series. The final expansion BioWare released for Inquisition in 2015 isnât just an epilogue for the RPG, but is pretty much the true ending. You say goodbye to all the companions with some silly, heartfelt scenes, engage in some politics, and fight some really memorable battles, but the meat of the DLC is in its final 10 minutes. Solas, the elven apostate who abandons your team at the very end, reveals that he is the Dread Wolf, the trickster god who led a rebellion against the rest of the elven pantheon. He plans to tear down the barrier between the real and spirit worlds, which he believes will revitalize the old world of the elves, granting them immortality once more and destroying everyone else in the process. But youâre given two choices that (before The Veilguard, at least) felt incredibly meaningful as a final word for the Inquisitor: Do you think Solas is beyond saving? And is your organization in a state to fight him? Ultimately, neither of those choices mattered in The Veilguard, despite them being imported into the game at the beginning. But back in 2015 it felt like a victory lap, a final declaration by a character you probably wouldnât get to play again.

BioWare has always been held up as a studio that spearheads inclusive design, but The Veilguard takes this one step further by letting you explicitly determine that your protagonist Rook is trans. This isnât just a cosmetic choice like giving them top surgery scars or picking a voice; it can be part of your characterâs backstory that you talk about from time to time with other characters. Few games have been this thorough about letting you define your characterâs identity, and The Veilguard approaches it with a great deal of care.

The Veilguard continues the trend, started with Mass Effect: Andromeda, of BioWare hiding some of a gameâs biggest lore reveals behind an optional collectathon, but this time they are so far-reaching and important that I canât believe some players may never see them. Collecting wolf statues throughout The Veilguard reveals Solasâ regrets. These are murals depicting memories from the elven godâs long life, and essentially write the creation myth of the Dragon Age universe. When I first played The Veilguard, I did these quests pretty late and they started to turn me around on the game entirely. I had mostly considered The Veilguard less a meal than a series of really good sides, but this was when I as a long-time fan felt like I was really eating. Each reveal was juicier and more surprising than the last, bringing connective tissue to a universe that had often felt disparate and disconnected. God, I canât believe theyâre optional.

A lot of The Veilguardâs choices are binary, but most of them are still pretty compelling. The first world-altering choice comes when you must decide which of two cities to save from incoming dragon attacks: Minrathous or Treviso. Thereâs a lot of emotion tied up in this choice, as well as tactical considerations to make. Your Rook might be from Minrathous, but pursuing a relationship with Treviso native Lucanis. You may be trying to develop partnerships with the radical Tevinter group the Shadow Dragons and feel like you should help them defend their city to not burn bridges. Whatever your reasoning and whatever the consequences, you have to choose right then and there. Your teammates are looking to you for an answer, and you realize that a mere few hours of gameplay ago you were just a contractor helping Varric track down Solas. Rookâs arc is all about them confronting the leadership role that has been thrust on them by circumstance and Varricâs expectations. This is the moment it becomes clear that they might not be cut out for the decisions they have to make, but theyâll have to learn to live with those choices one way or another.

The Mourn Watch necromancer Emmrich is The Veilguardâs best marriage of character and faction culture. He is fascinated by death because he has an all-consuming fear of the end. Emmrichâs goal is to become a Lich, an immortal keeper of the dead, willing to watch life begin and end forevermore. But as his personal quests unfold, his assistant Manfred, a reanimated skeleton, is killed in a battle with a rival Lich. Using his powers, he could bring Manfred back, but doing so would disqualify him from achieving the immortality he desires, as it would show an inability to accept death. How can you be immortal and watch everything live and die in an endless cycle if one death of a loved one compels you to defy the natural order? Iâve heard people make cases for allowing Emmrich to become a Lich, but I chose to advise him to bring Manfred back and leave Lichdom behind. The Lich order may believe his inability to leave Manfred behind as a weakness, but I saw it as an asset. Itâs proof that he loves too strongly to spend an eternity watching everyone he cares about disappear over and over again. Still, I see the argument for the other side. No other choice in The Veilguard so succinctly nails the companion-first format BioWare wanted while saying so much about the world in the process.

The Grey Warden headquarters of Weisshaupt has been referenced since the very beginning of Dragon Age, and after all those years hyping it up, our first experience of it is one hell of a followthrough. The Veilguardâs mission at the fortress is an action-packed and narratively rewarding setpiece packed with reveals about the state of the Grey Wardens and demonstrating just how much of a threat the remaining elven gods pose. Meanwhile, the drama it stirs between your team of usually harmonious heroes is a peak moment for the whole series, and holy shit, that boss fight at the end might be the most challenging BioWareâs ever created.

After you see all of Solasâ regrets, you meet a visitor in the Lighthouse: Morrigan. She gives you one last big lore dump, finally putting a bittersweet bow on the tragic story between her and her mother. She also reveals to you that the figure that has been looming over their hit-and-run relationship is Mythal, the elven god of love who once led the pantheon. Mythal is long dead, but her memories have transferred from host to host in the millennia since. Morrigan is the keeper of her memories now, and believes that if even a fraction of the old god were able to release Solas from all his regret, it might be enough to take him off this violent path. Morriganâs epilogue is introspective and melancholy, but as she directs you to one of the last pieces of Mythalâs soul trapped in the fade, all that family drama is given some meaning. The conversation in which you try to convince Mythal to help you is one of the best in The Veilguard. It branches into multiple topics, giving you several footholds to perhaps convince her that your cause is just. Who your Rook is can play into how effective you are in making your case, and if you canât persuade her, you can always fight her for her favor. Whatever route you choose, this is one of those moments in which you can feel Dragon Age history changing with every dialogue option you pick.

Dragon Age: The Veilguardâs final missions are a kind of greatest hits of BioWareâs best tricks. Itâs got everything: unavoidable sacrifice, avoidable losses determined by whether or not you know your team well enough to assign them tasks befitting their talents, and a culmination of all the strategic relationships youâve built with different factions. It might not be as interactive as Mass Effect 2âs Suicide Mission, but as a series of interlocking decisions bringing you to a myriad of mini conclusions, it far exceeds anything the studio has done in the past 20 years. I was nervous and shaking making those choices, and itâs all portrayed with a level of cinematic finesse that goes beyond anything BioWareâs done before.

When The Veilguard reaches its climax, it becomes clear that all the while, youâve been caught in a battle of ideals between Varricâs hope and Solasâ cynicism. Rook has been a pawn (no pun intended) for Solas. The elf has been manipulating them the entire time in hopes of trapping them in the Fade and resuming his plan. Heâs done this by projecting a vision of Varric who hypes Rook up until they can be cut off at the knees, falling into a state of regret so consuming it traps them within the spirit realm. Here, theyâre guided by Varric through the prison until they discover the truth: Varric died at the beginning of the game, and Solas used his image to nudge Rook along the entire game.

The reveal is incredible because you realize BioWare pulled off a Sixth Sense. No one else speaks to Varric the entire game, but heâs placed naturally enough in each scene that you donât really question that no one else responds to him. You realize that youâve been fooled by Solas just as much as Rook has, and when they mourn their mentorâs loss, theyâre effectively a stand-in for you, the Dragon Age fan. But as despondent as they might be, they still have a job to do, and Varric reminds them that theyâve done everything up to this point by themself. They donât need Varricâs guidance. They already have everything they need.

As frustrated as I was with The Veilguardâs decision to leave the Inquisitor behind for a new protagonist, this twist was what made Rook work for me. The whole game essentially emerges from Varric betting on someone to finish the job he couldnât. His belief in Rook is what keeps the game going, even as Solas tries to manipulate it to his own advantage. It may have been sad to watch Varric go from a city dwarf just trying to make it to a victim of Solasâ pride, but his belief in others lives on.

After four games, pretty much everything Dragon Age has ever been leads to one final conversation with Solas. The Veil is coming down, the rest of Thedas will be burned to ash in the aftermath, and the only way to stop it is for the trickster god himself to bind himself to it. No matter what you do, Solas will end up using his immortal life force to keep Thedas and the Fade separate. But the tenor of your decision still matters. You can knock him senseless and forcibly cast the blood magic spell to hold him there, you can trick him so his magic backfires and leave him helpless as you bind him to the Veil, or you can take the third option. Bringing Mythalâs essence out allows her to release him from her service, letting him lay down a lifetime of regret. Itâs the culmination of learning all the secrets left in this world, and once you have all that understanding, it feels like the most appropriate way to cap off a cliffhanger whose resolution weâve been awaiting for ten years.

Given everything thatâs happened to BioWare in the years following The Veilguardâs launch, what sticks out to me most is how much the game leans into finality. Closure is a key pillar of its storytelling, even if there are hints of a sequel we’ll never get. And if this is the note we had to leave it off on, I’m not upset. I hope the folks who were at BioWare at any point during the seriesâ development aren’t either.

#3685. Darializa Avila Chevalier Explains the DSA

In June, Darializa Avila Chevalier, the Democratic nominee for Congress in the 13th District of New York, burst onto the national stage when she won her primary against five-term incumbent Representative Adriano Espaillat. Along with several other candidates this cycle, Chevalier became emblematic of a new swell of progressivism in America. Almost immediately, she came under fire for inflammatory posts she had made on the internet—about defunding the police, abolishing prisons, and Israel’s actions in Gaza and the West Bank. She has what many would characterize as some pretty radical views.

Chevalier comes from the world of academia—she’s a PhD candidate, a longtime grassroots organizer, and a member of the New York chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America. But we don’t live in a theoretical world, and it seems to me that ideological purism often gets in the way of getting real things done. So, ahead of next week’s midterms, I wanted to know whether she stands by some of her most divisive statements and how she plans to govern once the race is over and she (presumably) takes office. And I really wanted to know who Chevalier is as a person. I sat down with her on October 26 for a conversation about how she views protests, being recruited to run for office, being compared to AOC, why President Donald Trump likes Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and more.

Mark Guiducci: Candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier, welcome to the show.

Darializa Avila Chevalier: Thanks so much for having me.

Thanks for being here. Darializa, you are the Democratic candidate and presumptive winner for Congress in the 13th District of New York. You’re also a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, one of many candidates this election cycle who represents a swelling progressive movement. Your national profile is growing.

You were photographed by Annie Leibovitz for our New Establishment Issue, and today I wanna talk to you about how you situate yourself in the political landscape and the leftist surge that we’re seeing right now. And I also wanna talk to you about you. So let’s start a little bit with your background.

New York is your home now, of course, but you were born in Florida and briefly lived in the Dominican Republic and in Venezuela before settling in Tallahassee, I think, as a teenager. And, you know, looking back at your childhood, I wanna know, what was the moment that you had your first political inkling?

Yeah. I mean, I moved around so much as a kid—not only around all those different places, but also within those different places, right? Because my mom was a working-class single mom. My dad wasn’t very involved, but he was also very working-class and, you know, he’s a truck driver. My mom’s a caseworker, worked multiple jobs, and it was not always easy.

And I think my first moment where I realized, Oh, we’re, like, very working-class, if not working-poor, was when I was driving to school with my mom one morning and we had to stop for gas, and my mom said to me, “Crouch down and look for coins,” because we weren’t sure whether we had enough to get gas to get to school.

And we crouched down; I think we barely got to a dollar, and I went into the, the gas station and I gave the man at the counter the dollar, and he looked at me, looked at my mom—who was waiting and looking into the gas station, watching me—and looked back down and said, “I put $5 on the pump.” And I think that was the first time, and I was small. I was still in elementary school at this point that I realized, Oh, this is not something that people normally experience, right? And we were literally relying on the kindness of a stranger that day.

When would you say that you were able to start putting language to that? You know, a five-year-old or a six-year-old probably doesn’t know that they’re working-class.

They know the situation, they know the emotions, but when were you able to start putting the language to it? ’Cause I think that’s an important piece to the politics, you know?

Yeah, I think, you know, as I got older, I was definitely aware that class was a thing.

I think I didn’t call it class, right, until I started reading more about, you know, people’s experiences. I think even in our society, we confuse what working-class means often, right? And we think about ourselves; everyone wants to be middle-class, right? And even folks who are really struggling, like they’re one paycheck away from losing everything, seeing themselves as middle-class [is] a point of dignity, right?

No one wants to see themselves as struggling so much that they could lose everything, but that is the reality for most Americans in this country. And once I was reading more, you know, just progressive, leftist, socialist literature, right, that was talking about these things in a very concrete way and giving language to it—I was reading folks like Baldwin and Du Bois and Angela Davis, right?

And they were really talking about these experiences in ways that really resonated.

Yeah, high school I was reading Baldwin; I was reading, you know, more class-conscious literature. And college, I guess, it was really where, like, things started to get a concrete definition for me, right?

I realized I just really wanted language for my experience, for the experience of my community, and, you know, I really felt really immersed in that world of literature and theory.

So you went to college at Columbia. You’re a New York transplant. How do you think your experience as a non-native New Yorker—I also didn’t grow up here—how do you think it influences your relationship to the city that you’re about to represent?

Yeah, I mean, I love the city so much because it made me the woman that I am. You know, I came and I was 18, but I also grew up coming here often because my mom’s side of the family was here, and New York always felt like the place where I could be all parts of myself. And having lived here since I was, you know, a teenager and 18 and growing into myself, I learned that I love organizing here, right?

I became politically active, and I became active in my community here. And, you know, if you ask me where my roots are, it’s here at this point, because this is where most of the people I love are.

I understand that. I moved here the day after college, and—

I get it. You were just saying your organizing started here.

And that really started when you were an undergraduate at Columbia as part of the Students for Justice in Palestine. I’m curious what you thought that movement was missing when you came across it and what you thought you could bring to it.

Yeah. Well, I actually started organizing earlier than that.

I was—well, in college, but before I joined Students for Justice in Palestine. I was organizing around ending sexual violence on campus. Emma Sulkowicz’s name is coming up a lot now because of the case at Cornell, but I was at school at the same time as her. And this was something that we, on campus, were really starting to build around and organize around to get the university to make meaningful change.

And I think, you know, unfortunately, clearly from what we’ve seen in the last few months, a lot has not changed on college campuses for a lot of people. But that was the work that we were already doing. And I was also organizing with the Black Students Organization, which takes its name because it was an organizing organization, whereas, you know, at other universities, it’s usually the Black Student Union.

We were actually invested in organizing Black students on our campus. And I joined SJP after having gone to Palestine. I’d spent a summer there in the West Bank. And having firsthand experience for, you know, just witnessing the apartheid system there, and—

That was 2014. And I was there as tensions were rising in the West Bank.

And the day after, or within a few days of getting home to the US, you know, Israel began bombing Gaza, and it was a very dark experience. I don’t have another word for it. I just felt so disempowered to be at home scrolling through the names and images of the people who had been slaughtered in Gaza, and people who look so much like the people I had just left behind in the West Bank.

And I think that was where I first started to really take an interest in the notion of power.

Because I’d never felt so powerless in my life.

You attended the pro-Palestine rally on October 8, 2023. What was your thinking in attending that event, and how do you think about it now? Do you regret that?

You know, I have always believed that protests are about power. Again, like, I think power itself is a morally neutral thing. It is about whether or not you can change the conditions around you, right? And so empowering communities to be able to change those circumstances is something I think about all the time.

Like, what are the conditions that you’re thinking, That’s the day to go?

Yes, and so, you know, as someone who’s an American citizen, as someone who pays my taxpayer money, the thing that I have power over in this cycle of violence is where my government uses my tax dollar in this cycle, and the party that we pay our tax dollars to and that we support and arm is the Israeli government, right?

And, you know, are there folks who say things you disagree with at any protest? Yes, of course. The same is true for many elected officials who attended the Israel Day Parade with Israeli officials who have openly called for the genocide of Palestinians, right? And I would hope that they have vehemently disavowed that, right?

But when it comes to advocating for the human rights and human dignity of Palestinians, there seems to be a double standard, right? Where we can’t express our outrage at our tax dollars being used in a way that denies people their human rights and their dignity, particularly when so many people in our communities are being denied those resources, right? Whether it’s in funding schools, whether it’s in addressing childhood poverty.

And I really deeply believe that we are responsible for having a power analysis when we engage in any kind of protest, right?

I think the people that you mentioned, especially public officials, should have to answer the question that you just posed to them.

But specifically on the October 8, you would do it—like, you would go back again on October 8, 2023, to that protest?

I would, because that same day, what I was thinking about was my experience in 2014, where I had sat in my bed and felt powerless, right? And knew in 2023 what was coming was Israel’s response would lead to more and more death.

And that same day, hundreds of people had already been killed, right, in Gaza. And to me, when we mourn human life, we have to mourn human life and prevent more loss of life.

I’m thinking about, on October 7, 2023, people who have done Birthright trips to Israel or have visited in some way and are scrolling through faces and names of people they knew. How do you feel your experience differs from theirs?

I think where, again, asking a question of, where are we positioned to interrupt cycles of violence? I think losing someone you care about is something that, universally, we can all empathize with, right? It is something that is tragic and heartbreaking and is hard to wrap our heads around. If in that moment I could’ve called up the president to yell at Netanyahu, to tell him to stop dropping the bombs, or if I could have, you know, called whoever at any point in the cycle of violence, of course you’d wanna do that.

That’s not a power I have. The power I have is to organize my community into creating that societal shift.

But do you see how those experiences are similar?

Again, the experience of losing somebody, I think that is a universal, like, experience of loss and trauma and pain and grief. Where I see things are different is, again, around a question of power.

Do you have the power to create a world where there is less grief, right? And I think if we look at things institutionally, our government currently is investing in continuing grief for a certain group of people.

Today you are no longer just an organizer. You are poised to be an elected official. When you were younger, did you ever think that you’d be running for office?

Can you describe the moment that you decided to run?

I was recruited to run by Justice Democrats, and I—you know, it’s an organization that takes community nominations, and they told me that someone from the community had nominated me, and that they had spoken to other members of the community and really were excited about this idea.

And I was like, All right, well, I’m just gonna take some time to think about it, ’cause this wasn’t something that I’d thought to do. And I had many conversations with other organizers, with members of my community, with folks who I was like, Oh, they’ll definitely tell me this is a bad idea. And to my surprise, everyone was like, “No, this is a great idea, but it really is up to you.”

This is the same organization that found AOC. How did they find you, and how did you start that relationship?

Yeah, I mean, I’ve been organizing for a really, really long time. And we actually had spoken with them about running somebody else, and a few months later, I get an email, and they told me that folks had reached out to them about me.

And the first question I asked was, “Why me?” And I was like, “And do you know—”

Well, I was like, “And do you know that, like, I have been very vocal,” right, “on a lot of issues?” And they said that’s why. Because they really just wanted someone who felt firm in their convictions and on their view of what this country can and should be for working people across this country.

And I had to really sit with that because it was not an easy decision to make, and so that’s why it took me so long to give them a yes.

How did you win? Because beyond grassroots organizing, moving out an incumbent like Adriano Espaillat in Harlem is no mean feat.

In the clearest possible terms, how do you think you did it?

And it was bringing groups together and building a coalition that knocked over 155,000 doors, that talked to their neighbors even when it was not an easy conversation. And it was, you know, organizing all of the members of our coalition into this larger vision, because not everyone was sold at first.

You have been using this word organizing. What is organizing?

So organizing is coming together with others in your community or who share your same understanding of what the problem is, right? And coming together to address that issue. It is about fundamentally shifting power away from the concentrated few toward the many, right?

So when we think about, for example, housing organizing or tenant organizing, right?

It is about tenants coming together, right, to build power among themselves to change the conditions in their building, whether that is because the tiles on the floor are actually dangerous for the grandma who might trip on them, right?

Or the leaks that are making it so that you are having to endure black mold and just deeply undignified conditions.

And coming together to build the power to have these repairs actually happen.

What does that look like on the day-to-day? Like, what are some things that I might not understand is organizing that you—you know, things that you did in your campaign that I might not understand as organizing, but that were effective?

I think a lot of people, they think there’s, like, this wow or flashy thing that happens in organizing that is what makes it like all of a sudden the power has shifted, but really, it is deeply unsexy work. It is the boring phone calls. It is the meetings that could’ve been an email.

It is the thing that, you know, just brings people together and [makes them] feel connected on a human level to build the trust necessary to move toward something else.

And what’s the role of the DSA in that? In that organizing and in that coalition, how did the DSA influence, impact, your race specifically?

Yeah. Well, I mean, DSA is such an incredible organization.

It is a member-based organization, so if you’re part of the DSA, it’s because you love organizing and you love being in that work, and you share this vision of a socialist, or democratic socialist, country. And once they were excited about this race, right, we knew we could win because we all of a sudden had an army of folks who were ready to knock on doors, were ready to talk about a politic that works for working people.

When you say “they” about the DSA, who’s they? I mean, because is it, like, Megan Romer, the co-chair of the national chapter? Is this the mayor?

Well, I’m a member of the New York City chapter of DSA, which is, you know, affiliated but separate from the national DSA. And I think maybe we take a step back and explain what DSA even is.

That’s perfect. Yes. Let’s do that. I had Ta-Nehisi Coates in this chair a few weeks ago, and the conversation went there, and even he was asking, “What is the DSA?”

Well, to Comrade Coates, I can explain that a little bit more.

It is a member-based organization that is focused on building people power in a democratic way.

And so if you share the values of a socialist, which, to us, is making sure that the wealth that working people produce is also wealth that working people can benefit from and enjoy in our society, then, you know, you can come organize with us to make sure that we’re building that world. And when I talk about socialism, I think sometimes people get stuck in the theory of it and don’t understand what that concretely means.

Sure. It’s a tough brand in America sometimes.

Yeah. And I think most of the most popular policies we’ve ever had in this country’s history, including now, are themselves socialist policies. So thinking, for example, of Social Security or Medicare, right? These are incredibly popular policies, to the point where we’re always fighting to defend them, right?

And we should be fighting to expand them. We should be fighting for more socialist policies that make the lives of working people better.

It is not a party. It is an organization.

I mean, many of us are members or are part of the Democratic Party, right? We’re registered as Democrats, but it is—

Yes. And I’m the Democratic nominee. But the DSA is just an organization. It is an organizing organization, right? And organizing, again, is really about shifting power away from a concentrated few toward the many.

The national chapter of the DSA has a published platform that includes aims like abolishing the presidency—

Abolishing the Senate, replacing the Supreme Court, open borders. How do you—do you agree with that? Or how do you address that with people who read that and are frightened?

Mm-hmm. I mean, again, I’m a member of the New York City chapter.

There are some of those things that I really just don’t agree with, like I don’t agree with abolishing the presidency, for example. But I do think that the beautiful thing about DSA is that it is truly a democratic organization. So as a New York City chapter member, right, I can participate in all of the democratic decisions that happen within our chapter.

And anytime we make a decision as a chapter, we are voting on it, right? And the beautiful thing is, if you have an idea for how to shift politics or policies to work for working people, inside the chapter, you can introduce that, right? You can introduce a resolution. And so—

So what I’m hearing is that it’s not—it’s more of an approach.

It’s not one specific policy or goal in mind, or even one specific worldview; that it’s flexible depending on—

Yeah. I mean, there is a huge diversity of thought within DSA, right? And even between national and the New York City chapter, there’s diversity. There’s, like, sometimes disagreement, right?

And that is what democracy is, right? And I think democracy is a practice, it’s an exercise, and it’s something we have to do often, right?

You have often been compared to AOC, also a New York DSA member. You’ve been called the next AOC; AOC but to the left. She recently endorsed you. What’s your relationship like?

It’s a positive relationship. She is someone who has really laid a path for so many people to be able to come into Congress as a working person. And, you know, I have a lot of respect for the congresswoman, and I’m really excited to see what she might do next.

What do you think are the key differences between the two of you?

Yeah. And, again, I think I’m my own person, right? So—

I think, as someone who comes from a different area of organizing but largely agrees with, you know, the vision that she came into Congress with, I think it’s exciting to be able to come in with a new perspective of where we can grow things even further, right?

President Trump has been recently praising AOC. He said—sort of begrudgingly, he said he doesn’t mind her so much, which is funny coming from the leader of the MAGA movement. And, of course, Mayor Mamdani and Trump have had very public meetings, cordial meetings at the White House and then Gracie Mansion.

I am also very fascinated by this. And I think part of it is that he’s a New Yorker, right? And I think that’s something for New Yorkers to also contend with, right? But I think he just also is someone who understands popularity, right? And I don’t mean popularity as like—

Yeah, he likes a winner, and I think he likes it when people are actually willing to stand on what they believe and not just, you know, kiss up to him.

Who do you think gets more from that relationship, him or them? That’s interesting. Specifically Mamdani.

You know, I think it has been really fascinating to watch the way that they’re cognizant of the power disparity.

He’s the president of the United States. That is just the political reality, unfortunately, for all of us, right? But to watch, you know, the mayor and to watch the congresswoman in the way that they interact and really move strategically to make sure that New Yorkers benefit from every interaction that they have with the president has been…

Honestly, I’m taking notes. Because I’m like, eventually, right, that will be something that I’ll have to do.

Yeah. It makes me think of something else too, which is, like, you know, so much of campaigning, certainly organizing, is about principles and ideology, and there’s a purity to that.

When you’re governing, you have to work with people, whether it’s centrist Democrats or even Republicans, and that often means compromise. How do you think about that? Are you prepared to compromise, or do you sort of—are you prepared to compromise?

I think that juxtaposition is funny and interesting because, even in a campaign, you’re organizing with people who you might not always agree with on everything, and that doesn’t mean that you compromise your ideology, that you compromise your vision of the world, that you compromise your principles, right?

I deeply believe that we have to be uncompromising in our principles and willing to move on strategy. Because if we are set on strategy, then what does that mean for our principles? Where are we bending there?

Can you give an example of where you’d compromise, or an example of AOC or someone else who has had to make compromise that you’d be okay with?

You know, I’ll actually point to myself, and that is that I’m running for office. I never thought that I would run for office. I’ve always seen myself as a grassroots organizer, and when I realized we had a strategic opening to meaningfully transform politics in this country, I said, Okay, let’s do this.

Let’s use this vehicle that I had for many years not really—like, that was not my world of organizing, right?

As much as I saw it as valuable, it just wasn’t where I was. But I stepped into it because I saw it as a really important vehicle for how we shift our politics more largely. And after winning, right, people told us that that could only happen in New York, and a week later, Melat Kiros won in Denver.

And then after that, 103 Democrats voted to stop sending arms to Israel. So we’ve already transformed the politics of what’s considered acceptable politics within the electoral world.

Sure. I was gonna say, when you get to Congress, do you see your role as someone that is there to make laws or to move the Overton window to the left so that the laws that are made are closer to what you and your compatriots are after?

Yeah. I think it’s both and. I mean, I think, like, if we are only ever talking about our values, but we’re not shifting the policies, then the world around us doesn’t actually change. And I think about—I mean, we’ll just continue down this example of the issue of the genocide, right?

We can talk about our values.We can convince an entire country of people. We’ve convinced the entire Democratic base on this issue, and yet we still have elected officials who are voting against the interests of their base, right? The material conditions have not changed, right? And that’s only going to happen when we have policy that also shifts with it.

And so that’s why it’s important that we are being, you know, good colleagues, right? And we’re talking to folks, finding those points where we do have something in common, and organizing our colleagues to see reason as well, right? Because it’s—yes, sometimes we have to, like, see reason of why something is difficult for them.

That’s what I was gonna say. Are you ready to see reason?

Yeah. And they have to also see that, like, their Democratic base wants them to move on these issues.

How much time have you spent with your future Republican colleagues?

Well, actually, I haven’t spoken to many, but I’ve spoken to, you know, folks across the spectrum on the Democratic Party at this point.

Have you met any Republican congresspeople?

Not actual members, but I’ve met plenty of Republicans.

Oh, plenty. I mean, I grew up also in Florida.

So there are plenty of Republicans there.

Who’s the Republican that you’ll reach out to first when you get to Congress?

Yeah. No, I mean, I’ll say this. I think that there are no two people who agree on every single issue, even as aligned as you might be, right?

And you’d be surprised how people who think very differently can still find a point of commonality and can build trust.

Exactly, and so that is what organizing is.

Earlier this month, ICE agents attempted to arrest 28-year-old Oscar Belgal in the Bronx.

They shot him in the neck while he was in the car with his five-year-old son in the back seat. As you pointed out in the aftermath of this incident, the shooter, an ICE agent, hasn’t been identified or charged with a crime. Can you talk me through what you think should happen now?

Yeah. I think there should be a full investigation into what happened.

I think Oscar should be released and returned to his family, and so that he could get medical care. He still has the bullet in his body and is losing hearing and feeling in his face. And, you know, I think we need to abolish ICE. I don’t see a world in which an institution that is a rogue militia, that is walking around in crowded streets with no uniform, no identification, masked, and shooting into cars—seven bullets into a car that had a five-year-old child in it—while people were returning home from school and work, is an agency that has any business operating in our country.

We’ve seen so many instances of communities and families being torn apart because of ICE’s actions, and the only reason that it exists at this point is to serve as Trump’s cudgel for fascism.

If the shooter in question was apprehended, what should happen to them?

I mean, they should be prosecuted, obviously.

But I also think—I don’t have faith in that because what we’re looking at is the institution that would oversee that is Trump’s, right? It’s Trump’s DOJ. And so I think what the solution here—

Yeah, I mean, this is attempted manslaughter at best.

It’s attempted murder, right? This was, like, ICE shooting at somebody in broad daylight.

I see a bit of a contradiction between wanting the shooter apprehended and your stance on prison abolition, and where’s the shooter going, if not to jail?

Mm-hmm. You know, abolition is a process and a vision, right?

It is the idea that we are constructing a world where a shooting like that doesn’t happen to begin with. And so when I talk about abolishing ICE, the point is that we are taking away the condition for this to ever happen again. We are taking these arms off the street. We are taking these people away from the power to do that to our communities, right?

And we are reinvesting those resources into things that actually make our communities more safe. Abolition is also the view that we should be proactive in safety and not reactive. Because right now we’re talking about an incident that already happened, where a man was shot, right? The world that we’re trying to build is one where that isn’t something that can come to pass.

I understand that, and I think that is a worthy vision, and to advocate for broad systemic reform to prevent murder is something I think a lot of people can get behind. But that’s a future goal, and I’m just curious about now. Now that you’re gonna become a lawmaker, do you believe that someone who is convicted of murder with intent should be physically confined to protect the public?

But that is what happens in the day-to-day.

And I know that because I’ve worked at a public defender’s office. I’ve seen this happen, right? What I argue, as someone who deeply cares about ending violence in our communities, is that if we don’t begin the process now of building this world where we are proactive in preventing violence instead of reactive once the violence has already happened, then we’re never going to get to that world.

I’m pushing you on this because I think people see this as radical. What you’re saying is an idealistic vision of the future that is worthy. I think most people, many people would think [it’s] a worthy vision.

But they’re concerned about that specific idea now. It feels radical.

Well, again, it’s not something that happens overnight. We’re not gonna depopulate and close Rikers tomorrow, even though the law, right, is that we are supposed to close Rikers, and we’re supposed to do that, like, now, right? But we need to also, of course, do that in a way that actually makes sense and functions for a society, right?

Where are these people gonna go? Do they even have homes to go back to, right? And I think what that is signaling is that we have a larger structural issue that has prioritized incarcerating people over taking care of communities, right? You know, I once worked with a client who would seek to get arrested because it was the only place he could take his bipolar medication.

That is a failure of our medical system, that is a failure of our housing system, and that is also a public-safety issue.

No question. But that ICE agent, in a perfect world where the DOJ behaves as they should, is going to prison.

In a perfect world, ICE wouldn’t exist, is my point, right?

And as a sociologist, we create our world.

We create the infrastructure and the structures that encourage people to behave in particular ways.

Have you ever heard the Tom Wolfe quote? He said, “A Democrat is a Republican who’s been through the criminal justice system, and a Republican is a Democrat who’s been mugged.” [Editor’s note: Wolfe’s quote is, “If a conservative is a liberal who’s been mugged, a liberal is a conservative who’s been arrested,” which builds upon the neoconservative aphorism “a conservative is a liberal who has been mugged.”]

It’s good. Let’s look forward. It’s January 3, 2027, and according to all prediction models, you’re gonna be taking office that day. What are your immediate priorities? Where do you begin?

So our platform was deeply important to our district, and we know that because not only after knocking doors did the folks say, like, “These are the issues that matter to us,” but also because I’d spent a year knocking on doors for the mayor and knowing that those were the issues that our community cares about.

So addressing childhood poverty, investing in our babies and not bombs, signing on to the Block the Bombs Act to stop the genocide, making sure that we are fighting to abolish ICE, and making sure that we’re winning housing for all so that everyone in our district has dignified housing.

You know, I have questions about impeachment. We’ve impeached him twice, and he seems to want impeachment, and I really want meaningful accountability.

And I’m looking at what is actually going to bring that about.

So instead, are you hauling administration officials and others into Congress after investigations? Is that a more meaningful approach?

I think hauling everyone who had any role in any of this corruption into Congress to answer to the American public, that’s what I think was a more meaningful approach, yeah.

So you haven’t committed to backing Hakeem Jeffries for Speaker, but you recently met with him. When it comes to deciding if you will cast your vote for him, what are you weighing? What are your considerations, the pros and cons?

I think this would be a really historic vote, and this would be a very historic moment—not just for myself, as it’ll set the tone for the kind of representative I’ll be for my district, but also for this country, where we’re talking about having the first Black Speaker, right?

And for the city, where we’re talking about bringing the Speakership to New York. I want that to mean something to the people of my district, to New Yorkers, to Black folks across the country, right? And so the things that I’m thinking about are, will we have a Speaker that’s gonna back and support getting the John Lewis Voting Rights Act across the finish line?

Are we gonna have a Speaker that is gonna push for “Medicare for All,” that’s going to push for blocking the bombs, for any number of policies, right, that matter to the people of this district? We have the most public housing units in the country in the city. Are we gonna have a Speaker who’s going to fight for investing in public housing?

Those are the things that keep the people of the city up at night, and I think that they should matter to our Speaker.

What commitment do you need from him for you to give your thumbs-up?

I think commitments on moving on all of these issues, right?

And actually bringing more power to Congress to take on Trump, right?

Reminding ourselves that Congress has the power of the purse. Trump can’t make all these threats around cuts to funding. It’s Congress, right, that has the final say on that.

Mainstream Democrat, pro-Israel, staunchly pro-Israel, is a congressman in your neighboring district. Do you know him?

I’m interested because you will have, when it comes to public housing, immigration, there are lots of issues where your—the fates of your districts are tied together.

So I’m interested to know if you plan on collaborating with him.

I mean, again, on things that I think both of our districts will benefit from. His district and my district, by many measures, are the two poorest districts in this country. I think there’s a lot that we need to deliver, right? And, you know, I’ve been meeting with members across the New York delegation and working to build those relationships, so I’m sure Congressman Torres and I will be talking very soon.

Would you support a primary to challenge him based on your disagreement on Israel?

I’m still working to get across the finish line on my race.

Okay. All right. So I wanna end by talking about the future. You and your colleagues in the DSA have presented a pretty transformational vision for the future of this country.

Do you think that’s achievable through incremental change, or do you believe a systemic overhaul, something monumental and dramatic in the moment, is necessary?

I think both. I think there are many things that we can be striving toward in a step-by-step manner, and then there are things where I think we have the opening now to really move forward on.

I think “Medicare for All” would be monumental. It would completely transform our society and benefit everyone in this country, right? And I think there is so much hunger and appetite for it across the ideological spectrum. And I think if we do the work to make sure that in the next two to four years we have the power to actually pass it—

That would be a monumental overnight shift for so many people, right? But we have to do the day-to-day work, right? That doesn’t just happen.

If you were to vote right now, who are you looking at for the presidency in 2028?

Well, you know, a lot of folks haven’t announced whether or not they’d run.

I don’t know. I mean, I think Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez would make a great president, but I also don’t know what her final decision is on that matter. But if she decides to run, I think she’d be great.

So, Darializa, the Proust Questionnaire is the longtime back page of Vanity Fair.

It lists a number of probing questions by Marcel Proust, and I’d like to put a few of them to you. What is your greatest extravagance?

All over. Thai, pizza, soul food. I just order a lot.

This was one of the things that I talked to Justice Democrats about. I said, “I, you know, I can’t lie. I don’t know if politics is for me,” and they laughed and they were like, “That’s actually a good thing.” So…

Oh, I mean, I think Trump is too easy of one, but we’ll go with that.

Netanyahu. There we go. Both of them. Maybe they’re tied.

What do you consider your greatest achievement?

Honestly, this campaign has been just the biggest honor of my lifetime. And to know that we have had thousands of people come out to support and volunteer and be activated in their communities again, that all of our coalitions saw growth in their membership—that, to me, has been my greatest achievement so far.

Candidate Chevalier, thank you very much.
