#3684. Here Are The Highest-Grossing Resident Evil Movies Ever, And The New One Is Now No. 1

Zach Cregger's Resident Evil movie got solid reviews and is making a lot of money at the box office, but where does it rank on the list of highest-grossing Resident Evil movies? Following its debut in China, it's now No. 1 overall with more than $399 million globally.

Director Paul W.S. Anderson made six previous Resident Evil movies, starring his wife, Milla Jovovich, and 2016's The Final Chapter previously ranked No. 1 in terms of money at the box office. Anderson's movies did not fare very well with critics, but had dedicated fans who kept going to see them. Together, Anderson's six movies made more than $1 billion.

Cregger's Resident Evil movie now ranks No. 1 with more than $399 million worldwide. It's also Cregger's highest-grossing movie ever, surpassing Weapons ($270 million).

Below you can see a rundown of the highest-grossing live-action Resident Evil movies ever, including domestic, international, and global figures. In addition to Cregger and Anderson, director Johannes Roberts worked on the series for 2021's Welcome to Raccoon City, the lowest-performing Resident Evil live-action movie ever.

The Resident Evil movies are produced by Constantin Films, which bought the rights back in the '90s and has retained them ever since. After Welcome to Raccoon City flopped, Constantin planned to put the film franchise on ice ... until Cregger showed up with a pitch.

While Cregger has said he has ideas for another Resident Evil movie, he's done with franchise movies and is instead making an original movie, The Flood, next.

#3683. Pre-K Teacher's Aide Filmed Himself Assaulting Kids In School: Prosecutors

A teacher’s aide is facing 61 charges after he allegedly filmed himself sexually assaulting multiple children inside the elementary school where he worked.

Shaun M. Stebbins of Somers Point, New Jersey, was previously arrested on March 29 on several charges, including aggravated sexual assault and child sex abuse material offenses in connection with allegations that he abused four children, who are siblings, over a span of several years.

That sexual assault investigation revealed additional alleged crimes involving students at Woodbine Elementary School in Cape May County, the Cape May County Prosecutor’s Office announced in a Thursday, October 30, news release.

Investigators discovered Stebbins, 44 — who worked at the school as a pre-kindergarten aide — allegedly took photos and video of children’s genitalia inside a school bathroom, per court documents obtained by WPVI-TV.

Stebbins also allegedly filmed himself sexually assaulting children in the bathroom and during their scheduled nap time.

Stebbins was charged on October 30 with 29 counts of manufacturing child pornography, five counts of aggravated sexual assault, 13 counts of sexual assault by sexual contact and 14 counts of endangering the welfare of a child, according to prosecutors.

“Children are among our most vulnerable population and we have a responsibility to protect their safety and well-being. Anyone who harms a child will be held accountable through our justice system,” Cape May County Prosecutor Jeffrey H. Sutherland said in an October 30 statement.

Stebbins was hired at Woodbine Elementary School in February 2022 and worked at the school for more than four years and until his arrest earlier this year in the separate child sexual assault case, prosecutors said.

In the other case, Stebbins allegedly sexually assaulted four siblings — all of whom are his extended family members — for over a decade, according to NJ.com.

Woodbine School District Superintendent Adrienne Breitinger previously said in a letter to families that the district immediately sought to replace Stebbins following his March 29 arrest, the outlet reported.

“The safety and well-being of our students remain our highest priority,” Breitinger wrote.

Stebbins attended a virtual court appearance Monday in connection with the alleged crimes against students and was ordered detained ahead of his next court date, which is set for November 4, per WPVI-TV.

Information on his legal counsel or whether he entered a plea wasn’t immediately available.

The Cape May County Prosecutor’s Office encourages anyone with information on Stebbins’ case to contact the office’s special victims unit at (609) 465-1135. Anonymous tips can also be submitted online.

If you or someone you know is experiencing child abuse, call or text Child Help Hotline at 1-800-422-4453.

#3682. Resident Evil Director Reacts To Backlash: “I Should Have Known Better”

Resident Evil is a huge success at the box office, recently surpassing $400 million globally. It's also received fantastic review scores. But hardcore fans of the game series took issue with the film and its direction because it did not contain any storylines or characters from the source material. Director Zach Cregger never intended to, instead opting for his own original story that is set in the world of Resident Evil. Now, Cregger has spoken more about the fallout, saying he became "frustrated at the conversation" around his movie and specifically how it "didn't have anything to do with the movie."

He said on The Town that the conversation from the hardcore Resident Evil fanbase was that the movie didn't live up to their standards, even though Cregger never said he was trying to make a movie that did that.

He said he really loves and is proud of the movie he made. At the same time, Cregger admitted, "I should have known better" about how fans of the game series might react. Anyone who has been on the internet and engaged with anything related to gaming knows how intense hardcore gaming fans can be about even the seemingly smallest of issues, but Cregger said he overlooked this for reasons he doesn't fully understand.

"I should have understood that that was going to be the case," Cregger said about the blowback. Cregger previously said he was naive to think gamers would embrace him and his idea for the Resident Evil movie.

Cregger previously said he would never make another franchise movie after Resident Evil, but he's softened somewhat, saying on the podcast that he has a "never say never" attitude about it. Asked if Cregger's anti-franchise stance might limit his job opportunities in the future, Cregger said that after Barbarian and Weapons, he feels like he is "playing with house money."

Cregger said he's basically already won in life and the rest of his career is gravy. He said he goes into his projects now thinking it could be the last film he ever makes, and he's OK with that. "I'm going to swing for the f**king fences," he said. "I'm going to pour it all out to make this as good as I am capable of making it. And whatever happens, whether it makes a lot of money or no money, I just have to make sure I left it all on the court. And if that's the end, then I've had an amazing run."

Cregger is, of course, not finished making movies. His next film is the deep space sci-fi movie The Flood, starring Jennifer Lawrence. He said in the interview that it's his biggest-budget movie ever; previously, that record belonged to Resident Evil (a reported $75 million before marketing costs). Cregger said he shouldn't admit this publicly, but he believes there are real benefits to making movies on lower budgets, in part so a filmmaker like himself has to get creative as he works against constraints.

The Resident Evil movies are produced by Constantin Films, which bought the rights back in the '90s and has retained them ever since. After Welcome to Raccoon City flopped, Constantin planned to put the film franchise on ice ... until Cregger showed up with a pitch.

In addition to The Flood, Cregger is producing the next Weapons movie, which is the spin-off, Aunt Gladys.

#3680. How To Pitch Stories To Kotaku

We’ve worked with a ton of different freelance writers at Kotaku over the years. Maybe you want to be one of them! Here’s what you need to know before pitching us stories.

The good ones. Especially if you have a unique angle or access to provide our readers with exclusive insights, information, or high-quality writing about something they never knew they wanted to read about before. This includes, but is not limited to, feature stories, opinion pieces, essays, reported scoops, sweeping investigations, and fascinating interviews.

Most of the pitches we get are for reviews and previews. These are also the easiest things to say no to because everyone else will be publishing them. What Kotaku is most interested in when it comes to freelance pitches are original stories that readers won’t be able to find anywhere else because of a unique angle you’ve crafted, insight you’ve unearthed, experience you’ve had, or information you’ve obtained.

This could be an interview with a developer that surfaces a fascinating insight about a game they worked on a decade ago. It could be a bizarre but intriguing drama that played out in a video game Discord community last month. It could be insights from a studio about why a troubled project still hasn’t shipped or a profile of a group of modders attempting something incredible in one of their favorite games.

The best stories inform and entertain. They have characters, conflict, and tension. Some stories have exciting conclusions. Others remain unresolved and are richer because of it. You don’t have to be pitching the next Pulitzer Prize-winning article to be thinking about these types of things.

Send us your idea for what you want to write with a projected word count and timeline for when it would be filed. Suggest a sample headline and explain what makes the story interesting, why we have to have it, and why there’s no version of it that we’ll be able to find online within five minutes of Googling for it. This pitch should be brief, punchy, and as exciting as the final version of the article you’re going to turn in.

Please also share a link to relevant past work and any public profile you maintain. We don’t need to know your entire life’s story or everything you’ve ever written, just one or two strong samples, whether published at a mainstream website or your personal blog, that help demonstrate your ability to execute on the ambitious idea you just pitched us.

Send them to [email protected]. Or you can reach out to individual members of staff. Don’t hesitate to follow up if you don’t get a response right away. And while we can’t guarantee we’ll get back to every pitch, we definitely read them all. We do not accept work produced by AI agents or drafted with the help of them.

Our rates start at $50 for short news posts (300-450 words). Our standard rate for short features (750-1,000 words) is $150. These include light research and some original sourcing (quotes or information revealed for the first time in this story), and often try to show a trend, convey a larger point, or make a broader argument about gaming and the world, although they certainly don’t have to. Sometimes hyper-detailed anecdotes or chains of events within niche communities make for the most interesting reads of all.

We pay up to $300 for more in-depth articles that require multiple interviews, more intensive research, or lots of hands-on time with a game. Rates for everything in-between and beyond are negotiable on a case-by-case basis. If you show up with a leaked build of Half-Life 3 or an exclusive interview with Shigeru Miyamoto, we can talk.

#3679. Gears Of War: E-Day’s Apparent $500 Million Budget May Not Tell The Full Story – Report

How much does a true console exclusive cost to make today? If recent reports are to be believed, Gears of War: E-Day had a production cost $500 million, but there's more to that figure than just a single game.

That's according to Windows Central writer Jez Corden, who says he spoke with multiple sources familiar with the story behind the half-billion dollars paid over several years to The Coalition while it was working on Gears of War: E-Day. The studio emerged from the COVID-19 pandemic as a Swiss Army Knife developer that assisted not only on several Xbox games, but also worked on the technology powering them.

As Corden explained, The Coalition worked with Epic Games on the oThe Matrix Awakens and Alpha Point tech demos for Unreal Engine 5 demonstrations, and used that knowledge to help other developers in the Xbox Games Studio portfolio. The Coalition reportedly worked for over 18 months on a prototype game that was eventually canceled, assisted on Avowed, Hellblade 2, Clockwork Revolution, State of Decay 3, Grounded, and Grounded 2, and even contributed to the upcoming StarCraft at Blizzard.

Once Mike Crump was appointed studio head, development on Gears of War: E-Day reportedly kicked into full gear. That makes for a busy developer, and one that brings a lot of institutional knowledge to Xbox with its work on Unreal Engine 5, which is one of the most popular engines for video game development. "I can't help but feel like the '$500 million' figure being shared around internally is being used to justify potential cuts, layoffs, or worse, a studio closure targeting The Coalition. Perhaps to 'soften the blowback,' should Microsoft target the studio. For what it's worth, I've not heard that Xbox is planning to close The Coalition," Corden added.

Gears of War: E-Day has reportedly not sold well either, but this can be attributed to various factors. It was only released for PC and Xbox Series X|S, is also available through Xbox Game Pass, and it happened to launch during an exceptionally busy time, as the last couple of months have been loaded with several major game releases, creating a lot of competition for a person's attention and money.

Circana analyst Mat Piscatella recently commented on the game, saying that making Gears of War: E-Day exclusive to Xbox "hasn’t made any difference" in terms of selling more Xbox consoles.

#3678. 'Elsinore' Stars Andrew Scott and Olivia Colman on 'Fleabag', Auditions, and Acting Through Illness

Olivia Colman and Andrew Scott’s friendship pre-dates Fleabag by a decade, though Colman wouldn’t know it. “Was it in the garden for the wedding of Fleabag? Was that the first scene we [did together]?” she asks as the pair sits down in London.

“Oh darling, we met about 10 years before,” says Scott with a laugh. “We did a radio play, which you never remember.”

Colman giggles, and insists she does. It was a BBC Radio 4 adaptation of Harold Pinter's classic play Betrayal, which aired in 2012.

“The big thing that you have to do when you’re playing a radio play is not make the paper make any sound,” says Scott, revealing that another actor once told him a trick to keeping his script silent: “You scrunch it right up, and then you unscrunch it so it’s rigid…so even if you move them, they’re never going to [make a sound].”

The pair have a natural chemistry, which isn’t a surprise after seeing their work on Fleabag. Colman played Godmother, a passive-aggressive, vulgar villain who ate up every scene she was in. And Scott, of course, played the “hot priest” in the second season, the charming and slightly unruly clergy member that became a sensation.

This year, they reunited in the much more dramatic Elsinore, a moving drama about Scottish actor Ian Charleson (Scott) who attempts to perform Hamlet at the National Theatre while secretly living with AIDS. Oscar winner Colman plays Charleson’s doctor, Margaret Johnson, who discourages him from taking on the strenuous role because of the threat it poses to his health.

An exploration of art, ambition, and mortality, Elsinore is centered on a career-best performance from Scott, who had previously played Hamlet (150 times!) onstage in London in 2017.

Earlier this month, Scott and Colman looked back at their favorite Fleabag memories, the way Elsinore brings out comedy within the tragedy, and their best tricks for acing auditions.

This interview has been condensed and edited.

Vanity Fair: What was the first scene you did together on Fleabag?

Olivia Colman: Was that the wedding or was it the dinner party?

Andrew Scott: No, I will never forget it. I had to say that I was pulling out of the wedding and we were in the house and I'd say, you were like, “Oh no, that's absolutely, it's perfectly fine.” And you see me out. And there had to be a door slam and the camera stays in the living room and you just hear the door slam and then we hear you saying—

Scott: Exactly. But I wasn't able to leave because of sound. So I had to crouch down. And then you were, “What a cunt!” And I remember thinking, Hold it together. Do not laugh because I'm going to ruin it. I was in the room and I couldn't laugh. And it was so funny.

Colman: And we had the dinner and the wedding.

Scott: I remember so much about that dinner scene because you'd just come back from Venice, and you just won that big fancy prize. All of these had to be filmed on the weekends.

Colman: Yes, because I was doing The Crown Monday to Friday.

Colman: That's why I can't remember anything. That's in my defense. There was one month, was it September? Where I didn’t have a single day off.

Elsinore opens in theaters beginning Nov. 20.

How did you each get involved with Fleabag?

Colman: Phoebe [Waller-Bridge] and I were doing a play, and she was writing a lot and she'd written Fleabag and she was doing a crowdfunder to get it to Edinburgh. And [English actor] Kevin McNally and I were two of the people who sponsored it to go to Edinburgh. Then I think before [the festival], they did a little read-through of it somewhere. I saw it. Then I also said, just shamelessly, “Can I be in it? Or can I be in anything that you write?”

Scott: So you gave money for the original Edinburgh show? Wow! I never knew that. You must feel so proud of that.

Colman: I’m pretty thrilled with myself, yes. But also just trying to buy Phoebe's friendship.

Scott: A perfect way to buy friendship. That's how you got mine and I'm still getting those direct deposits every month.

Scott: Phoebe and I had done a play at the Soho Theatre about 10 years before Fleabag. And so the first [season] had come out and everybody loved it. And then she called me and said, "I'm thinking of writing this other character. Can we have a sort of talk about it?" We hadn't seen each other in a few years, and we ended up having this incredible walk around Soho and talking about love. And she had this idea of this priest and we talked about religion and what that means. And I remember bringing her into this place in Soho and it's on St. Martin’s Lane, which is the Quaker meeting hall. Have you ever been in there?

Scott: You know that scene where we go into the Quaker meeting hall? Anyway, I brought her into this place and I said, "This is where I come to sort of chill out sometimes and you can go into some really silent room in the middle of St. Martin's Lane." And so we sat in there for about two hours and we just talked about love and life. And then she incorporated it into the story. I sort of signed up to it with no script. So the day before the read-through I was like, "Oh my God, this is incredible." She's so brilliant that she just incorporates things and that amazing mind is always at work.

Olivia, when the “hot priest” situation happened, what was it like seeing Andrew, your friend, suddenly catapulted into this sensational online narrative?

Colman: Well, I remember my girlfriends just going, "Oh my God, the hot priest! I'm having awful thoughts about him!” And I loved it. I thought it was hilarious. All my women friends, just thinking filthy thoughts about you.

Scott: People do get very feral. It's the priest thing. It's the collar.

Colman: It's the taboo. It's the transgression of it.

Scott: Who would have thunk it? I knew that it was kind of funny and sexy and actually very soulful, that relationship between those two characters, but you never think it's going to be…

Colman: I was so cross with Phoebe when I first read it though, and the ending that they weren't together. Why can't you make a happy ending? I want to re-watch it all now.

Scott: We should have a little Fleabag party. That would be so fun.

Colman: Fleabag holiday. Oh my God, let's get a nice big house in a countryside. I want to have dogs and just watch Fleabag every night.

What do you remember about shooting that dinner scene together?

Colman: It took two days to film that scene. And it felt like, “I can imagine film students are going to study this one day.” It's so brilliantly written.

Scott: And I remember at the time I had a 103-degree temperature. I was so sick. But it's that amazing thing about when you're acting, you sort of forget about it.

Colman: I don't want to make this about me, but I had pneumonia when filming Wicker.

Scott: Did you really? How long did you have it for?

Colman: I can't remember. I started to sort of get better as they sort of fell in love, weirdly. Otherwise, I don't think I could have done the marriage dance thing. But it is amazing how you just—and maybe we're sort of a bit old-school, but maybe it's silly.

Scott: Probably it is a little bit silly. You just do those things…

Colman: The fear that you're going to get replaced. Still in the back of my head that someone else will take the job.

Scott: Absolutely. And in a way, it might be a little bit foolish. I had to have a sort of affect having a weird panic attack in [his one-man stage adaptation of Uncle] Vanya, and towards the last two weeks, I was like, "This isn't really stopping." Because I think your brain knows, but your body doesn't know and you sort of continue. It is a sort of corny, nuts thing to do for your life.

Colman: This rather beautifully ties in with Elsinore, doesn't it?

Scott: You're acting and you sort of forget about it for a little while. And in some ways, on a much, much more serious scale, Ian Charleson was really suffering with illness, and he went on and he did this heroic, Olympian part. And then he would just collapse at the end.

Scott: Yeah, six weeks later. I suppose it's about quality and quantity, right? Dr. Johnson basically said, "You can have more time. If you just give yourself a bit more time, then there might be some developments in the treatment. But if you play this part, it's going to mess up your immune system and it's going to mess you up. It could be fatal." And that's their big conflict. And then bit by bit, it's about art and what it means and how we use our time. And eventually—

Colman: They had come to an understanding.

Andrew, how did performing Hamlet onstage back in 2017 inform your performance as Ian Charleson playing Hamlet?

Scott: It was kind of difficult because all the scripts leave my head almost immediately. So I had to relearn Hamlet.

Colman: Do you find, when you're auditioning, the audition scene is the hardest one to film if you get the job?

Scott: Oh my God, totally. Because you're like, “You liked that. Can I do it again?” Because you feel like that must have been what they liked because otherwise I wouldn't be here. You're so right. Did you like auditioning?

Colman: Partly because I really enjoyed forcing them to like me. I'd go in and they'd go, "What the fuck? She's not right for this." I go, "I'm going to win you over. I'm going to do it." And so there was a job where I was playing a mom to some really tough lads and I really enjoyed it and they went, "Oh." Now with everyone taping, I wouldn't get the work I got if I had to do tape. I had to be in the room to win people over.

Scott: And also, I think what's difficult is that if you're putting yourself on tape, you present what you think that your instinct is. But if someone goes, "Oh, actually no, I think a person is much less friendly or more generous or whatever." You go, “ok,” because acting is so much about going, “I can do it a different way.”

Colman: It’s great for people who are far away and can't afford to get the train fare, but I think it's tough for actors now.

Scott: I remember auditioning for Sherlock and exactly the same experience as you had where I think they were like, "Who is this tiny little fella that's coming in?” And I remember thinking, "I'm going to frighten you. I'm going to frighten you." I remember I sort of shouted in the audition and I could tell they were like, "He's a bit creepy actually."

Do you always know when you’ve gotten the part?

Scott: No, you never know after an audition, do you? You sort of have an instinct.

Colman: Occasionally I knew that I didn't get it. I used to do a little thing: I'd go, "Do you want me to leave the script?" And if they went, "Yes, that'd be great. Thank you," I knew I hadn't got it.

Do you prefer dramatic parts or comedic ones, or is there even a difference in your approach?

Scott: If we were to meet for dinner, I don't think we'd go, “We'll do the sad bit. We'll do the funny bit.” I think you've got to be prepared for all the colors. You know what I mean? That is why you are truly exceptional. I don't think you can be a really great, great actor to my mind without having a terrific sense of humor. And that's just what you have. You just have that interest in the lightness of human beings. I don't love overly serious acting, just because I don't think it's real to human beings.

Colman: I think the funny has to be based in realism and if you're trying to lay on funny, play funny. It's not funny. But you are naturally funny and you're naturally feeling and giving.

Scott: I think that's why even though we had some serious scenes to do, but also we should say that the screenplay was just massively funny. And they have a sort of antagonistic relationship and I always think antagonism is a funny thing to play. It's a great fun thing to do. And then they gradually sort of warm to each other.

Olivia, what’s your approach to awards acceptance speeches? Because some have gone viral, like your shoutouts to Lady Gaga, or calling your Favourite costars Emma Stone and Rachel Weisz “my bitches.” What goes through your head in those moments?

Colman: No idea. I can't remember any of it. The Oscars, it's like a wedding day. I remember my dad saying, "There'll be moments, just stop and just look at it. Take it all in. Look at all the faces. Who's there?" And that was amazing advice. And on my wedding day I remembered it. And it was before phones and things—that magic of theater— when it's gone, it's gone. And so that was rather beautiful. But the Oscars was such a head fuck because it’s such a huge occasion. You just sort of can't believe that's happened, and you wake up the next day and go, can't remember any of it.

Scott: I think it's a testament to you because you come on and you're just completely yourself and what's completely yourself is just completely adorable and sincere. That speech is just so incredibly sincere and it's fun and it's also ridiculous, but also meaningful.

Colman: It means so much. And that's why in the buildup when people talk about it, I really understand how it's, “Please don't, please don't” because you can't help but sort of dream about it. And then it happens and then you wish you'd paid more attention.

What role of each other’s would you have loved to try to take on?

Scott: I don't want to do anything that you've done. I'd just be shitter.

Colman: I want to be in more of the stuff that you've done. I want to be in scenes with you.

Scott: Would you do a play? Do you feel you just don't really want to do a play?

Colman: I think until my youngest [child] has left home, I find going out to work just as everyone's getting cozy heartbreaking.

Scott: It's so hard. Or even in the summer when everyone's like, “Oh, we might go to a beer garden,” you think—

Scott: I'm going in the dark. I’m going to scream in the dark.

Colman: The camaraderie is extraordinary. I love that. I miss that. I miss rehearsals, but I might not go back to it until I know my kids are all grown.

Is this something that you’d want to see each other do in the future?

Colman: Well, we talk about doing a little thing together about houses.

Scott: We think we should have a reality show about houses and beach walks. We might not have a huge viewership.

Colman: We walk around and we go, “I wouldn’t put that there.” We'd be a bit bitchy going around people's houses. We thought that'd be fun. Probably no one will see it.

Scott: Nobody would watch that. They’d think, “What awful, horrible people.”

#3677. Spencer Pratt Defends Staying in $1,200-a-Night Hotel During L.A. Mayor Race

Spencer Pratt is setting the record straight about why he stayed at a luxury hotel during his campaign to become Los Angeles’ next mayor.

“Remember when you first met me? For those of you in the [Pacific] Palisades, that was likely many years ago, but the majority of folks met me when my first campaign ad dropped back in April,” Pratt, 43, wrote via X on Tuesday, November 3. “I showed Karen Bass’ and Nithya Raman’s multimillion-dollar homes and then showed everybody the grim reality of what became of my home. A sleek, Airstream perched precariously on my hillside lot, a stark contrast to the nuked out wreckage where my home used to be.”

After Pratt and his wife, Heidi Montag, lost their home in the January 2025 Palisades fire, The Hills alum worked to get an Airstream trailer installed at his burned property.

While running to become Los Angeles’ next mayor, however, Pratt found himself in controversy when outlets claimed he was actually staying at the Hotel Bel-Air, which has a nightly rate between $900 to $1,200 for standard luxury rooms.

“When the media found out I was staying there, they were most certainly not cozy nor at ease. The backlash was intense, and predictably so,” Pratt shared via X. “Now, in many ways, our campaign was perfectly fine with the controversy, because the kerfuffle over me staying at a hotel just reminded everyone of my opponent’s biggest failure; Karen Bass is the reason I didn’t have a home to go to. But, nonetheless, it was becoming such a big controversy, it was eating up all the oxygen in the room, and it was a distraction from all my winning policy ideas; instead of talking about the campaign, we were talking about a damn hotel.”

Pratt consistently criticized Bass, 73, for not being present in Los Angeles at the time of the Palisades fire. He also claimed she was not prepared to deal with a fire that destroyed more than 6,800 structures. (Bass and Los Angeles City Council member Nithya Raman ultimately received the most votes in the June primary, leaving Pratt off the ballot for Tuesday’s election.)

In his X post, Pratt answered the question some may be asking about his pricey accommodations.

“Why is he spending $1,200 a night? Why couldn’t he stay somewhere for $300 a night? Well, the answer to that question is not as pretty as any of us may like to hear,” he said. “Most people simply presumed that I was being a bougie spoiled brat, and that I was abusing campaign funds. … At the time, I couldn’t explain the math to people, and my campaign staff told me I wasn’t allowed to divulge the real reason I had to stay there, but now that the election is coming to a close, I don’t need to listen to anyone anymore.”

According to Pratt, he endured “numerous death threats” to the point where he had to hire full-time security.

He described the Hotel Bel-Air as a “unique” property “surrounded with a fortress wall.”

“Unlike normal hotels, it is a very secure facility, which is why Presidents and Royalty like the Prince of Wales or Saint Thomas of Cruise feel comfortable staying there,” he explained. “When my security team dropped me off behind the walls of the Bel Air, they felt good about leaving me alone in the secure facility. Had I stayed anywhere else, I would have needed to book out 3 rooms for my team to maintain overnight security, which would’ve cost an additional $3,000 per night. Paradoxically, by this calculation, I was actually saving a ton of money by staying at the secure Bel Air; even staying at a Motel 6 would’ve cost me more money, and in a campaign…money is everything.”

Pratt said he appreciated having security “watching everything and everyone around me.”

“Now that there’s no campaign, I can’t afford that level of protection, even though I still deal with death threats and trespassers at my property, routinely,” the Guy You Loved to Hate: Confessions from a Reality TV Villain author claimed before promoting an app called Patrol.

Pratt continued, “This is the way of the future, and I’m doing everything in my power to keep my family safe. … I’m done leaving our lives in the hands of government. We are on our own.”

#3676. We Finally Know Who Made The Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Remake

Fans have speculated on which studio is leading the development of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake since it was first announced, and a new Ask the Developer feature from Nintendo appears to give us the answer.

The interviewees in Nintendo's online feature include longtime Zelda producer Eiji Aonuma and several members of Nintendo Entertainment Planning & Development (EPD) Production Group No. 3, which is the team behind the mainline Zelda games. In other words, the usual Zelda people are making the new Zelda game, as opposed to another studio like Monolith Soft or Grezzo.

Those other two studios have come up in fan discussions about the Ocarina of Time remake, due to their respective histories contributing to the Zelda franchise. Grezzo was behind the 3DS remakes of Ocarina of Time and Majora's Mask, along with the Switch remake of Link's Awakening. The studio also co-developed Echoes of Wisdom with EPD No. 3.

Monolith Soft, the Nintendo subsidiary behind the Xenoblade games, has taken more of a support role with Zelda games in recent years. The studio is credited with contributing to Skyward Sword, Breath of the Wild, and Tears of the Kingdom.

Fans had guessed that either or both studios were working on the Ocarina remake for Switch 2, theorizing that EPD No. 3 was working on a new, mainline Zelda game. Neither Monolift Soft nor Grezzo are mentioned in the first two parts of the Ask the Developer feature (parts 3 and 4 will be published on November 3), but it's still entirely possible that they could be involved in the production as support studios. We'll have to wait and check the credits when the game launches on November 5.

For now, be comforted knowing that development on the Ocarina remake is being led by veterans of the beloved series, satisfying the fan desire to know exactly who's making these Nintendo games.

#3675. I Enjoyed Backrooms, But Can We Finally Admit It Wasn't That Scary?

I have an annual tradition of watching the best horror movies, and given that Backrooms was so buzzed about earlier this year, I streamed it with my HBO Max subscription. I'd heard some people who saw it found it boring, and while I disagree on that front, I do think it isn't really scary.

The concept of "the backrooms" has existed on the internet for a long time, and I've seen it portrayed across many short films, video games, and horror stories. I wouldn't say I went into this movie with high expectations, but I certainly went in feeling like I'd leave feeling more scared than I was.

The problem, I think, is that I went into Backrooms expecting it to be a horror movie. As mentioned, people generally tackle this premise with a horror bent, typically with weird, deformed monsters and jump scares. This movie has zero jump scares, which bucks the trend of many modern horror movies, but I think it did it no favors.

All this to say, Backrooms is a fascinating thriller, and I really enjoyed the movie. Once I set aside the fact that I expected it to frighten me, I genuinely enjoyed the film and look forward to any future installments. In that way, it reminds me of The Silence Of The Lambs, which is another movie I'd associate with Halloween that isn't really that scary.

A sequel to Backrooms could, and certainly should, be much scarier. Now that the mainstream gets the general idea of how it all works, this is the time for director Kane Parsons to really flesh out how horrifying that concept is and what oddities can come from this space.

I've Been Looking Into Backrooms Theories, And Whoa, There's A Lot More To Unpack Than I Realized

As I mentioned before, we've already seen a lot of other works do this. A lot of what Parsons would need to add to a sequel is sitting there on the internet, and he has the power to make the mythology around it even scarier. It's what made it disappointing that the movie itself was more about being surreal rather than scary.

Without jump scares, Backrooms had me wondering how many people younger than me are genuinely terrified of a generic office layout from the 1990s. Or furniture that's clipped into walls and doors? We saw that all the time in video games growing up! That's not scary to me, that's bad graphics!

The good news is the movie did well and crushed it on streaming, so I think we're going to see the concept further evolve in the coming years. I'm fully on board with showing up for a sequel, but if this next one isn't scary, I don't think I'll stick around for the ride.

#3674. Doom Dev Says “We’re Doing Great” After Half The Studio Was Just Laid Off

Doom developer id Software was among the numerous Microsoft-owned game studios that cut staff recently as part of the big Xbox "reset." What's the vibe like internally at the studio in the wake of that? Studio co-director Marty Stratton said in a recent interview, "We're doing great."

He said he wasn't trying to "handwave" the layoffs, and isn't shying away from acknowledging that "half of our studio" was laid off, IGN reported. Stratton said the layoffs were part of a "deliberate effort" to ensure id Software would succeed.

Stratton is an executive at id Software, and his perspective on the situation no doubt differs from other people at the studio. He didn't share any commentary on what the vibes are like internally at id currently for other people who survived the layoffs.

Stratton also mentioned how the shift brought id and MachineGames closer together--the two studios had always been "very close," but now the pair are working closer "than ever."

"We're at a point with technology development that both teams are incredibly talented and have incredibly talented engineers and we're really on an amazing path that had started pre-[layoffs]. The studio's latest release was 2025's Doom: The Dark Ages, while MachineGames released Indiana Jones and the Great Circle in 2024. It's rumored that MachineGames is now making a new Wolfenstein game.

#3672. Marilyn Monroe and Arthur Miller’s Tragic Love Story

“I think you’re the saddest girl I ever met.”

“You’re the first man that ever said that. I’m usually told how happy I am.”

This exchange, from The Misfits, written by Arthur Miller, shows Marilyn Monroe drawing closer to something other than the “dumb blonde” persona for which Hollywood praised her.

After all, the actor—who was born in Los Angeles in 1926 and died in the City of Angels in 1962 at the age of 36—wanted to be taken seriously as a performer. She never fully identified with the image Hollywood created for her. She spent her limited free time enjoying uncharacteristic pastimes, as evidenced by one of her most famous photographs, which depicts her reading James Joyce’s Ulysses while donning a striped tank top, black shorts, and a deep, melancholic gaze.

Marilyn Monroe reads a book in her room at the Hotel Ambassador in midtown Manhattan, March 1955.

“A sex symbol becomes a thing. I just hate to be a thing,” said Monroe to Life magazine in 1962, reflecting on her strained relationship with Hollywood.

Miller, who was born in New York in 1915 and passed away in 2005, initially believed he would be a good partner for Monroe, whose life was marked by great successes, but also abandonment and her unfortunate inability to have children—one of the most painful issues for Monroe.

Monroe and Miller first met in 1950, when he was in Los Angeles with director Elia Kazan. It was Kazan who introduced them.

Monroe and Miller began talking, and he emphasized her potential to become a dramatic actor on New York stages. He struck a chord.

In the mid-1950s, the star left Hollywood and moved to New York to study, attending The Actors Studio and working with Lee Strasberg. She met with Miller again in the Big Apple, and in 1955, they began dating seriously, joining two seemingly distant worlds.

Marilyn Monroe and playwright Arthur Miller play with his dog Hugo,at Miller’s summer home on June 25, 1956.

Monroe felt respected by him, unlike the way she felt in Hollywood, which she once called “an overcrowded brothel, a merry-go-round with beds for horses,” in her unfinished memoir, My Story.

Miller, who had won the Pulitzer Prize in 1949 for Death of a Salesman, was captivated by her and ended his failing marriage.

The subsequent marriage between Monroe and Miller—her third marriage, his second—took place on June 29, 1956, in White Plains, New York. A few days later, a private Jewish ceremony was also held, following the actor’s conversion to Judaism.

The first major rift in their marriage stemmed from ongoing tension between public and private life. Miller wanted a more secluded, domestic life; Monroe wanted a family, but she was not willing to give up the career she had so painstakingly built.

For the 1957 film The Prince and the Showgirl—directed by and starring Laurence Olivier, with Monroe as the female lead and coproducer—the actor and her husband moved to England, where tensions rose.

Arthur Miller and Marilyn Monroe after their wedding.

Monroe found some of Miller’s notes, in which he expressed disappointment with their marriage and admitted to sometimes feeling embarrassed around his friends in the cultural world.

It was one of the hardest moments in their relationship: Monroe discovered that the man who seemed to recognize her talent and intelligence also viewed her through the very same lens from which she was trying to free herself.

In her own notebooks, she reflected on her fear of becoming “someone’s wife” and losing her independence.

Miller would later say that he wrote very little during the years of his marriage.

Monroe, meanwhile, was struggling to become a mother. During her marriage, she experienced a miscarriage, an ectopic pregnancy, and another spontaneous termination of pregnancy.

On the set of The Prince and the Showgirl, her difficulties increased: She often arrived late, struggled to work consistently, and her relationship with Laurence Olivier became strained.

In the background, Miller faced a trial, as he had refused to name Communist Party members and sympathizers. He was convicted of contempt of Congress in 1957, but the conviction was overturned the following year.

Marilyn Monroe and her former husband Arthur Miller as they leave Doctors Hospital on August 10, 1957, after she recovered from a 10-day hospital stay following an ectopic pregnancy.

Despite Monroe publicly expressing her support for her husband, the cracks in their marriage turned into chasms. Arguments, a lack of trust, disillusionment, drugs, alcohol, all of it became too difficult to contain.

The point of no return was another feature film, The Misfits, written by Miller for Monroe.

The desert setting where it was filmed didn’t help. Amid hellish temperatures, Monroe and Miller were no longer on speaking terms, even though they were staying at the same hotel. Intermediaries were needed just to get them to communicate.

It was during this shoot that Miller met the photographer Inge Morath, whom he would later marry in February 1962.

They divorced shortly after The Misfits was released in theaters.

After The Misfits, Monroe went through one of the most difficult periods of her life. In 1961 she was admitted to the Payne Whitney Psychiatric Clinic in New York. Joe DiMaggio intervened to have her transferred to another facility.

Marilyn Monroe’s photo shoot at Hollywood agent Johnny Hyde’s backyard in Beverly Hills, California, 1957.

Before her death, Monroe nevertheless continued to work, seek roles, and imagine a life different from the one others intended for her.

In a 1988 interview that aired on the Italian network Rai, journalist and writer Enzo Biagi asked Miller: “How do you want to remember Marilyn Monroe?”

He replied: “She made everyone believe she was very happy, but I didn’t believe it. She was very depressed, but she had the extraordinary talent of being able to mask her state of mind. #3671. Claude Code Just Got A New Rule: Stop Copying Other People’s Games

AI clones and vibe-coded copycat games have become a huge headache for developers recently, but it looks like an update to Anthropic's Claude Code's "rules" has been pushed out. Listed under "tengu_heron_brook," the tweak to the AI now directs it not to copy games and assets, and users cannot disable this setting.

Spotted by Chasm on X (via Game Developer), the full rule reads, "Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don't build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original". Anthropic's Addy Osmani added that "two sentences" were added to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5, to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game, as "using Claude to infringe IP " is against the company's policy. "Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working. We'll continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance."

AI clones have been running rampant for months now, as the tools have let pretty much anyone crank out copies of successful games in surprisingly little time compared to traditional methods of cloning a successful piece of work. This all came to a head during Steam Next Fest last month, when the demo showcase was flooded with low-effort games and AI slop. This has also led several developers to cancel demos outright, fearing bad actors could take the code, whip up a copy in Claude, and release it before their game ships.

Valve has vaguely mentioned that it's "aware of the situation" and that "a significant number of people are thinking about how to solve" the problem. At the same time, Valve has encouraged developers to focus on building communities and support for games, which isn't exactly an ideal solution. Creating a community around a game takes time, whereas AI slop clones can be generated fast enough to capitalize on virality, and in an ideal situation, make a quick buck for the prompter on the other end--just look at all the video games about needles in haystacks that have popped up recently, copying the viral success of Needle in a Haystack Simulator, which isn't out yet.

The rampant reverse-engineering got so bad that the creator behind Needle in a Haystack Simulator, NasNakarus, poked fun at it by teasing a joke mode for the game where players will have to sift through piles of cloned games to find the original.

While tweaking Claude is good news, it doesn't mean developers are out of the woods yet. Claude prompters will likely look for ways to work around the new restrictions, and if they're unsuccessful, other AI agents are available without the same safeguards.

#3670. GTA 6 Buying Guide: Get Ready For Sticker Shock

Rockstar's GTA 6 finally releases on November 19, and if you're looking to play the game, you'll also need a console--and those are more expensive than ever. Here's a quick buying guide to help you understand what you need and how much the items will cost. 

A console

First, you'll need a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X|S console. The least expensive option for buying a new system outright is the Xbox Series S, which costs $500. Unfortunately, that's $200 more expensive than the system cost at launch in 2020--there are a number macroeconomic and AI factors that drove prices up significantly.

A new Xbox Series X, meanwhile, costs $750 for a system with no disc drive, or $800 for a console with a disc drive. GTA 6 is not available on a disc, but having a disc drive may still be important to you for other games and media like DVDs and Blu-rays. 

Switching to PlayStation, the least expensive system on Sony's side is the $600 digital edition, scaling up to $900 for a PS5 Pro (with a disc drive). PS5 Pro, as the most powerful of these options, is likely to provide the best experience from a technical and graphical standpoint, although the gameplay itself should be identical across all platforms.

These are all prices for brand-new units, but Sony offers certified refurbished PS5 consoles starting at $500. A certified refurbished Xbox Series S, meanwhile, goes for $400. These are the prices from Sony and Microsoft directly, but you can find secondhand consoles at a variety of other retailers, along with places like eBay, Facebook Marketplace, and Craigslist. As usual, check your local or preferred retailer to see the latest prices.

New and certified refurbished consoles come with everything you need--including the system, controller, and power cords. You will need a TV or monitor, but the odds are good that if you're looking to play GTA 6, you probably already have one. 

People on platforms outside PlayStation and Xbox are out of luck, as GTA 6 has not been announced for Switch 2 or PC. A PC edition is expected to release in early 2027, but there is no word on a Switch 2 version. 

The game

To play GTA 6 you will need to buy GTA 6. The game's standard edition goes for $80, with its Ultimate Edition selling for $100. As mentioned, the game is not available on a disc. That being said, retailers are selling the $80 edition in stores, though you only get a code in the box. The $100 edition appears to be exclusive to digital storefronts.

The $100 Ultimate Edition includes loads of extras, including a variety of cosmetics and even in-game shops that people who buy the $80 edition cannot access. Since GTA 6 is a digital-exclusive game, there is no reason to worry about units selling out, but if you do want to preorder, you get the Vintage Vice City Pack and a free month of GTA+.

GTA 5 launched at $60 back in 2013--adjusted for inflation, that's about $85 today.

You will also need an internet connection to install GTA 6, since it's a digital only game. It's a beefy one, too, weighing in at a reported 201GB. Thankfully, preloading begins on November 12, a full week before the game launches. That means you'll be able to begin downloading it early in the hopes of being ready to go on November 19.

November 12 is also when GTA 6's code-in-a-box copies will be available to buy at physical stores. You're not getting a week of early access, though, as the game does not unlock fully until November 19.

Do you need PS Plus or Game Pass?

GTA 6 is a strictly single-player game, and as such, you likely will not need PlayStation Plus or Xbox Game Pass to play. Rockstar has yet to confirm this, however. 

Rockstar is surely going to release a new version of GTA Online at some point--some believe that will happen in early 2027. And at that point, you'll likely need a membership. But for launch, there is no online or multiplayer support, so we don't think a subscription to PS Plus or Game Pass would be required. 

Why no disc?

Neither Rockstar nor studio owner Take-Two have provided a reason for GTA 6 being a digital exclusive, but the answer seems pretty obvious: It's all about money. Rockstar makes more money from digital game sales, and having no disc eliminates the secondhand market. 

“A disc can be resold or rented a hundred times, and Rockstar earns nothing after that first sale," Rhys Elliott of Alinea Analytics said. 

The code-in-a-box strategy for physical games has been around for a long time already, and while people might complain online about the lack of a physical edition of GTA 6, the game is going to sell phenomenally no matter what, Mat Piscatella of Circana says.

Beyond these factors, consumer spending patterns have trended increasingly toward digital since the early 2010s. GTA 6 is such a large game in terms of its file size, so making it digital-exclusive also saves Rockstar and Take-Two money by not needing to print a second disc, if one was ever needed.

Full House might not be hailed as one of the best sitcoms of all time by many, but I have always been a massive fan of the show. I used to watch it every night on Nick at Nite and even own the entire series on DVD. I’ve always adored the Tanners and their extended family and can’t imagine any of them being played by any other actors; but it turns out that Lori Loughlin almost didn’t get to play Aunt Becky.

A majority of the Full House cast reunited at ‘90s Con in Connecticut and appeared on a panel discussing the show. During the panel, John Stamos shared his experience with the show’s creator, Jeff Franklin, when it came to casting Aunt Becky, aka his eventual long-term love interest on the show.

Lori came on at first, and I was like — I think we did some readings together before. I told [series creator] Jeff [Franklin], ‘I don’t know. She’s cute, and she’s adorable. I don’t think she’s tough enough to put Jesse in his place.’

Good casting can make or break a project, especially when it comes to the chemistry between two actors who are playing characters that are romantically linked. At the time, Full House wasn’t considered a hit by any means, so it makes sense that Stamos would want to get the casting right to ensure the show would continue.

While Stamos’ Uncle Jesse and Lori Loughlin’s Aunt Becky eventually became the best couple on the show, their relationship wasn’t always a walk in the park. Jesse was instantly smitten with Becky, as he was with most women on the show, but the same was not true for her character. Thus, it was important that Loughlin be able to play off Stamos’s character in order to build up that will-they, won’t-they tension.

Thankfully, the show’s creator didn’t listen to Stamos and did go on to cast Loughlin in the role. In turn, the When Calls the Heart actress proved Stamos wrong and put him and his character in his place on the first day of set.

Scene one, she came and she put me in my place fast. She had the perfect combination of this adorable, sweet girl. But, when it was time for me to get in trouble, you had no problem [playing] that out.

For those who don’t remember, Jesse meets Becky at the Tanner house and instantly tries to hit on her. Unlike most of the women who swoon at his feet, Becky challenged Jesse’s flirting attempts and even compared him to her baby brother, which gutted him. However, despite Becky’s apprehensions, she did end up falling for Jesse’s charm, and the two got together (for the first time) during the second season’s Christmas episode.

Hiring Loughlin turned out to be one of the best decisions, and the show steadily started to grow its fan base. It’s wild to think that she was initially only hired for six episodes and went on to become a fan favorite character. It turns out Aunt Becky was the missing piece all along.

#3668. Model Sahara Ray's Death Certificate Reveals New Details: Report

The death certificate for Sahara Ray has reportedly revealed new details about where the model died and more.

Ray’s remains are set to be cremated on November 10, with her mother’s Los Angeles home listed as the place of final disposition, according to the certificate obtained by TMZ on Tuesday, November 3.

The certificate also confirmed that Sahara died at age 34 on October 18 at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles. Her cause of death remains deferred.

Ray’s family previously announced her death in a statement on October 19.

“She passed away last night surrounded by family at the hospital,” the family told TMZ. “She was so loved.”

Sahara, the daughter of Australian pro surfer Tony Ray, was born in Australia and grew up in California. She gained fame through her modeling career and developed a large following on social media. She also launched a swimwear line called Sahara Ray Swim.

Sahara made headlines in 2016 when she was spotted vacationing with Justin Bieber in Hawaii. She has also reportedly been linked to singer and future Traitors star Cody Simpson.

In 2024, Sahara revealed she was diagnosed with Guillain-Barré syndrome, a rare neurological disorder in which the body’s immune system attacks the nerves and causes weakness, numbness or paralysis.

“My whole life changed in an instant,” she wrote via Instagram at the time. “So thankful for my family and doctors for helping me get stronger everyday. Attitude is everything.”

In a video, she added, “Right now, I’m paralyzed from the tops of my upper thighs all the way down to my feet. I can’t walk at all.”

Sahara’s condition improved over time, and she announced in August 2025 that she was expecting her first baby. She welcomed a daughter named Snow in January.

Sahara’s sister, Ruby Ray, paid tribute to the content creator via social media after her death.

“My beautiful big sister, Sahara,” Ruby wrote on October 19 alongside several throwback photos with Sahara. “The most vivacious, intelligent, hilarious, kind, empathetic and breathtakingly beautiful soul. A force of nature. A light so bright that this world feels impossibly dimmer without her in it.”

She continued, “Sahara has moved from this life into another, and I am left trying to comprehend how someone so full of life can no longer be here to live it.”

Ruby called her older sister “everything extraordinary about being human” and “the most incredible person to ever walk this earth.”

“How cruel it is to love someone so deeply and have nowhere for that love to go. To have a lifetime of memories behind you, but no more tomorrows together,” she continued. “I don’t think there are words in any language capable of holding the weight of this heartbreak. I don’t know how to make sense of a world that keeps turning when mine feels as though it has stopped. … I just want my big sister.”

#3667. Phantom Blade Zero Put Up Some Massive Sales Numbers

Developer S-Game's action-RPG Phantom Blade Zero launched on October 29 and had a massive start across PC and PS5.

The game sold more than 4 million copies over its first 72 hours. That works out to 926 units sold per minute or about 15.4 per second over the first three days.

"Thank you everyone from the bottom of our hearts for all the love and support," the studio said in a social media post.

The 4 million figure counts copies sold across both PC and PS5--the game is not available on Xbox. The game reached a record of 833,921 peak concurrent users on Steam on November 1.

The game's developer is based in China, and the majority of preorders for the game came from China, Taiwan, and Hong Kong.

Phantom Blade Zero's sales out of the gate are strong, but do not come close to another hit game from the Chinese game developer scene, Black Myth: Wukong. That game sold 10 million copies over its first three days. The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, meanwhile, sold 10 million copies in three days as well.

If you’re looking to get started, you can check out our Phantom Blade Zero guides hub for many walkthroughs on increasing your power and finding rare items.

Inside the NBA fans were hit with some major news last week, as longtime co-host Ernie Johnson confirmed his plan to leave the show at the end of the professional basketball season. Right now, many are simply taking the time to pay tribute to the man affectionately known as “E.J.” However, there are those who are also questioning what lies ahead for the show in the long run without Johnson. The man himself recently expressed his hope that the show will go on, and there’s also been an update on ESPN’s alleged feelings about that.

To put it mildly, Johnson is one of the mainstays of Inside, given he’s been hosting the show for 37 years now. 70-year-old Johnson announced his intention to exit the show nearly a week ago in a social media video that’s since gone viral. The veteran sports journalist confirmed that he wasn’t retiring from broadcasting entirely, though. He’ll continue to serve as a March Madness analyst and produce content under his 32 Bowties production company. Nevertheless, he’s stepping down from Inside as a way to “slow down a bit.”

Johnson recently caught up with Front Office Sports Tonight to discuss his big decision and plans for the future. When addressing what may lie ahead for his long-running basketball talk show, Johnson expressed optimism:

I don’t want to be blamed for ending Inside the NBA. I’m stepping away from my role on there. I would hope that they could continue the show in some form. And there are plenty of great studio hosts out there who could do what I do.

On paper, it would definitely make sense to keep the TNT-turned-ESPN sports show on the air, considering its popularity. It’s still hard not to wonder, however, how viewership may be affected by Ernie Johnson’s absence next season. Plus, there’s the fact that Charles Barkley has been discussing retirement again as well. With that, sources are now saying that ESPN has been giving the future some thought amid these developments.

Shaq Explains Why Inside The NBA Works, But I’m Just Loving The Ernie Johnson Detail He Revealed

Weeks before Johnson confirmed his intention to leave Inside, Barkley already indicated that his longtime co-star would do just that. The “Round Mound of Rebound” also said at the time that he was planning to exit the show after this current season as well due to him and Johnson being a “package deal.” Considering that Johnson and Barkley have shared the screen for over 25 years, their dual exits would mark a major shift. However, per FOS’ sources, ESPN remains committed to keeping the show going even without the pair.

That would theoretically leave co-hosts Kenny Smith and Shaquille O’Neal alongside two others. Interestingly, since Johnson shared his news, Barkley hasn’t said anything more about whether he’ll ride off into the sunset as well. Johnson was also asked about Barkley’s plans when he appeared on FOS Tonight, and he had this to say about him:

As for what Chuck is going to do, I have learned many many moons ago, you never try to predict what the Chuckster is going to do. But he and I have had a lot of conversations in the past about what we’re going to do, so I will leave that final word to him.

If any other Inside the NBA fans are like me, they’ll be waiting with bated breath for Charles Barkley to deliver a definitive decision. The fact that Ernie Johnson is leaving (for some well-deserved time with his loved ones) is already tough to think about, so Barkley’s exit would also be a lot. At the very least, though, it’s encouraging that ESPN is reportedly still aiming to keep the show on the air for the foreseeable future.

#3662. Former Xbox Exec Shares Her Side Of The Story After Mysterious Depature

Helen Chiang, the veteran Xbox staffer who got promoted in July and left the company amid mysterious circumstances just recently, has shared her side of the story--but her response doesn't close the book on this saga.

In a LinkedIn post titled "Clarity is Kindess," which itself is a reference to her former boss (and Xbox CEO) Asha Sharma's much-ridiculed and cringey mantra, said it's "not accurate" that she was "fired for a policy violation" as multiple reports said.

Chiang said she will not "turn this into a play-by-play" and reveal the specifics, but she wanted to speak out to dispel rumors. "What has been said about my departure, and what has been left unsaid, has created a picture of me that I hardly recognize."

She went on to "set the record straight" by claiming she did not leak confidential company information to the press as some had speculated. "I have never communicated with any journalist outside the limited, company-authorized interviews I’ve done as part of my job," she said, adding that this includes having no contact with any journalist who reached out to her before today to ask for her side of the story.

Chiang went on to say she did not leave Xbox to join a competitor. "You don’t spend two decades somewhere without developing a deep loyalty to the people, teams, and businesses you’ve helped build," she said

"Xbox was never just another stop in my career. My end game was always to keep building here," she said.  

That may all be true, but it's also unquestionable that people regularly spend lengthy periods of their career at one company, in high-level positions, and then move to other companies.

Third, Chiang said she "did not engage in discrimination, bullying, harassment, insider trading, embezzlement, or other fraudulent activity."

"I stand by my record: both the results I delivered and the way I have treated people throughout my career. I won’t let speculation define my character or erase that record," she said.

Chiang added that she did not leave Xbox because she was "passed over for a bigger role." She said that since having children, she became more "intentional about how I define ambition and success." She said she has purposefully not sought out bigger roles or jobs with more responsibilities; she said she hadn't interviewed for a job since 2011.

"My reputation and results paved the way for the opportunities that followed. I went where the company believed I was needed and where I could have the greatest impact," she said, adding that she did not ask to become Xbox's first-ever COO.

"I believe in fairness, accountability, and holding ourselves to the standards we expect of others. Those standards only mean something when they’re applied consistently," she said.

Chiang said she has "serious concerns" about how those standards were applied in her case, and she said those concerns "deserve to be taken seriously."

"I share this because I don’t want my departure reduced to an inaccurate story about incompetence, ambition for the next big job, or a Nelson-level scandal. My story is about staying true to your core values, especially when it is hard," she said. "That’s the legacy I hope to leave behind."

Chiang's statement doesn't spell out the specific nature surrounding her departure from Xbox, so many will naturally want more answers. Those could come in time, as Chiang said this is "not the whole story."

Another former Xbox executive, Shannon Loftis, commented on Chiang's post to say she is "Team Helen all the way." Loftis said she wonders who may have leaked the "false information" about Chiang and what their motivations may have been. In any event, she says it shows a "loss of moral character and 'clarity' in leadership at Xbox."

"A real leadership team would have relentlessly pursued the 'leaker' and taken appropriate action because 'confidential personnel matters' actually are bases for defamation lawsuits," she said. "It's a clownshow up in there and I feel terrible for anyone that still has to deal with it."

A spokesperson for Microsoft told Windows Central that the company does not “discuss individual personnel matters.”

According to a source speaking to Eurogamer, Chiang was “terminated for policy violations.” The Verge’s Tom Warren backed this up, saying Chiang was cut loose due to a “policy violation,” but the exact nature of that is unknown.

In July, Sharma announced that Chiang would become Xbox’s first-ever COO, with “end-to-end” responsibility for the financial future of Xbox’s content, hardware, platform, and services.

Chiang had worked at Microsoft for 20 years, in that time playing a key role in the creation of Xbox Live and later shepherding Mojang and the lucrative Minecraft franchise. As COO, Chiang was expected to “bring our businesses together under one operating model, making sure we make clear investment decisions, learn from our successes and failures, and hold ourselves accountable for results,” Sharma said.

For her part, Sharma said she will have an update to share on the COO position at Xbox at some point, but she didn’t divulge more.

The Xbox business was “not healthy” when Sharma took over, she said, and Chiang no doubt had a challenging road ahead of her. As for now, however, people can only speculate as to the real reason she left Xbox.
