      • Stormstrike: Now deals 150% normalized weapon damage, up from 100%. Cooldown reduced to 6 seconds from 8 seconds.
      • Mental Dexterity: Now increases the Shaman’s Attack Power by 50/100/150% of Intellect, up from 33/67/100%.
      • Flurry: Now increases attack speed by 6/12/18/24/30%, up from 5/10/15/20/25%.
    • Restoration
      • Riptide: Mana cost reduced by about 40%. Cooldown increased to 12 seconds from 6 seconds. Riptide no longer deals any initial healing, just healing over time.
  • Warlock
    • Spellstones now correctly only increase Shadow damage (was increasing Shadow and Fire damage).
    • Pets now gain 2 Health per point of Master’s Stamina (was 7.5 Health per point of Master’s Stamina).
    • Bane of Agony now correctly dynamically updates its damage.
    • Drain Soul: This chance for this spell to grant a Soul Shard on dealing damage (not a kill) has been reduced significantly.
    • Affliction
      • Amplify Curse now correctly affects Curse of Exhaustion and Bane of Agony.
      • Improved Drains: Now increases Drain Mana’s amount of Mana drained but no longer increases Wrack damage.
      • Wrack: Spell damage coefficient doubled, to match the expected coefficient per cast time of 0.286 per second. Base damage per second now increases with each level by 2.5. Base damage per second at level 60 effectively increased from 36 to 86.
    • Destruction
      • Shadow and Flame: The damage bonuses from this talent now increase Fire or Shadow damage by 4/8/12/16/20%, up from 2/4/6/8/10%.
  • Warrior
    • Fixed an issue with the tooltip of Victory Rush incorrectly displaying the amount of damage it would deal.
    • Defensive Stance: Threat bonus increased from 30% to 80%.
    • The cooldown of Slam has been reduced to 15 seconds (was 18 seconds).
    • Arms
      • Improved Tactical Mastery changed to a 3-point talent granting the ability to retain 5/10/15 additional Rage when changing stances (was a 5-point talent granting 3/6/9/12/15 Rage retention).
      • Two-Handed Weapon Specialization changed to grant 2/4/6% increased damage when using a two-handed melee weapon (was 1/2/3% increased damage).
      • Bloodthrill changed to a 2-point talent granting your Main Hand melee attacks against enemies afflicted by your Rend a 10/20% chance to allow an activation of Overpower (was a 5-point talent granting a 4/8/12/16/20% chance).
      • Improved Slam’s reduction to Slam’s cooldown changed to 2.5/5 seconds (was 3.0/3.0).
    • Fury
      • The Blood Craze and Gore Drinker talents no longer generate threat when restoring Health to the Warrior.
      • Blood Craze will no longer activate when sitting.
      • Booming voice now also reduces the Rage cost of Piercing Howl by 5/10/15/20/25%.
      • Enrage moved to Row 3 (was Row 4).
      • New Talent: Reckless Swings. Row 4. 1 Point. 15 second cooldown. Costs 25% of base health. Your next 4 melee attacks generate 5 additional Rage. Lasts 8 seconds.
      • Gore Drinker moved to Row 5 (was Row 6) and is connected to Blood Craze now instead of Enrage.
      • Death Wish is no longer required for Flurry.
      • Flurry changed to a 3-point granting 10/20/30% increased attack speed for 3 swings after a critical strike (was 5 points granting 5/10/15/20/25% increased attack speed).
      • New Talent: Improved Whirlwind. Row 6. 2 Point. Passive. Reduces the cooldown of your Whirlwind ability by 1/2 seconds and increases the damage it deals to the closest enemy by 15/30%.
      • Bloodthirst now has Death Wish as a required talent.
    • Protection
      • Defiance: Threat bonus increased to 7/13/20% from 5/10/15%.

Player versus Player

  • In the Darkspear Islands battleground, dropping the flag no longer places the “Recently Dropped Flag” debuff on the player who dropped it.

Races

  • Dwarf
    • Earth Fury (2% increased critical strike damage and healing) removed.
    • Added: Artisan’s Precision - Increases hit chance with spells and attacks by 1%.
  • Human
    • Ruthless now increases critical chance by 1% (was 2%).
    • Human Spirit now increases Spirit by 10% (was 5%).
  • Orc
    • Savage removed (1% increased critical strike chance).
    • Command re-added, increasing Warlock and Hunter pet damage by 5%.
    • Blood Fury’s cooldown reduced to 2 minutes (was 3 minutes).
  • Skyborne
    • Wind-Blessed Haste bonus reduced to 2% (was 3%).
    • Read Leyline now increases Mana and Health regeneration by 50% (was 100%), with a 15-second duration. This ability cannot be used while Innervate is active, and will be replaced by Innervate as a more powerful effect.
    • Using Read Leyline at a Ley Line now also grants “Attuned” for 1 hour. While Attuned, the benefit of Read Leyline is increased to 100% regeneration increase. Attuned persists through death, and is removed upon entering a raid.
    • Skysight is now a 15% increased movement speed (was 10%), with a 15-second duration.
    • Using Skysight at an elemental convergence now also grants “Charged” for 1 hour. While Charged, the benefit of Skysight is a 30% movement speed increase. Charged persists through death, and is removed upon entering a raid.
  • Tauren
    • Plainsrunning now grants 2% movement speed per stack (was 1%), for a total max increase of 60% (was 30%).
    • Plainsrunning no longer increases mounted movement speed.
    • Endurance no longer provides any modifiers beyond 5% increased Health (no hit chance or critical damage modifiers).
  • Troll
    • Berserking duration increased to 15 seconds (was 10 seconds).
  • Undead
    • Cannibalize can once again be used while immune to Physical damage.
    • Fixed an issue where Touch of the Grave was not activating frequently enough.
    • Fixed an issue where Touch of the Grave was leaving a beam visual behind.
    • Touch of the Grave internal cooldown reduced to 15 seconds (was 25 seconds).

Gamepad Support

  • Gamepad Support has entered a complete functional state.
    • In World of Warcraft: Forever, all major gameplay and core user interface experiences can be played with a controller, including movement, spells, interactions, UI navigation, etc.
    • Gamepad settings can be customized through Edit Mode and the Options menu.
  • Action Bars
    • AoE items bound to the Gamepad Action Bar can now be used and placed at a targeted location.
      • Press the Action Bar button again to confirm placement, consistent with ground-targeted AoE spells.
    • Fixed an issue where changing the current keyboard and mouse Action Bar page would cause Gamepad Action Bar buttons to be offset.
    • Fixed an issue where Gamepad Action Bar settings were not immediately reflected while in Edit Mode.
  • Add-ons
    • Improved Gamepad UI compatibility with user-created add-ons to reduce the likelihood of add-on conflicts causing interface issues.
  • Bags and Inventory
    • Fixed an issue where Gamepad focus could move away from the inventory after confirming or canceling the destruction of an item.
    • Fixed an issue where horizontal Gamepad navigation could behave incorrectly when moving between bag columns of different heights.
    • Fixed an issue where navigating the inventory with a Gamepad during a trade could cause a Lua error.
    • Fixed an issue where opening individual bags with the keyboard and mouse UI could cause a Lua error after switching from the Gamepad UI.
    • Improved bag management when using a Gamepad.
    • Improved the Gamepad Bag UI.
      • Added updated visuals and clearer bag states.
      • Added remaining bag space and ammo count indicators.
      • Improved bag prompts and interactions.
      • Improved Keyring navigation and highlighting.
      • Improved the inventory search layout.
  • Character Select & Ruleset Selection
    • Added Gamepad support for navigating and interacting with ruleset selection screens.
    • Fixed an issue where newly created characters were not automatically selected when returning to the Character Select screen while using a Gamepad.
  • Cinematics
    • Added Gamepad support for skipping or exiting cinematics.
  • Combat and Targeting
    • Added Gamepad support for targeting a previously assigned Focus Target.
      • LB + RB + Face Down can be used to select your Focus Target.
      • The target context menu displays Clear Focus when your current target is also your Focus Target.
    • Friendly corpses can now be targeted with a Gamepad.
      • Friendly Analog Targeting can target friendly corpses.
      • Friendly Tab Targeting can target friendly corpses.
    • Improved Gamepad targeting for critters.
      • Hostile Analog Targeting can target critters.
      • Soft Targeting can target critters.
    • Improved Gamepad targeting of enemy players.
      • Enemy players can no longer be selected by Friendly Analog Targeting.
      • Enemy players can be selected by Hostile Analog Targeting regardless of PvP flag status.
    • Units behind the player can now be selected with Analog Targeting when they remain visible on screen.
    • Feign Death units that remain attackable can now be targeted if and only if the Gamepad reticle is positioned over them.
    • Fixed an issue where certain attackable enemies could incorrectly display an Interact icon when using a Gamepad.
    • Fixed an issue where looting or closing the loot window could leave a corpse incorrectly locked as the player’s target.
  • Flight Paths
    • Added Gamepad support for ending a flight path early using the Back/Cancel action.
      • Players will dismount at the next available flight point.
  • Navigation and Focus
    • Fixed an issue where Gamepad focus could be lost from the Options panel after closing a graphics settings confirmation dialog.
    • Updated popup behavior so non-user-initiated popups no longer automatically steal Gamepad focus.
      • These popups can be explicitly focused using the View/Select action or equivalent controller input.
    • Updated Gamepad navigation prompts to use LT and RT button indicators when navigating between supported UI panels.
  • Pets
    • Added Gamepad support for the Pet Move command.
      • Pet placement can be confirmed using the Interact button or by activating the ability again.
  • Professions
    • Fixed an issue where Gamepad users could not use the Train action at Profession Trainers when a skill upgrade was the only available option.
    • Fixed an issue where the Gamepad prompt for removing a Profession did not indicate that the button needed to be held.
  • Quests
    • Fixed an issue where viewing quest details in a different map region with a Gamepad could cause a Lua error.
  • Swing Timers
    • Fixed an issue where the Off-Hand Swing Timer could fail to appear after logging in on dual-wielding characters.
  • Tooltips and UI
    • Added Gamepad support for adjusting opacity in the Color Picker.
    • Fixed an issue where Gamepad LB and RB prompts could incorrectly appear in the Equipment Manager while using the keyboard and mouse UI.
    • Updated Gamepad tooltips to remain visible rather than allowing them to be toggled on or off with the controller.

Items

  • Bags
    • Bags will no longer automatically equip into available bag slots and must now be manually equipped by the player.

Quests and World

  • Adjusted respawn rates for many different areas in the world.
    • Developers’ notes: Our goal with these adjustments is to properly support large player volumes at launch, so that players aren’t hitting hard bottlenecks and can continue to enjoy the game. Some contention for spawns is expected and part of the experience - it is not our goal to remove that. These adjusted rates are generally on the faster side in lower-level zones - with starting zones being the fastest - and gradually fall to slower rates as you level up, consistent with when players naturally spread out across the many zones available in WoW Forever. Once the initial launch surge of low-level characters has settled down, we will adjust the lower-level zones down to more typical rates.
  • Adjusted experience values on various quests.
  • Adjusted pre-requisites and level settings on some quests to improve flow across the world.
  • Added mouseover tooltips for objectives on various quests.
  • Added missing point-of-interest markers and adjusted incorrect ones on various quests.
  • Fixed incorrect zone sorts in the quest log on various quests.
  • Fixed various quests where destroying the associated item would not abandon the quest, and vice versa.
  • Fixed an issue where some satyr were classified as humanoids instead of demons. They are now 100% more scared of Paladins.
  • Alterac Mountains
    • Fixed an issue where Dalaran Summoners were really amazingly good at summoning and would summon until their little hearts couldn’t summon anymore. And then they’d summon some more anyway.
  • Barrens
    • You can now speak to Rethgar Deathgate to begin the event for “Counterattack!” if it is not currently active.
    • The Alliance Outrunners now spawn in random locations.
  • Darkshore
    • The quest “Holy Diver” now gives an XP reward.
  • Mulgore
    • Gloomrise Hatchlings now give lower XP, commensurate with their lower health values.
  • Orgrimmar
    • Fixed an issue during “Hidden Enemies” where the Lieutenant’s Insignia would remain in inventory after quest completion.
  • Ruins of Lordaeron
    • Ruins of Lordaeron dungeon quests now consistently require a minimum of level 15 to start (was a mix of 15 and 16), and some pre-requisites have been adjusted.
  • Teldrassil
    • The Cleft - There are now slightly fewer spiders in this area for the quest “Twisted Hatred”.
  • Wetlands
    • Fixed an issue where Carnage reset near the end of the fight for the quest “Carnage”.
    • Fixed an issue during “Destruction in Deadmines” where Alba Fairmoon would become unavailable to turn-in the quest.

#3627. Riley Green Just Picked The Only Singer He Could To Continue On The Voice After THAT Performance

I Didn't Expect Adam Levine To Get So Emotional With Another Coach On The Voice, But His Reason Was Totally Valid

Fans Aren’t Sure If A Survivor 51 Castaway Is Getting A Winner’s Edit Or Being Set Up For Heartbreak

I Totally Get Why Riley Green Is Excited For The Voice's Live Shows And How It Impacts One Brutal Element Of The Show

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

A standing ovation from all four coaches turned one The Voice singer into a frontrunner.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Spoiler alert! This story discusses Cut Week on The Voice Season 30, which aired November 2. Episodes are available to stream the day after they air with a Peacock subscription.

Season 30 of NBC’s long-running singing competition The Voice, currently airing on the 2026 TV schedule, is heating up with the first ever Cut Week. Due to audience demand, the Live Shows are back with six weeks of live competition, but before the singers could get to that next step, coaches Kelly Clarkson, Queen Latifah, Adam Levine and Riley Green had to make the biggest elimination in one week ever in the history of the show.

To get into the specifics, Cut Week saw each coach send two artists straight through to the Live Shows while the remaining five had to sing their hearts out as they battled for the last remaining spot. That’s three singers for each coach going through to the next round, with one additional pick made by America to round out the Top 13. While some coaches agonized over who to fill their final slot with, The Voice newbie Riley Green had the easiest selection of the night.

This latest episode breezed by, as five singers for each team, 20 in total, gave everything they had to their performances in the attempt to win their individual coach over. The thing that surprised me the most about this new twist that was replacing the Knockouts, also known as Adam Levine’s least favorite part of the competition, was that each artist sang on a level where any of them were deserving of being sent through to the Live Shows. I’ve got to say, Cut Week was painful, with more than half of each team getting dropped all at once and having to say goodbye to truly talented competitors.

For me, the most shocking decision was the Maroon 5 frontman choosing to let Brandon Diaz, his steal from Team Queen, slip through his fingertips. Not to take anything away from Dakota Cohen’s performance of “Hemorrhage (In My Hands),” which was a worthy rock rendition that had Queen Latifah singing along.

However, Brandon’s version of “Dare You to Move” showcased expertly skilled vocals, and they prove he has what it takes to win. Not only that, but performance also ahd the Equalizer star and American Idol winner giving Brandon a standing ovation. That’s why I couldn’t believe Levine didn’t send him through to the next round.

While Riley Green didn’t get every single country singer on Season 30 for his team, he came pretty close, often pulling out all the stops to get them to choose him as their coach. From the beginning, 19-year-old Joe Henley has been a stand-out, so it was surprising when he didn’t get one of the automatic spots for the Live Shows. But his rendition of the Keith Whitley song “Don’t Close Your Eyes” was so heartfelt from the first note to the last that he earned the only four coach standing ovation of the night.

While the Marshals guest star said he thought he knew he was going to pick before Joe took the stage, Kelly Clarkson declared that she would be mind blown if he didn’t make it to the finale. It made Green’s decision to put Joe Henley through an absolute no-brainer, because he really could end up winning the season.

After the craziness of Cut Week, what I’m most curious about with next week’s episode is to learn who America will pick out of everyone the coaches eliminated. Clearly, I’m rooting for Brandon, but there wasn’t one bad performance from the 16 remaining singers. On that note, we’ll see how that turns out.

While we already know the competition series will be shaking things up with Season 31’s The Voice: Celebrity, we won’t learn who Season 30’s winner will be until December. So, be sure to keep tuning in to NBC on Mondays at 8 p.m. ET until then.

#3626. GTA 6 Is Getting A Physical Map–Here’s How To Get One For Free Or Very Cheap

Rockstar Games has confirmed more details about Grand Theft Auto 6's impending release on November 19, including more information about physical goodies. While the game itself won't be available on a disc, Rockstar is offering a printable physical GTA 6 cover art poster and a map of the game's setting, Leonida.

The poster and Leonida map will be available for free as digital downloads on GTA 6's official website on November 19. A double-sized physical version of the poster will be available "shortly after launch" from the Rockstar Store for 99 cents. Alternatively, it's free with any purchase from the Rockstar Store.

Back in the day, Rockstar used to include fold-out posters in the box for GTA games featuring the game's cover art and map. But GTA 6 is a digital-only game. Players can buy a physical GTA 6 box at retail stores, but it won't include a disc, only a code for a digital download. Rockstar hasn't said if it will include anything extra in the box.

Some retailers are apparently trying to sweeten the deal to encourage people to buy from them. It was recently reported that Walmart orders of GTA 6 will include some kind of "surprise." When the Switch 2 released, some Walmart orders for the console included "game-ready" snacks like soda and chips.

In other news, Rockstar just recently announced when GTA 6 preloading begins and when the game unlocks--players in the US will be among the last people in the world to get in.

#3625. How Greg Brockman’s Wife Anna Became a Trump and MAGA Mega-Donor

It was weeks before the election and spirits were low in MAGA’s top ranks. The president’s approval ratings had plunged to historic depths. Polling suggested his endorsement had become an albatross for many of his preferred candidates. And so Donald Trump had retreated to the gilded comfort of Mar-a-Lago to attend to “matters of national importance,” including, on October 17, a candlelit dinner with some of his most loyal supporters.

At the head of the table were just four seats: Google cofounder Sergey Brin, President Trump himself, OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman, and his wife, Anna Brockman.

Anna Brockman, Greg Brockman, President Donald Trump, and Sergey Brin during a MAGA Inc. event at Mar-a-Lago. October 17, 2026.

The Brockmans, worth nearly $30 billion, have used their wealth to become the 16th-biggest political mega-donors this midterms cycle: Last year, the couple donated a combined $25 million to MAGA Inc. and $25 million to the pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future. Greg has said that he and his wife are “single-issue donors,” their lone cause being AI, the technology he’s helped build. “It’s not popular,” he recently acknowledged, so “we really want to support politicians who really lean into [it].” And it has been “we” at each of these turns—the Brockmans working in tandem toward a shared vision of the future.

Yet despite Anna Brockman’s frequent presence amid the backdrop of this pivotal scene in history, next to nothing has previously been reported about her. When The Wall Street Journal profiled Greg Brockman in May, they wrote of his elusive wife, “She is intensely private: almost no information, including her maiden name, is available online.”

Anna Chang has an unlikely past—one that raises some new questions. How did a onetime registered Democrat and ambitious tech worker who “loves everything that positively changes the world” become the retired wife of one of the wealthiest men on earth, Donald Trump’s frequent guest, and one of the single-largest donors seeking to hasten a future where artificial intelligence is developed with minimal regulatory oversight?

Sources close to the Brockmans and to OpenAI suggested that Anna is no bystander, and is worthy of scrutiny as a significant player herself. “She’s not a silent sidekick to Greg,” says one AI industry insider. “She is a force.”

When Greg and Anna met at a Silicon Valley dinner party in 2018, Greg said they “instantly connected.” She was the daughter of Korean immigrants, and he had a long-standing reverence for Korean culture: He has a black belt in tae kwon do, and even attended Korean summer camp as a teenager, picking up some of the language. They had also both worked at the payments-software start-up Stripe in the 2010s, though their tenures never overlapped. (Both Greg and Anna Brockman declined Vanity Fair’s request for comment for this story.)

In 2015, Greg had left his position as Stripe’s chief technology officer to cofound OpenAI with 10 fellow visionaries out of his San Francisco living room. A gifted and relentless coder, he muscled his way through seemingly impossible projects in the hopes of eventually achieving artificial general intelligence, or AGI (the point when the technology can match or exceed human-level capabilities at every possible task). He sometimes clocked 90-hour workweeks. Greg’s colleagues from over the years describe him as fiercely competitive, not just with work projects but also with hobbies like running and weight lifting.

Anna was a quirky and exuberant animal lover from Texas—one source estimates she and her husband live with over 20 animals—who had worked for AmeriCorps mentoring working-class students after graduating from Wesleyan University, well known as an ultraliberal school. (In a total coincidence, I discovered midway through reporting that Anna and I had overlapped there during our college years.) When she became one of the first 100 or so employees at Dropbox, her idealism persisted. In an introduction to her new colleagues, she told them she spent her free time “taking on adventures to help save the world.”

While a source close to Anna said she doesn’t drink alcohol, sources who’ve spent time with her said she has sometimes drawn attention for her juvenile humor and unconventional manner. She “curses like a drunken sailor,” said one. Another described her as “fratty.”

Early in the Brockmans’ relationship, Anna experienced a series of mysterious health mishaps. The couple spent years visiting doctor after doctor, and eventually discovered she had Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (hEDS). Greg has also said that she has Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS) and Mast Cell Activation Syndrome (MCAS). She believed that with the right AI tools, her arduous investigation might have been made much simpler. “Her whole passion for AI is driven by this medical journey,” said her friend and former colleague Sujay Jaswa.

In her late 30s, Anna was also diagnosed with autism. “Her autism can come at a cost, one of which is requiring a lot of alone time (the fur kids and myself excluded) and downtime to rest and recover,” her husband wrote, referring to their many pets. “A beautiful trait of her autism is her deep connection to animals and attention to understanding their needs,” Greg posted on X.

He, too, required patience from his partner while he focused on his interior life. During their first holiday season together, he decided to teach himself machine learning, scratching out equations in a notebook. “She was there with me no matter how many planned activities it meant skipping,” he wrote on his blog. He described her as “someone who made me feel it was ok if I failed.” Greg said on the Tetragrammaton With Rick Rubin podcast that they even put off having children so that he could focus all his energy on AI.

Anna’s early adoption of AI tools helped her practically float up the corporate ladder, but it also opened the door to loftier visions. In a 2018 blog post, she wrote, “I believe in the power of AI to allow us to become more human, today and in the future, by alleviating monotony and opening the space for creativity and intuition.”

Meanwhile, Greg sounded like he was experiencing vertigo from the progress they were making at OpenAI. His journals from this period, portions of which were later made public as part of discovery for the Musk v. Altman trial, ricochet between self-doubt and megalomania. “No person should have control over what we’re creating,” he wrote in August 2017. Then three months later, he appeared to copy and paste a chat with an unknown correspondent into the journal document. “It is better for us to become increasingly kings of this industry,” one of them wrote. “Being the kings of AI is not so bad.”

In Anna, he found the ultimate support system. According to the WSJ, he took the other side of a bet with his then OpenAI colleague (and later Anthropic cofounder) Daniela Amodei, who wagered $100 that Anna was not the one. He won. As Greg put it, they “have been inseparable ever since.”

At the Musk v. Altman trial, Anna was by her husband’s side almost every day. Some observers noted that she held his hand right up to the last second as she walked him to the witness stand. Sources who know the couple described Anna, 38, as “very devoted” and Greg, 38, as “the ultimate wife guy.”

When Anna and Greg got married in 2019, they held a civil ceremony in OpenAI’s office officiated by fellow OpenAI cofounder Ilya Sutskever. The ring bearer was a robotic hand.

As wife to the “wife guy” at the helm of one of the most powerful companies on earth, Anna has enjoyed a front row seat to scenes of such intrigue that they have inspired multiple books, and the highly anticipated upcoming film Artificial. (Cooper Hoffman, the actor who plays Brockman in the film Artificial, recalls director Luca Guadagnino’s guidance on how to approach the role: “Greg is all-American,” Guadagnino told him. “He’s like a cheeseburger.”)

The Brockmans attended the Met Gala in 2025.

While it isn’t uncommon for spouses and partners to turn up in the offices of start-ups, sources who’ve spent time with the Brockmans noted that by the late 2010s Anna was unusually engaged in his work life, having left her own job at the venture capital firm Basis Set Ventures. While, per The Information, Anna has never been formally employed at OpenAI, over the years she has appeared in live product demos; accompanied executives on trips, like one to South Korea to meet with local start-ups; and even been spotted at high-level meetings at the OpenAI office.

When OpenAI’s top executives were appointed drivers and private security, Anna would sometimes be spotted in the car with Greg, taking him to work, according to former colleagues.

As the money piled up, the relationships between the company’s early team—including Sam Altman, Greg Brockman, Ilya Sutskever, Jakub Pachocki, Mira Murati, and Dario and Daniela Amodei—began to fray. While the imaginations of many of their Bay Area peers ran wild with sci-fi visions of uploaded consciousness and unfathomable abundance, and AI doomsayers warned of extinction events, the Brockmans’ hopes for an AI future felt relatively pedestrian.

Greg was firmly in the pro-commercialization camp, according to OpenAI researchers who’ve worked with him, believing that above all, AI can empower individuals to transform their own lives. Anna, meanwhile, is driven by the “idea that AI for all is gonna take all these major social problems, like the extreme cost of health care and education [and] extreme inequality in access…and it’s gonna democratize all of it,” according to Jaswa.

And to do that, the Brockmans understood that AI leaders needed to win over the policymakers that, in their view, could stand in the way of AGI.

Following the release of ChatGPT in 2022, OpenAI’s founding team found themselves on the other side of overnight fame—at least in the insular tech bubble of the Bay Area. While some of the more socially awkward researchers chafed at the attention, Greg—who’d been promoted to president of the company—and Anna have seemed to bask in it.

The Brockmans have dined with Sylvester Stallone at the Kennedy Center, attended black-tie events at the White House, and even walked the blue carpet at the Met Gala, where Anna wore a black-and-white ruffled gown by Korean designer Ashlynn Park.

The power she’d been quietly amassing by Greg’s side played out in a more significant and dramatic way in November 2023, when the board of OpenAI removed Sam Altman from his position as CEO over concerns that he was untrustworthy. Sutskever, who was on the board, also compiled a memo detailing allegations against Greg, and Greg was removed from his position as chairman of the board (but allowed to stay on as president). When the board called Greg to inform him of their decision, the first thing he did was talk to his wife. He told her, “‘We have to leave.’ And she said, ‘Yes, we do,’” he said on the Tetragrammaton With Rick Rubin podcast. He warned her they would have to be prepared for his equity to disappear if he quit. “‘Still want to do it?’ And she said yes.”

But when the board began to reconsider its decision, Sutskever became the deciding vote. In an oft-repeated piece of OpenAI lore, Anna allegedly begged Sutskever in a tearful encounter to reconsider. (Sources familiar with the events have suggested that the impact of this encounter has been overstated.) According to the WSJ, when Sutskever decided to reverse his decision, Anna left him a cactus as a gift.

After a long negotiation over his place at the company, Sutskever left to start his own venture, Safe Superintelligence. “There were some deep and bitter things” that went down during this period, according to one high-level employee at the time.

After this dramatic inflection point, which has come to be known as the blip, Greg took a three-month leave of absence. This period allowed him to dedicate himself to a project he was passionate about: developing a biological foundation model for genome modeling and design at the Arc Institute—“a domain that’s very personally meaningful to both me and and to my wife,” he has said.

Meanwhile, the company had replaced nearly all the board members who’d risen up against Altman with what one former senior OpenAI employee called a “more loyal and ‘normie’” board who were supportive of the company’s commercial push.

The center of gravity began to shift in Greg’s direction, solidifying his place as Altman’s second in command, soon to be tasked with an even more fraught assignment: building political goodwill. What wouldn’t the billionaire couple do to help the technology that they consider vital to humanity’s future?

“He thinks big, but he is also very practical, kind of a realist,” Peter Welinder, OpenAI’s vice president and general manager, says of Greg. Others felt that his techno-optimism, and subsequent push into Washington to defend those ideals, is “naivete,” says the former high-level employee. “I don’t think he’s very carefully thinking through the political and power implications.”

When Donald Trump was reelected in late 2024, OpenAI found itself facing down a new threat. Elon Musk, an original cofounder of the company who left in 2018, had grown increasingly antagonistic toward his onetime colleagues while also growing close to the incoming administration. According to Kevin Roose’s The AGI Chronicles, OpenAI, and Altman in particular, feared political retribution from Musk, who now had his own competitor company in xAI, if he was allowed to take up all the oxygen in Washington. At the same time, OpenAI’s need for energy and compute had grown so insatiable that the company had no choice but to seek the government’s help. In an administration run on quid pro quo, OpenAI would have to make nice.

Brockman found himself uniquely well-positioned to lead the infrastructure-scaling bonanza, thanks to a preexisting relationship with Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum, who hailed from his home state of North Dakota. Greg was also “the most credible” face of the political donations, said one former OpenAI employee.

And so Greg and Anna Brockman became White House mainstays. They have attended state dinners for foreign leaders like Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman and Xi Jinping, and joined top tech executives at a White House event about the future of AI. Brockman, rather than Altman, flanked Trump during the signing of the White House Accord on Super Intelligence in September.

When the political pendulum began to swing back this summer, it began to appear as though whoever had made the call on those political donations might have made a severe miscalculation. Following a steady drumbeat of negative headlines about Leading the Future’s work and significant internal dissent among OpenAI employees, the Brockmans rescinded their second planned $25 million donation to the PAC. Greg wrote in a Slack message, obtained by The New York Times, that Leading the Future had become a “distraction” from OpenAI’s work.

When I reached out to OpenAI to discuss the Brockmans’ political giving, it directed me back to the Brockmans’ team. In an interview this October with Vanity Fair’s global editorial director Mark Guiducci, Altman said, “I did not ask him to donate or stop donating. He can make his own personal decision.” It seems the Brockmans’ donations are a hot potato no one is eager to catch.

Regardless, their $25 million checks have helped provide the funds to enable a torrent of preelection ads, including warnings like, “This is the final battle” to “liberate America from these villains, once and for all.”

Some observers of the company have come to believe that the plan was “to have Greg be the scapegoat if/when the Democrats come back into power, but to allow OpenAI to privately (with the White House) claim credit for the MAGA PAC donations with the Trump administration while privately (with employees) distance itself from them,” according to the former senior employee. (OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment.)

Meanwhile, Greg has returned more of his focus to the product realm, and he and his wife have found a less controversial way to spend their millions. When the couple found out that the Big Bear Valley habitat of two publicly beloved eagles, Jackie and Shadow, was under threat, they donated over $5.5 million to preserve the land this summer. “[Jackie and Shadow] inspire perseverance and a sense of connectedness to something greater,” Anna said of their donation.

“It was clear in talking to her that she loved her husband very much and that she loved the eagles,” says Jenny Voisard, the communications and PR leader for Friends of Big Bear Valley, of her experience working with Anna on the donation. They never talked about politics.

#3623. WoW: Forever Won’t Get More Class Balance Changes Any Time Soon

World of Warcraft: Forever is gearing up for launch with some major class balance changes, but don't expect any more for at least a month.

As detailed in Forever's launch patch notes, Blizzard is making some dramatic class changes, including major reworks to Rogue and Paladin talents, in time for release that will result in a big spike in player power. Blizzard said it has used all the data from the game's month-long beta to "get everything tuned to a reasonable place."

However, don't expect additional changes in the near future. Blizzard said it won't be making significant balance changes until sometime next month.

"With the exception of bugs and serious outliers, we don't plan on making big tuning changes between now and the opening of the raids next month," Blizzard wrote in its patch notes. "Once we have sufficient data from players leveling past 30 and engaging in a wide range of content, we expect that we will do a large tuning pass based on our data."

Forever's three launch raids will open December 9, meaning there will be a little over a month without class changes. But launch and its subsequent months will just be the beginning, Blizzard said.

"This is all merely a starting point for the classes in Forever, which will continue over the course of the months and years ahead just as they did following the original launch in 2004," Blizzard said. 

Blizzard is in it for the long haul with Forever, telling GameSpot in an interview it hopes the game will continue to receive updates for the next 10-20 years (or potentially forever). It recently announced its plans to release major Forever content updates every four months, as well as teased how its controller support will eventually lead to players being able to play the MMORPG on "whatever you want." 

WoW: Forever launches November 4, but you can make your character now. In other Forever news, Blizzards revealed it will be making major improvements to the game's divisive layering system, how it's avoiding the problem of "dead" servers, and announced big changes to racial abilities alongside its newly announced class changes.

I’ve been thriving off Marvel nostalgia thanks to repeated trips back to the age of Iron Man. First with VisionQuest, and now with some hilarious trivia. I’m always up for some fun BTS stories about the shared universe, but even I couldn’t have predicted how the MCU connects to spy guinea pigs. Yes, you read that correctly. So imagine my reaction when I heard the wild (guinea pig-related) story behind Jon Favreau casting one star for Iron Man 2.

Turns out, we have a family-friendly spy movie to thank for Sam Rockwell’s role as Justin Hammer. For those of you who don’t remember (or hasn’t strayed from the MCU re-watch list for Doomsday), back in 2010 Tony Stark dealt with two villains: Ivan Vanko (played by Mickey Rourke) and Hammer who was Vanko’s benefactor in his crusade against Iron Man. While the second movie doesn’t get as much love, it’s clear that the Galaxy Quest actor enjoyed playing the cheeky bad guy, and even has a connection to Justin Theroux who penned the script. He dished to Esquire on the unique way he landed the part while sharing BTS stories behind some of his popular roles:

Justin and I were friends, and I was dating Leslie Bibb and she had done the first Iron Man. And I went over to Theroux’s apartment just to get coffee, and he's packing a bag. And I'm like, ‘Where are you going?’ He's [like,] ‘I'm going to LA. I'm going to write Iron Man 2.’ I'm like, ‘Get the fuck out of here. I want to be in that. What's the part?’ said, ‘I want to be the bad guy. Let me be the bad guy.’ And he goes, ‘Yeah, yeah, OK, whatever.’

While he’s not involved in any upcoming Marvel projects, I’m glad he got to live out his dream. Not only did he get a part in the movie, he also got to play a bad guy. Justin Hammer has everything you love about Bond villains (plus Sam Rockwell’s cheekiness), and was the perfect charismatic foil to play off of Robert Downey Jr. Though what exactly do guinea pigs have to do with him landing the role? Well, Rockwell explains:

And then, like, six months later, a few months later, I’m doing G-Force, and Jon Favreau and I are in a room playing guinea pigs, and we’re like wrestling around with each other in the sound studio, and he says, ‘Hey, there’s this thing Theroux’s writing.’ I said, ‘Oh, is it Iron Man?’ So he said, ‘I got the Marvel guy coming. We're going to take the villain. We're going to split it in two and we're going to make one the fast talking guy and then sort of alpha. So they got me and Mickey to sort of do both do the villain sort of as two parts.

I shouldn’t be surprised by this story and yet I didn’t expect the two to connect while pretending to be guinea pigs. Am I the only one who can’t stop picturing Happy and Hammer running around pretending to be adorable rodents? Though Favreau has a gift when it comes to picking actors, as he ignored the pushback against RDJ and chose to back him as Iron Man anyway. At the time, he explained that he “just saw it” regarding RDJ in what would be his most famous role. Clearly something about Rockwell’s performance as Darwin (the no-nonsense leader of G-Force) that was perfect to play Hammer.

The actor gave a shout out to a memorable moment. Before you guess, it’s not when he’s fine-dining while interviewing Vanko. Turns out, when Hammer gave the gun demonstration, the actor had to use an earwig as they changed up the props right before filming. What apparently stood out most in the interview was Rockwell’s willingness to return to the MCU if asked. He’s just waiting to get the call. Although Hammer’s return would be the least surprising thing after VisionQuest Episode 6 blasted us back to 2008 with Faran Tahir reprising his Iron Man 1 character. Somehow I missed that casting news prior to watching.

At this point, Justin Hammer could easily come out of the wood works, and I wouldn’t be shocked to learn that he escaped from prison. This would be relatively simple to achieve, especially since our characters keep making trips to the island of Madripoor and it’d be believable that he’d hide out there. Plus, Tony’s rival would easily fit in with the lawless chaos.

So why not include a Benefactor that can face off against the Power Broker?

#3621. Ta-Nehisi Coates on Haley Stevens, Abdul El-Sayed, and the Right’s “Campaign of Hate”

When Michigan congresswoman Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Mike Rogers yesterday, she offered a curious framing. “I’m choosing country over hate,” Stevens claimed. “This is not anti-Muslim at all.”

Rogers, for his part, invoked Martin Luther King Jr.: “You cannot solve darkness with darkness; you have to solve it with light. You can’t solve hate with hate; you have to solve it with love.” For the site of their hard launch, the odd couple chose Perfecting Church, a Black church in Detroit, evidently seeking to exploit the aura of social justice implicit in the Black faith tradition.

Aura farming aside, it is very hard to square the claims of patriotism and love with the actual campaign that Stevens now supports. Indeed, since the moment Abdul El-Sayed triumphed in the Democratic Senate primary, Rogers has made his views of his opponent clear. “I spent years hunting terrorists and bringing Osama bin Laden to justice,” he claimed the morning after El-Sayed won. “Never in a million years did I think that I would be running against someone who believes America deserved 9/11.” (Never mind that Hasan Piker, not El-Sayed, said the 9/11 quote, which El-Sayed has disavowed.)

Indeed, a consistent theme of Rogers’s campaign has been the implication that El-Sayed is a tool for shadowy forces originating in the East. “The Muslim Brotherhood celebrated exactly one victory in the United States in the primary this year,” Rogers claimed. “Abdul El-Sayed’s.” As a factual matter, the attack is highly dubious. But facts are not the point, so much as the deployment of “Muslim” as a slur.

To understand this, one need only look to the overlord of the Rogers campaign, President Donald Trump. As is his wont, Trump delights in mangling El-Sayed’s name, referring to him as “Abduladadalalalala” or simply “Mohamed.” “Somebody said his name isn’t Mohamed,” Trump told attendees at a rally. “I’m the president, I can call him whatever the hell I want. To me, he’s Mohamed.”

The Trump theory of El-Sayed holds that his ascendance is being facilitated by the machinations of Wayne County, a “strictly Third World” jurisdiction that seeks to elevate to Congress a “jihadist” who shouldn’t even be eligible for “a seat on an airplane.” If seated in the world’s greatest deliberative body, El-Sayed, the theory holds, would execute his dastardly plan to ban Christmas and—you guessed it—impose Sharia law.

Trump’s attacks have been echoed and amplified by right-wing news outlets like Newsmax, which has lambasted El-Sayed as an “anti-Israel Muslim,” an “immigrant from another Muslim country,” and a Midwest variant of that other alien, Zohran Mamdani, the “socialist Muslim who’s always smiling.” For those too dense to catch the message, the Newsmax chyrons have helpfully driven home the point—“THE LEFT IS FORGETTING THE HEINOUS ATTACKS OF 9/11,” “DEMOCRATS DROOL OVER NON-WHITE SOCIALISTS,” “MUSLIMS TELL US THEY’RE TAKING OVER, AND THEY ARE.”

Lest one think that this bigotry is merely limited to the crude ramblings of unlettered ogres, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has stepped in to offer some intellectual heft to the attack. The Muslim Brotherhood, according to Kennedy, is responsible for not just the menace that is El-Sayed, but also the dark age that has fallen over the entirety of the Arabdom. “There’s 500 million Arabs in the world,” Kennedy claimed, “and yet they don’t produce science, they don’t win the Nobel Prize, they don’t win the Field[s] prize, they don’t win the Wolf Prize, they don’t produce the literature they used to produce.”

Again, facts aren’t really the point here, and there is no wisdom in debating a quack whose brain has literally been infected by a worm. Nonetheless, it is worth noting the particular history at work. During both his run for president and his time in the White House, Barack Obama endured his share of racist attacks. To Rush Limbaugh, Obama was “Barack the Magic Negro.” To Newt Gingrich, he was America’s “food stamp president.” At the Value Voters Summit, a vendor hawked “Obama Waffles,” a product featuring a racist caricature of the president on the packaging. The tagline was: “Point box toward Mecca for tastier waffles.” That last line deserves particular attention. Indeed, by 2016, the political scientist Philip Klinkner would find that the best way to discern whom a voter would support in the upcoming election was to pose a simple question—“Is Barack Obama a Muslim?”

Stevens, in joining Rogers, has allied herself with this odious culture war, one that is itself tied to a very real war. The campaign of hate, of which El-Sayed is the latest victim, has a simple goal: to render Muslims and Arabs more killable. The latter does not require the former. In 1953 the CIA backed a coup that overthrew a democracy in Iran. In 1965 it supported a coup in Indonesia, the country with the largest Muslim population in the world, that killed between 500,000 and a million people. During the Cold War, the justification for this death toll was the threat of communism; post-9/11, it is racism. In 2008, John McCain confronted a supporter and disputed the claim that Obama was Arab. “No, ma’am,” McCain told his supporter. “He’s a decent family man.” This moment is often referenced as an act of patriotism, and perhaps it was one. But the notion that “decent” people exist in one place, while Arabs exist in another, is the major premise for a syllogism of violent, chauvinist power—wedding parties droned, governments overthrown, schoolgirls bombed, and inconvenient people eliminated.

This long war on the Muslim and Arab world has reached its apogee in the concentration camp of Gaza, where every single bomb was dropped from a plane of American extraction. And the genocide is but the latest chapter in a book authored by Israel, a state whose own basic laws reserve full rights for its “decent” people and something less for everyone else. This is the state that Haley Stevens has claimed to literally see in her dreams. And it is ultimately the defense of this state that drove Stevens into the arms of Mike Rogers. From this perspective, Stevens’s defection isn’t a story about party intrigue. It is a story about Stevens waking up and choosing violence.

In the weeks since You Can See Everything hit the 2026 movie schedule and started tearing up the box office, it's no surprise that some of those tickets have been sold to former Theranos employees. Whistleblower Tyler Schultz spoke out shortly after the Nathan Fielder/Lance Oppenheim-directed documentary about the company’s founder, Elizabeth Holmes, was released, and now more employees are speaking out about their takeaways from the movie. Two of them recently spoke to The Times about it. Here’s what they have to say.

According to the article, former Theranos creative director Gage Clegg and former chief creative officer Patrick O’Neill saw the movie together, and they described their complicated feelings to the paper. O’Neill is glad that people are finally seeing the real Holmes, in his estimation, telling the paper:

No one’s asking me any more how I could possibly work for someone like that; people now understand it … I’m excited that the world is going to experience Elizabeth in the way that I did. People will finally understand her ability to persuade and to connect, and how that gave her such enormous power. [Fielder] fell for it, too.

Much has been said of Holmes’ ability to manipulate people, and some have said Fielder fell under her spell while living with her and her partner, Billy Evans, while he and Oppenheim shot the movie. Personally, I’m not sure he did, but it's easy to see how people fall for it when watching You Can See Everything. Clegg was more direct, saying the documentary:

Sees her as being kind of on the spectrum, a person who doesn’t understand regular people, as a way to garner sympathy and to make people think that maybe she didn’t really understand that what she was doing was wrong. That is crazy. The person I knew was smart, capable and decisive. She walked into the room and owned the room. She is a night and day different person from who was in Fielder’s movie.

As to whether or not they think people should believe the Holmes they saw in the movie, Clegg’s answer was clear: No. He told the paper:

Hearing her say that she didn’t know she was lying made me want to jump out of my seat in the cinema.

Clegg and O’Neill were not alone in pointing out both the deception and the role-playing they see in Holmes. A former in-house lawyer for Theranos (yikes!), Brad Arington, summed up seeing the movie the same way.

She’s always performing. She’s very convincing. I wasn’t going to fall for it again.

Whether or not Fielder fell under Holmes’ spell is one of the big questions the movie leaves audiences wondering. It’s even brought up in the movie itself when he is questioned by another star in the movie over whether he’d gotten too close to his subject.

In fact, the last scene in the movie, with Fielder and Holmes swimming together in the ocean, harkens back to an earlier scene when Holmes tried to convince Fielder to go on a swim with her. Fielder demurs, saying he doesn’t want to, but obviously did swim with her at some point. Was that Fielder reinforcing the notion that Holmes can sell anything to anyone? The film doesn’t answer that for us.

Like so much in the movie, we’re really just stuck asking more questions than getting answers, and for me, that is part of what makes the movie an Oscar contender, and one of the best movies of the year.

Hugh Scott is the Syndication Editor for CinemaBlend. Before CinemaBlend, he was the managing editor for Suggest.com and Gossipcop.com, covering celebrity news and debunking false gossip. #3619. WoW: Forever Shamans Are Protesting Class Changes After Being “Completely Ignored”

World of Warcraft: Forever just received a massive batch of class-balance updates ahead of launch that have boosted power across the board, but one group of players isn't happy with the changes: Shamans.

Developer Blizzard recently released Forever's launch patch notes based on feedback and data accumulated during the beta, resulting in a power spike for all classes and major reworks for classes like Paladin and Rogue. Shamans, too, received some significant changes, most notably the removal of a key Elemental specialization ability, Lava Burst, along with any interactions other abilities had with it.

It's that change, and other changes to specialization-specific abilities like Restoration's Riptide and Enhancement's Maelstrom Weapon, that have resulted in the WoW Classic Shaman Discord going into lockdown in protest. The entire server, which has around 80,000 members, has been made read-only, with a message declaring the reason for why it took what it described as such a "drastic measure."

"Community feedback gets completely ignored and class fantasies are getting destroyed," the server declared. "With this we intend to give them [Blizzard] a sign and show them that the community is not [happy] with how they approached our beloved class. Give us back our class and spec identities and fantasies."

While the protest is in regards to class changes in Forever specifically, the server is also home to Shaman discussions as they relate to other "classic" versions of the game as well, including WoW Classic and Mists of Pandaria Classic. As of writing, all of those channels are also locked and set to read-only. 

In a follow-up post, the server went into more detail about its complaints in regards to how Blizzard has approached Forever's Shaman design. It stated its complaints aren't about "damage output." It also made clear the server will re-open "regardless of the outcome," but that it felt like its feedback through "legitimate" channels were being ignored. 

The server then proceeded to list what it viewed as wrong with various ability changes for each Shaman specialization. It additionally called attention to what it called the "hybrid spell power issue," where spell power and intellect gear seems to be better for not only Elemental but also Enhancement, muddying the identity between the two specializations. 

Blizzard has previously said it doesn't want "hybrid" classes that can deal damage and heal, like Shamans, to deal more damage than dedicated DPS classes. Players in the WoW community refer to this idea as the "hybrid tax," something those running the Shaman Discord said they are fine with if it means Shaman class design is improved.

"Truthfully, hybrid tax us all you want if the result is a cohesive class with strong class fantasy elements that are actually represented in our playstyles," it said. 

This isn't the first time a WoW class Discord shut down in protest of how class changes. As pointed out by Wowhead, back in August 2025, the modern WoW Paladin Discord was partially closed in protest of the Retribution specialization's raid performance. In that case, only Retribution-specific channels were locked, and the entire protest lasted less than 24 hours. Blizzard did announce Retribution Paladin buffs shortly after, though it's unclear if those changes came at least in part due to the server protest or not.

How long the WoW Classic Shaman Discord remains in lockdown remains to be seen, but Forever launches November 4. Blizzard recently said it doesn't expect to make any more major class changes for at least another month.

#3617. This Custom Xbox-Inside-An-Alligator Console Is Actually One Big Ad For GTA 6

Given that Sony holds the marketing rights for Grand Theft Auto 6, Microsoft has had to get creative to promote the open-world crime game for Xbox--and the company's latest effort in that department goes big.

Say Hello to the X-Bite, a playable Xbox Series X console that was designed to look like it was swallowed whole by one of Florida's millions of alligators. Microsoft only made one of these ornate consoles, and you have to win a contest to get it.

Microsoft's blog post doesn't mention GTA 6 or Rockstar Games, but Xbox marketing boss Josh Munsee said the system has "pure Miami vibes," and that's a pretty obvious reference to GTA 6 given the game takes place in a stand-in, Vice City, for the popular Florida city. The blog post says the winner of the console can play "some of the biggest games of the year" using it, and that's no doubt another nod to GTA 6.

"This November, Xbox is heading to Florida--home to incredible wildlife, unforgettable places, and every now and then, stories you have to see to believe," Microsoft said in its announcement of the X-Bite.

The X-Bite is about five feet long, and the console itself sits inside the alligator, with the Nexus/Guide button illuminated through the gator's skin. The lucky winner will also get a custom Xbox controller with simulated bite marks on it.

The custom console was designed by creature animatronic specialist John Nolan Studio, which did work for The Witcher and Jurassic World Dominion.

Microsoft's fine print states that the gator console is a "custom fabrication" and wasn't made from a real alligator. "No actual alligators were used or harmed in the making of this console," Microsoft said. The estimated value of the console is $800, Microsoft said.

You can enter for a chance to win the X-Bite by following Xbox on X, Instagram, or TikTok, reposting the sweepstakes post, and then add #XbiteSweepstakes to your repost. You'll also need to have a public account.

The sweepstakes runs now through November 10. The winner, who will be chosen by a random draw, will have 48 hours to respond if they're selected. "Miss the window, and this gator makes a clean getaway," Microsoft said in yet another reference to GTA 6.

GTA 6 is getting special treatment for its PS5 edition, and this has so far included a limited-edition DualSense controller inspired by the game and trailers for GTA 6 that end by telling people the game "plays best" on PS5. The game's recent launch trailer does not include the Xbox logo, either.

GTA 6 is of course not exclusive to Xbox, and there is no evidence that it "plays best" on PS5.

According to Sensor Tower, GTA 6 has sold about 2 million copies so far on Xbox Series X|S, compared to 5.75 million on PS5. Xbox is not worried the PS5 version massively pacing ahead of Xbox, in part because the 74%/26% split in favor of PS5 over Xbox reflects Xbox's current share of the console market. GTA 6 is breaking records already for Xbox, the company has said.

Microsoft takes a 30% cut of games sold on the Xbox platform, so that could end up being a huge number when the game launches, even if it's far behind PS5. At about 2 million copies sold on Xbox so far, according to Sensor Tower, that's $192 million in gross revenue; Xbox's cut would be about $57.6 million. Sensor Tower has said the majority of GTA 6 preorders should come in the final week before release, and could reach 25 million.

If the split stays about where it is now, that would be about 6.5 million units on Xbox by launch, generating more than $170 million in platform fees paid to Xbox. Of course, these are just ballpark estimates, but it's a sure thing that GTA 6 is going to be a big deal for Xbox. Microsoft already alluded to this, as the company forecast major growth for Xbox content and services in the current quarter, and while management didn't attribute this to any particular title, the gargantuan release of GTA 6 is no doubt factored in.

GTA 6 launches on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S.

#3616. Even Pierce Brosnan Is “Eagerly” Awaiting News of the Next James Bond

Like the rest of us, Pierce Brosnan has been following the seemingly endless and exhaustive search for the next James Bond. Having played 007 across four films, Brosnan says he admires all the actors in the running, but Callum Turner, who played his angsty Manhattanite son in The Only Living Boy in New York, gets a particularly warm mention. “Callum is someone I’ve worked with, and he’s so strong,” Brosnan tells Vanity Fair. As for Dune director Denis Villeneuve’s vision for the franchise, Brosnan is already sold. “I think we are going to be blown away.”

Away from Hollywood, the Irish actor stars in Burberry’s new holiday campaign, celebrating 170 years of the luxury fashion house, alongside actor Fiona Shaw, his son Dylan Thomas Brosnan, and a cast of characters including Dwyane Wade, Cara Delevingne, Gabrielle Union, Nico Parker, and more. Set at the cinematic Longleat House in Wiltshire, England, it’s a festive British Christmas, complete with Burberry’s signature checks and partygoers draped in classic garments. On set, Brosnan found a kindred spirit in Shaw. The two bonded over their shared love of art—though he wishes they had much more time to chat, “It was all too brief with Fiona,” he muses.

Pierce Brosnan in the Burberry Festive 2026 Campaign video.

Pierce Brosnan and Fiona Shaw in the Burberry Festive 2026 Campaign video.

Brosnan is no stranger to good style. Having spent a career playing some of the most impeccably dressed men on screen, from James Bond to Thomas Crown, Brosnan has come to re-embrace the joys of good tailoring after an era of rebelling against the gentlemanly image he created for himself. Now, he’s looking forward to seeing a new generation of leading men step into some of those familiar roles, including Michael B. Jordan, whose upcoming take on Thomas Crown he’s cheering on.

In conversation with Vanity Fair, the former 007 talks favorite Christmas traditions, the Burberry Mac he’s kept for years, the art of playing it cool, how filming MobLand shaped his personal style, and the paintings waiting for him in London.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Vanity Fair: The new Burberry campaign celebrates 170 years of the fashion house with a festive Christmas party in the English countryside. How was your time on the campaign set?

Pierce Brosnan: I was with my son, Dylan Thomas Brosnan, which was just absolutely wonderful, and we had the most magnificent time. I’d never seen so many people on a set in all my days for such an event. Everybody was very charming.

Do you typically go all-in on Christmas? What’s your favorite holiday tradition?

I think it starts with the Christmas tree, and my wife really decks the halls, as it were. She loves decorating the tree, and that becomes a great ritual. The boys are much older now, but we do have grandchildren joining us for Christmas. My son Sean Brosnan and his family will be coming down. My wife is a wonderful cook; she’ll make a feast for us all.

Midnight Mass is a tradition and a great joy if we’re in London. Friends, family, and reflection on the year past. Having been brought up within the Catholic religion, the season and all of those traditions are very much ingrained in me.

Harmony Korine (Gummo, Kids, Spring Breakers) directing a holiday campaign feels like such an inspired choice, given how experimental his films can be. What was it like working with him?

I thought he was charming! Very charming. It moved very fast. He was busy and deep in the workload of the day. The highlight was meeting and being with Fiona Shaw. That was just absolutely magnificent. I’m such a huge fan of the lady’s work.

The Burberry trench is such a cornerstone of British style. Is there a clothing item in your wardrobe that holds that kind of status for you?

Oh, dear. There are so many beautiful items in my closet. One of my favorite suits has become a workhorse because it’s so durable. The cloth is wool, and it’s just a two-piece, beautifully tailored suit by Anglo-Italian. I’m very partial to my shoes and belts by Bottega Veneta. And of course, a Burberry Mac, which I’ve had for many, many years. It is the classic, dream trench coat of anyone who has grown up on the movies.

It was wonderful to celebrate such a garment of classic time, and to be in the company of Fiona Shaw. [She’s] someone who I would adore to work with again on any level, really. We had a wonderful time talking about art. We’re both painters, and art is very much part of the tapestry of our lives now.

Pierce Brosnan in The Thomas Crown Affair, 1999.

Speaking of art, I wanted to ask you about playing Thomas Crown in The Thomas Crown Affair. Michael B. Jordan is stepping into that role now, in a new version of the film, which he’s also directing.

I love Michael B. Jordan. I think he’s an outstanding actor and artist, and I wish him every great success with his vision of Thomas Crown. There’s something just beautifully cinematic about the character. He was brought onto the stage by one of the great actors, Steve McQueen, who was so gifted in the art of film acting, stillness, and inner life. For me, the romance with the film came from his body of work as an actor and has always been with me since I was a young lad in Ireland. These characters are very hard to really understand, but they create a sensation.

He was so cool, Steve McQueen. How do you play cool? You play it with sincerity. You play it with stillness, with just the knowingness—and hopefully some humanity and humility, and a kind of inner knowing of being the actor you are.

What do you think makes Thomas Crown such an enduring character?

When I made my rendition and produced it with my late dear friend Beau St. Clair, I wanted to steal art. I didn’t want to steal diamonds or money. I wanted to steal paintings. It was against all the political correctness of his time and space. Thomas Crown was a man who had everything in life: wealth, fortune, intellect. But he didn’t have love. So it was a love story for me.

When we were looking for the film’s art, I suggested René Magritte: the bowler hats, the red tie, the great coat. Magritte is someone I find spellbinding, captivating, and always has a narrative which is almost cinematic. So that’s where the bowler hats came from. The visible and the invisible: Visible with an apple in front of a face, but you don’t see the face. And I thought that translated well to the enigma of Thomas Crown.

Pierce Brosnan and Callum Turner, The Only Living Boy In New York, 2017.

Having played James Bond yourself, I’m curious how you’re following the conversation around this upcoming chapter.

[Laughs.] Oh, I’m just an audience member now. I’m just the man in the street who is eager to see who is going to play this epic role of cinematic history. All the men who are on the list now are actors I admire. Callum, Callum Turner is someone I’ve worked with, and he’s so strong. They all have a voice and a physique, and a presence on film. They all have longevity as actors, all of these young men.

Pierce Brosnan as 007 in The World Is Not Enough, 1999.

What would you say to the next actor stepping into 007?

Whoever plays the role, I wish him the very best of life and strength and courage. You know, it’s hard to tell who it would be, but I eagerly await to hear the news and the celebration of the next James Bond.

Martin Campbell gave your era such a memorable introduction with GoldenEye. Now, with Denis Villeneuve taking on the franchise, what are you most curious to see him bring to Bond?

I think we are going to be blown away. I really do. [Villeneuve] is such an iconoclastic director. His work is visionary, and his stealth and imagination of camera work and storytelling is so visceral and sensuous. It’s going to be great. It’s going to be truly magnificent. Of course, we all get sentimental and nostalgic, and you have to give it time and be patient, and it’s always such a delightful game. But Villeneuve is someone who I have great admiration for, and I look forward to seeing the work.

Pierce Brosnan as Remington Steele, 1986.

Pierce Brosnan as Remington Steele, 1986.

You’ve played some of cinema’s most impeccably dressed men! Have those characters influenced the way you dress in your own life?

I have always been, I suppose, a clothes horse. When I played Remington Steele, I delved into the work of Cary Grant, another emblem of cinema that I’ve admired. Bob Butler, who directed it, said, “We’re making an old movie,” so I styled myself and had the joy of wearing beautiful suits every week. That continues through my life.

As I’ve gotten older, I used to try to rebel against the look, character, and style of actor I had created for myself. Now I embrace it more because it excites me. I love the elegance of tailored clothes and dressing up, and fitting into the season, the gale of emotion, the world around you.

You’ve got some great hunting coats in MobLand too.

Rebecca Hale, the costume designer, has brought so many great ingredients to the world of Conrad. He’s an Irishman from a hard part of Irish life, the Troubles, a mangled life of abuse and violence. He wants to fit into the world of the Cotswolds and be the gentleman. There’s this magnificent coat in MobLand, where Conrad has a shootout, and they made a magnificent overcoat, which I managed to keep from last season. And, of course, I step back and just revel at what Dame Helen Mirren does. She is such an empress of fashion herself.

When Vanity Fair last caught up with you, around your first solo exhibition, you’d already been painting and curating work for years. How has your relationship with art evolved since then?

I had, yes. I had the exhibition three years ago, and it was a great success in the sense that I had the courage to step out and show the work. I have a body of work now that has progressed, and hopefully I will have another showing here, maybe in London.

Do you find that painting gives you something different from acting, or do the two creative practices feed into each other?

Both are essential to my life. Acting is how I make my living and provide for my family. And to be able to have a lifestyle that is not only creative but productive, and then is hopefully entertaining, because you’re working towards an audience.

The practice of my art is a constant exploration of inner life, inner thoughts, inner emotions expressed through color and form. Having lived in Kauai for 25 years, there’s a wonderful artist there who’s become my teacher, Saim Caglayan. Both are necessary to my life. They soothe me and frustrate me and challenge me and exhilarate me—sometimes all in the same space of day and time.

Yes! I was sketching when I was doing Burberry. There was a lovely landscape down there, and I have my sketchbook with me at all times. I wanted so much to be an artist, to be a writer, a poet, to live a creative life. I have no real head for figures or the abstraction of figures, but I certainly have a great love for art and the power of art on the wall.

With the holidays coming up, and hopefully a little time to slow down, is there anything you’re hoping to make more time for, creatively or personally?

I have a little time left before I go back to London with my wife, Keely. London is home, and my mother of 94 is there, so I’m looking forward to seeing her. In my studio, I have a number of paintings that I’m quite pleased with, and I’d like to finish a couple more. And I’m really excited to jump into season three of MobLand. I have no idea where the story is going. Conrad is slowly, slowly going bonkers. But the thing is, he’s aware of it, and the love story of Maeve and Conrad lives on. It’s very exciting.

Parks and Recreation has been off the air for over ten years, but I still find myself coming back to the workplace sitcom whenever I need to improve my mood. Pawnee feels like home; the characters always make me laugh, the heartwarming moments always make me cry, and I feel like I walk away from every rewatch having been taught a new life lesson.

Tom and Donna’s “Treat yo self” mantra, Leslie’s endless optimism, and Ron’s quiet way of loving and supporting those around him are just a few of the life lessons I’ve learned as a fan. As fans, we’re always more susceptible to latching on to characters and learning lessons because of how many times we’ll rewatch something; but stars themselves can also learn something from their time on a show. Case in point: Amy Poehler recently opened up about what playing one of the most beloved television characters of all time taught her.

Leslie Knope taught me a lot. Playing her really did improve my life. It made me a much better listener and more engaged person in the world. And it was really nice to come to work and, like, spend the whole day telling everybody how much you love them. I had to have a lot of energy to play her. And she gave me a lot of energy when I played her.

Parks and Rec was full of hilarious characters with big hearts, but it was Leslie who centered them all. Sure, sometimes she tried too hard and failed, but she always did things because she thought it would make a difference for the people of Pawnee. She’s definitely the reason why I always come back to the show and consider it one of the best sitcoms of all time.

To me, Poehler and Knope are basically the same person. Anyone who has ever listened to the Saturday Night Live alum speak over the years can attest to the way she seems to embody the Pawnee native. I’d never considered that she wasn’t always that way, but in listening to her mock job interview for WSJ Magazine, that wasn’t always the case.

That’s not to say Poehler was some terrible person pre-Parks and Recreation; anyone who worked with her on SNL would vouch for her kindheartedness — especially Andy Samberg, who credits Poehler with him pursuing Brooklyn Nine-Nine. There’s no denying she’s become an even better person because of Leslie. As she went on to say:;

So what I like about her and what I try to remember, and why I think I deserve this job, she never thought it was lame to care about things. So when I catch myself not caring about things, I do think about her. Because she wouldn't have that.

Not being afraid to care deeply about things is definitely the biggest message I’ve taken away from watching Parks and Rec, and it’s nice to hear the same is true for Poehler. She’s definitely taken that to heart in how she carries herself on her podcast and even with her charity endeavors, like back in 2020 when the Parks and Rec cast reunited to benefit Feeding America.
