#3614. Parties That Changed the World: Barbie’s Premiere and Gone With the Wind’s Debut

The world’s most famous doll was inspired by a spunky, high-end call girl named Lilli. Described as a “gold digger, exhibitionist, and floozy,” the character of Bild Lilli was created in 1952 by German cartoonist Reinhard Beuthien after he was asked to draw a filler cartoon for the inaugural issue of the tabloid Bild-Zeitung. Lilli, a buxom blonde with a perky ponytail and sky-high stilettos, sat beside a fortune teller. “Can’t you give me the name and address of this tall, handsome, rich man?” she cooed. The cartoon was an instant hit, and in 1955, Lilli was immortalized in plastic.

A year later, Ruth Handler discovered the Lilli doll while on a vacation in Europe. She bought several. One was for her teenage daughter, Barbara, to keep; the rest were brought back to Mattel, the toy company she had cofounded with her husband, Elliot, and businessman Harold Matson. (Mattel is a portmanteau of both men’s names.) Lilli—with comically large breasts, chic outfits, and heavy makeup—was precisely what Handler had been looking for.

Robin Gerber, author of Barbie and Ruth, wrote: “The doll looked too much like a prostitute for the company’s taste,” so Mattel’s design team (slightly) softened Lilli’s exaggerated proportions, renamed her Barbie, after Barbara, and before long, she would become the physical ideal for generations of young girls and women everywhere.

Sixty-four years after Barbie hit shelves, she finally got her close-up in Barbie, a feminist manifesto in a pair of pink stilettos. The film’s premiere and after-party at the Shrine Auditorium marked Warner Bros.’ largest premiere to date—and the cherry on top of a bubble-gum-flavored, years-long marketing blitz. According to Event Marketer, “the affair was like Barbie herself: high-energy, glamorous and very, very, colorful.”

It was a beautiful day in Hollywood. Even by Los Angeles standards, the weather on Sunday, July 9, 2023, was almost impossibly perfect—sunshine, low 70s, and a cool breeze—as if Hollywood itself has been dropped into the fantasy world of Barbie Land.

The event kicked off with a splash. The pink carpet was tricked out with replicas of pieces from the film’s beach scenes: a lifeguard station, a towering lighthouse, faux palm trees, and a 3D ocean wave, with carpeting that shifted colors to mimic sand. A wide range of influencers were invited to get first dibs on photo ops before the stars arrived. But the real showstopper was the two-story replica of Barbie’s Dreamhouse, complete with a 2D faux pool, a DJ spinning tracks, and the trademark spiral slide. “We had to have that slide,” Wendy Robino, SVP of Warner Bros. marketing events, said at the time.

On Sunday, they wore pink: Writer and director Greta Gerwig, along with cast members Issa Rae, America Ferrera, Kate McKinnon, Ryan Gosling, and Michael Cera, turned out for the premiere in every shade of Barbie’s signature color, turning something long dismissed as girly into a celebration of individuality, joy, and girl power.

But the belle of the ball wasn’t one to blend in. After weeks of thinking pink, Margot Robbie—the film’s star and producer—arrived in black. Her custom Schiaparelli look re-created 1960s’ Solo in the Spotlight Barbie: a black sequined dress with a single red rose stitched onto her tulle skirt, matching opera gloves, Manolo Blahnik mules, and a diamond necklace. Movie Star Barbie fully committed to the bit, even clutching a pink handkerchief as she posed in front of a pink Corvette. Robbie’s blond hair was swept into a high ponytail—reminiscent of the one first worn by Lilli.

Following the official screening—marking the first time Barbie was revealed to the public—it was time to party.

The theme was “Barbie’s Blowout Disco Party.” Fittingly, one attraction invited guests inside a glittering, 12-foot pink disco ball. Justin Lefkovitch, whose company Mirrored Media, partnered with Mattel to create it, tells VF the entrance created “a shroud of mystery” for partygoers. Inside, a six-foot 1:1 Dreamhouse showcasing the new Barbie the Movie doll collection was surrounded by gold and silver streamers and over a dozen custom pink disco balls. The goal, Lefkovitch recalls, was to “transport guests into the world of Barbie.”

Nicki Minaj was the first guest to arrive at the party, event producer Austin Johnston tells VF—“five-foot-long hair all the way down to the floor.” A theme park designer by trade, Johnston and his company, AKJohnston, transformed the after-party into what he calls a “pop-up museum.” Barbie Land’s pastel-colored cul-de-sac was re-created as “a 65-foot-tall, 70-foot-wide” inflatable, its landmarks crammed together like a kitschy postcard. At the end of Barbie’s driveway, Mark Ronson presided over a hot pink DJ booth, playing hits from the soundtrack by Ice Spice, Dua Lipa (a.k.a. Mermaid Barbie), and Nicki Minaj—whom Johnston had to “very kindly” ask to get off Barbie’s Corvette.

Tucked beneath the second-floor mezzanine, a series of alcoves became larger-than-life photo sets, with photographers on hand to capture guests in action. Partygoers could retrace Barbie’s journey to the Real World—by bike, boat, and rocket ship—or step inside the Kendom man cave, Weird Barbie’s house, and life-size Barbie and Ken toy boxes. Not everyone hired to re-create Barbie Land had actually seen the movie by then; only a handful were invited to be part of that “really restricted small group,” Johnston says.

At the center of the room, guests sipped pink cocktails under a giant disco ball while an 11-foot, glitter-coated pink B twirled above. Another bar doubled as a fashion show, with four life-size mannequins dolled up for disco in original costumes from the film’s dance number, including Barbie’s gold sequined jumpsuit and the Kens’ matching white-and-gold tracksuits.

Obviously, the food was on theme too. Wolfgang Puck catered the evening’s Barbie-Q, serving grilled salmon, summer melon salad, roasted Pink Fir apple potatoes, char siu glazed grilled chicken, and charred tricolor cauliflower.

Even the night’s corporate sponsors knew better than to steal Barbie’s spotlight. OPI set up a nail salon, and Xbox provided a gaming station where players had their pick of two General Motors rides: Barbie’s Corvette or Ken’s Hummer. A highlight for Johnston was spotting Robbie racing a virtual Hummer while her Australian parents cheered her on. “No one paid her to do that,” he says. “She’s just like, I want to have a drink and play a video game at my premiere.”

For one night in Hollywood, women could be anything. And 84 years earlier, another city had hosted another rager in honor of another larger-than-life heroine. While Los Angeles turned pink for Barbie, Atlanta resurrected the Old South for Scarlett O’Hara.

All hell broke loose when British actor Vivien Leigh was cast as beloved heroine Scarlett O’Hara in the big-screen adaptation of Margaret Mitchell’s epic, Gone With the Wind. Fans and journalists were outraged that such an iconic Southern Belle would be played by a foreigner. At the time, Leigh was yet to star in a Hollywood film and was best known stateside for her affair with Laurence Olivier. Gossip columnist Hedda Hopper sniped: “Out of millions of American women, [producer David O. Selznick] couldn’t find one to suit him.”

Hopper was exaggerating, but not by a lot: During a grueling two-year nationwide search for his leading lady, Selznick reportedly met with over 1,400 actresses. After angry fan letters poured in, Selznick’s publicity machine kicked into overdrive—and eventually, the public came around to the idea that a refined Brit was somehow easier to swallow than a Yankee.

But perhaps the most convincing endorsement came from Leigh’s own leading man. Even Clark Gable, who initially considered Leigh “too demure” for the Southern firecracker, was won over by her dedication and declared she “was Scarlett every minute.” His own casting, meanwhile, had been a dream come true from the thousands who flooded MGM and Selznick’s offices with letters demanding he play Rhett Butler

The shoot was famously plagued by drama, and by the time filming wrapped, the cast and crew had earned themselves a party.

But Selznick had bigger fish to fry—namely, finishing the movie in time for its premiere. He left the party planning to local organizers and his trusted story editor Kay Brown, who had convinced her boss to buy the film rights in the first place. But since Atlanta was still tightly in the grip of Jim Crow, not everyone could join in. Leigh’s costars Hattie McDaniel and Butterfly McQueen were excluded from the festivities.

Selznick argued, unsuccessfully, with local organizers to get McDaniel on the guest list. Gable threatened to not attend the premiere in solidarity with his friend, The Hollywood Reporter stated, but McDaniel ultimately talked him out of it. “While it was unfortunate to exclude Mammy, it was the wisest policy,” Brown wrote, per Matthew Bernstein, former professor of film and media studies at Emory University.

Meanwhile, white Atlanta was gearing up for the party of the century. Former president Jimmy Carter later called it the South’s “biggest event” in his lifetime. According to Time, then governor Eurith D. Rivers was prepared to call in the National Guard, while Mayor Hartsfield urged every woman of Atlanta to dust off her hoop skirts and each man to “sprout a goatee, sideburns, and Kentucky colonel whiskers.”

Hollywood came in hot. Leigh and Gable made their grand entrance by limousine, waving to the 300,000 spectators who lined seven miles of streets in downtown Atlanta—including a number of nonagenarian Confederate veterans who were invited as special guests. Leigh arrived with Olivier while Gable brought his new wife, Carole Lombard. Fun fact: Gable reportedly hadn’t even wanted to play Rhett Butler until Louis B. Mayer offered to help bankroll his divorce so he could marry Lombard.

Of the motorcade, Time wrote: “Crowds larger than the combined armies that fought at Atlanta in July 1864 waved Confederate flags, tossed confetti till it seemed to be snowing, gave three different versions of the Rebel yell, whistled, cheered, goggled.” Leigh wept as the crowd welcomed the British actress “back home,” as if she’d just returned from battle.

The multiday event included a costume ball thrown by the Junior League that would have Abraham Lincoln rolling over in his grave. Decked out in hoop skirts, bustles, and Confederate-era uniforms, 6,000 guests descended on the Municipal Auditorium, which had been transformed into a recreation of the film’s Monster Bazaar. Black participants were relegated to serving or entertaining. Among them was the Ebenezer Baptist Church choir, whose singers reportedly performed dressed as enslaved people in front of a façade of Tara, a fictional plantation from the film. One of the singers was 10-year-old future civil rights hero Martin Luther King Jr.

Vivien Leigh arrived in a velvet gown designed by Walter Plunkett. Though Olivier escorted her costar Olivia de Havilland instead—to keep up appearances—Leigh was the belle of the ball, especially in hometown hero Margaret Mitchell’s absence. Eighteen years earlier, the young novelist had performed a risqué “apache dance” at a charity gala, which cost her her Junior League membership. Now, with Hollywood celebrating her masterpiece, some suspected Mitchell was getting the last laugh by snubbing the biggest party in town.

Young women fangirled all over Gable. According to Time, one woman fainted at the sight of him. Another was given a choice: a Christmas gift or a chance to meet the heartthrob. She chose Gable. After he kissed the 11-year-old, she gasped, “Now am I a woman?”

Governor Rivers declared December 15, 1939, a statewide holiday in honor of Gone With the Wind’s world premiere, the grand finale of the three-day extravaganza. Searchlights swept the Southern sky, and flashbulbs popped as 18,000 spectators crowded Peachtree Street. Even Loew’s Grand Theater got a glow-up. Its Romanesque façade was disguised as a grand Southern plantation—four towering white columns were erected to support a temporary façade with floral garlands, potted trees, and an enormous portrait of Leigh and Gable hung above the entrance.

Inside, all 2,000-plus seats sold out at $10 a pop—the equivalent of about $240 today. That’s not exactly chump change, considering Atlanta was still licking its wounds after the Great Depression. Young women in antebellum costumes greeted guests before Mayor Hartsfield took the stage to kick things off. Selznick and the film’s stars received standing ovations that lasted a full minute. But the loudest cheers were for Mitchell, now in attendance, who joined Leigh and Gable onstage.

The lights dimmed for nearly four hours of melodrama. When Rhett Butler delivered his immortal parting shot—“Frankly, my dear, I don’t give a damn”—the audience reportedly gasped, then erupted in applause as he left Scarlett in his dust.

Before Gone With the Wind—still the highest-grossing film of all time when adjusted for inflation—premieres were usually exclusive screenings in Hollywood or New York. 1939’s antebellum extravaganza turned an entire city into a movie set, setting the stage for modern spectacles like Barbie.

Both parties also offer a revealing snapshot of the societies that threw them. For Gone With the Wind, the industry glorified an imagined past; for Barbie, Hollywood toasted an imagined future. The Barbie premiere wasn’t just a love letter to a feminist film: It was also a giant corporate juggernaut designed to sell a product whose history was tangled up with the very stereotypes the film was questioning. It paid off: Following the film’s theatrical release, Mattel reported a third-quarter increase in worldwide gross billings of 27%, and Barbie toy sales in the United States increased 25% for the July-August combined months compared to the same two-month period a year prior. The immersive premiere, brand collaborations, worldwide activations, and fan participation blurred the line between marketing a movie and creating a cultural event.

The film also became Warner Bros.’ most successful release of all time, grossing $1.4 billion worldwide and making Greta Gerwig the first solo female director admitted into the hallowed halls of the billion-dollar boys club. The premiere celebrated a movie that changed the cultural conversation while handily outgrossing the testosterone-fueled Oppenheimer—a spectacular rebuke to the assumption that chick flicks have a glass ceiling.

Its timing made the celebration particularly potent. In that moment, Hollywood was still finding its footing after the pandemic; the premiere offered something audiences were missing. “It eventized going back to the movies. It eventized the premiere,” says Lefkovitch.

For one night, partygoers got to revel in a fairy tale where women ruled the world. But outside Barbie Land, the irony had all the subtlety of Ken’s Mojo Dojo Casa House. Hollywood was throwing an enormous party celebrating a fantasy of female empowerment while women were still fighting for equality in the real world. There is “definitely some hypocrisy,” agrees Lefkovitch, who made a point of thanking his all-female team.

Decades earlier, Atlanta had thrown its own enormous party, celebrating a fantasy of Southern womanhood while reinforcing the racial and social hierarchies of the real South—and conveniently leaving the horrors of slavery out of the picture. (The film itself did just that, presenting a fictional plantation where the most loyal individuals enjoyed being enslaved.) Black performers were welcome to entertain white audiences, but not to celebrate alongside them; not a single seat inside Loew’s Grand Theater was available to Black moviegoers.

Together, these indignities galvanized the local Black press. In a column for Atlanta Daily World, Reverend John Clarence Wright wrote, “As Atlanta goes mad with the Wind one hundred thousand of her citizens should become more thoughtful than ever of the course that must be pursued to gain their rights as free men and citizens in a land where the spirit of secession and slavery still lives.” With Black moviegoers barred from Southern theaters, the Pittsburgh Courier dryly observed, “Negro reaction… will have to wait until the film comes North.”

The premiere and the film’s success helped propel the NAACP to fight not just individual films, but toward a broader campaign to change Hollywood itself. In 1942, NAACP leader Walter White spoke directly to studio heads in an attempt to persuade them to steer away from demeaning Black stereotypes—like the ones onscreen in Gone With the Wind—and to increase the roles available to Black actors in Hollywood.

White’s approach infuriated the very woman whose absence from the Atlanta premiere had helped expose Hollywood’s hypocrisy: Hattie McDaniel. As a Black woman, McDaniel’s choices were limited—“I’d rather play a maid than be one,” she once said. Writing for Vanity Fair, Hadley Hall Meares noted that McDaniel was “incensed” that White had negotiated with the studios on her behalf, and believed she and her fellow Black actors deserved their own seat at the negotiating table.

McDaniel did get a seat at the 1940 Oscars—but it was at a small table at the edge of the room, separated from her Gone With the Wind costars. The ceremony, after all, was held at the Cocoanut Grove nightclub, which had a strict color line. When her name was called, McDaniel gushed: “I sincerely hope I shall always be a credit to my race and to the motion picture industry.”

Meares described McDaniel’s life as “a tightrope walk.” She was expected to satisfy the white executives who controlled her career, the Black audiences who wanted better representation, and her own ambitions as an actress.

Vivien Leigh also made history that night, becoming the first Brit to win the Oscar for best actress. She dedicated her award to Selznick for his “energy, courage, and very great kindness.” After all, he had been partly responsible for convincing an initially outraged public that Leigh was worthy to play their beloved Scarlett O’Hara. Years later, the Academy lavished Barbie with eight nominations, though it snubbed Gerwig for best director and Robbie for best actress. (Frankly, my dear, they didn’t give a damn about the two women who created Barbie Land.) If Hollywood could build an entire universe in which women ruled the world, why was it still so difficult to imagine one outside the movie theater?

Billie Eilish and Finneas O’Connell took home Barbie’s only Oscar, for best original song. Their winning composition poses Barbie’s existential question while echoing the expectations heaped upon Scarlett, Leigh, McDaniel, Robbie, and Gerwig: “What Was I Made For?”

It turns out the inspiration for Barbie—the quintessential American toy—wasn’t even made for little girls. Lilli dolls were sold to grown men in European tobacco shops and adult toy stores, becoming popular gag gifts. “Men… put them on their car dashboard, dangled them from the rearview mirror, or gave them to girlfriends as a suggestive keepsake,” Gerber wrote. Long before Barbie could be anything, she was something for men.

Eighty-four years apart, Hollywood threw two spectacular parties for women who refused to play by the rules. But the rules were still very much in place when the lights came back up.

The saga of It Ends With Us has lasted for years, with the two leads becoming synonymous with the book to screen adaptation and their long legal battle. Namely Blake Lively and Justin Baldoni, who have been battling in court due to allegations made about about the film (which is streaming with a Hulu subscription). The saga has taken another twist, as Baldoni reportedly sold his LA home in the wake of all the drama.

Blake Lively's complaints against Wayfarer Studios started a years-long legal battle between her and Justin Baldoni, who also directed and starred in It Ends With Us. Despite the pair issuing a joint statement and settling, the drama hasn't slowed down much. The latest update comes to us from Page Six, which claims that Baldoni sold his home in Los Angeles for over $2 million, after moving to Nashville in the midst of the drama with Lively.

The outlet claims that he sold the house back in August, and ended up making a profit of around one million dollars. Considering how wildly expensive lawyers fees were for both Lively and Baldoni, perhaps this sum will help to settle up with his representation.

The report also clarifies that the actor/producer/director still has a home on Ojai, so there are still some roots in California. Although it seems like his primary residence will be in Tennessee, where he'll presumably be able to operate with more anonymity than staying in California... especially as the It Ends With Us drama continues to make headlines.

As previously mentioned, the legal drama surrounding It Ends With Us has been going on for years, starting shortly after the movie arrived in theaters back in 2024. After his co-star's complaint Justin Baldoni filed his own defamation case, naming both Blake Lively and Ryan Reynolds in the process. Both of the movie's stars made allegations about what the other did on set, with the Jane the Virgin star claiming that Lively tried to take control of the movie. What's more, he also claimed that used famous friends like Taylor Swift to try and intimidate him in the midst of their drama.

The saga definitely captured the attention of fans, with the court of public opinion making their own judgements. It also seems to have negatively affect both of its stars' careers. For his part, Baldoni largely hasn't been working while dealing with his legal battle again Lively. Luckily for him that's about to change, as his company Wayfarer Studios will produce Gina Rodriguez's upcoming directorial debut. We'll just have to see if/when he gets in front of the camera again.

It Ends With Us is streaming now on Hulu. Baldoni didn't have projects on the 2026 movie release list, but maybe that'll change now that the drama is settling.

#3612. Why Your Smartwatch Size Really Does Matter

“Is my watch too big?” is a constant question on forums dedicated to smartwatches and fitness trackers of all kinds. (Some, but fewer, wonder if their watch is too small.) Personally, I don’t much care how a watch looks, but I’ve noticed that size can make a big difference in how accurately a watch functions. If your watch is too big, your numbers may be off.

Watches measure heart rate through an optical sensor on the back of the watch. (That’s what you see glowing green back there.) The heart rate sensor detects how that light reflects off the blood vessels in your skin. To get a proper reading, it needs to be snug against your skin, ideally in a way that blocks out ambient light.

If the sensor loses contact with your skin, or if too much light sneaks in, heart rate readings may be inaccurate. If a watch fits you well to start with, you can generally get an accurate heart rate by simply making sure the watch is snug during workouts.

But if a watch is too big, it can move around, letting light in. When you run, if a watch is bouncing around, the sensor may detect a flash of light with every footstep. This can lead to your watch reporting a heart rate that is the same as your cadence (footsteps per minute), which is sometimes called “cadence lock.” Some runners will cover their watch with a sleeve (especially in cold weather) to minimize this possibility.

No matter how you wear it, a big watch on a small wrist is likely to have a lot more difficulty than one that fits properly. Very small devices can have a similar problem: The device isn’t large enough or can’t be tightened enough to block light. This isn’t usually a problem with wristwatches, but it may explain why smart rings tend to be so poor at daytime heart rate tracking.

Now, is this a real-life concern, or just a theoretical quibble? I wasn’t sure, until I took the Forerunner 265 and 265S for a run at the same time. These are the same watch, with the same heart rate sensor, differing only in size. You can read about my results here, but the graph tells the story pretty well: The smaller 265S (42 mm) captured my heart rate more accurately than the 265 (46 mm).

If heart rate accuracy were the only issue, I would tell you to get the smallest watch you can find. It wouldn’t even look weird; before smartwatches became popular, wristwatches were often much smaller than a person’s wrist. (Watch old movies and you’ll see some tiny watches, even on people who don’t have tiny wrists.)

But watches are big and seem to be getting bigger. A bigger screen means numbers, text, and icons are easier to read. This is great news if your vision isn’t the best anymore, or if you use the watch while exercising and want to be able to see what’s on your screen with a quick glance.

Bigger watches can provide bigger screens, but also bigger batteries and more room for other internals. This is probably at least partly why more “premium” watches come in bigger sizes. That said, it’s hard for me to distinguish when a watch is huge because it needs room to pack in its hardware features, versus when the company is making the watch bigger so it will seem fancier and thus justify a higher price.

And this brings me to something I need to rant about. Smartwatch and fitness watch companies know that watch size matters: They often offer two sizes for at least some of their models. The Apple Watch Series 12 comes in 42 or 46 millimeters, while the Garmin Forerunner 570 comes in 42 or 47 millimeters, to give a couple of examples.

But when it comes to premium models, those options often disappear. The Garmin Forerunner 970, far more feature-rich than the 570, only comes in a 47-millimeter size, matching the larger size of the 570 but without a smaller option. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 only comes in a 49-millimeter size, which is even larger than the larger size of the Series 12. I’m about to start testing a Hyrox feature that only comes on Amazfit’s Balance 3 or Balance Ultra watches; those watches are 51 and 52 millimeters, respectively. This is getting ridiculous.

As a woman reporting on tech, I can’t ignore the way gender plays into this. According to ANSUR II, a U.S. Army study, women have an average wrist size of 154 millimeters (about 6.1 inches), and men have an average wrist size of 176 mm (about 6.9 inches). My wrists are right around 6 inches, making me very average for a woman.

When companies make two sizes of watch, the smaller size usually fits the average woman’s wrist fairly well, and the larger size is a better fit for men’s wrists. This isn’t a perfect match, of course, since plenty of women may fit or prefer the larger size, and vice versa. I’m glad the companies market these as “small” and “large” or just by the numerical size.

But as a person with six-inch wrists, I can’t wear a large watch without dealing with bouncing, rubbing, and potentially inaccurate data. I’m no twig; I’m perfectly average for my half of the population. But those larger watches just aren’t going to be as accurate for me as they are for the average man. I noticed a similar phenomenon when I tested the heart rate tracking in Powerbeats Pro 2 earbuds: They barely worked for me, but did fine when I tried them on a man with larger ears.

There's also an uncomfortable intersection between this gender dynamic and the way watch companies use size as a signifier of how fancy a watch is supposed to be. While Garmin only offers the 970 in a large size (47 mm), they only offer the cheaper 70 and 170 in smaller sizes (both 43 mm). Garmin’s Venu 4 comes in both 41 and 45 millimeter sizes, but the cheaper Vivoactive 6 is only available in 42. Having a small wrist can save you money, but it still shuts you off from some of the more premium options out there.

For my work reviewing and testing watches for Lifehacker, I’ve worn smartwatches ranging from around 40 millimeters (an older Apple Watch) up to 48 millimeters (a tie between the Kospet Tank and the Amazfit T-Rex 3 Pro). I love a watch in the 40-42 millimeter range; I can tolerate one around 46 millimeters if it’s lightweight enough that it doesn’t bounce too much; and I really have a hard time with anything larger.

Those bigger watches are hard to snug up sufficiently for a workout; get them tight enough not to bounce, and they’ll feel like you’re nearly cutting off your circulation. After a long run with a big, heavy watch, I’ve sometimes gotten red, irritated spots on my wrist from the inevitable friction. You may not be able to judge how badly a watch will fit when it's still in the box, but I do have a rule of thumb for when you try it on.

To judge visually, I find it helps to put a watch on your wrist, rest your arm on a table, and look directly down at it. If the lugs of the watch extend past your wrist, it’s too big. You want the watch to fit on your wrist, not overhang the sides.

And if you prefer a watch size that isn’t going to be the most accurate for heart rate, remember that you can always pair a chest strap to a watch that supports it, or to your phone if you don’t have a compatible watch. If you prefer a larger watch for more readable text or maps, or if you want a premium feature that doesn’t come in smaller sizes, a chest strap may be the way to get the best of both worlds.

#3611. David Baldacci, John Grisham, and Scott Turow Know How a Story Can End. They Say Losing the Rule of Law to Trump Would Be a “Death Sentence for America”

In July, for the first time in seven years, sitting justices of the US Supreme Court testified at the Capitol. Chief Justice John Roberts has been shy about letting members of the Court answer legislators’ questions, viewing it as a violation of the separation of powers. However, in this case, there was apparently no choice, since the Supreme Court requested millions of dollars to enhance its very own security in the face of sharply growing threats to lower court judges—threats that have grown exponentially over the last decade.

We are all lawyers as well as novelists. We have appeared in court on various matters before both judges and juries, and thus believe that respect for the rule of law is absolutely essential to have any hope for a civilized society. Recent events, like the reasons for justices Elena Kagan and Amy Coney Barrett to testify before Congress, have prompted us to write this, because we want all Americans to understand that we are drawing perilously close to the rule of law becoming optional. For any free and open democracy, not only is that unacceptable, but it is a death sentence for America.

Respect for the rule of law must come from everyone, and it most certainly should come from the highest officeholder in the land. Unfortunately, with the current administration, we have witnessed the exact opposite result.

Donald Trump with Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts, and Supreme Court Justices Elena Kagan, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett in February 2026.

Consider the fundamental text: The Declaration of Independence, which celebrated its 250th anniversary this year—and established what the framers viewed as the bedrock principles for a just government, starting with the declaration’s most hallowed statement, that all persons are created equal. But the document went on to list many grievances against the tyrannical rule of King George III, including the fact that the king had made “Judges dependent on his Will alone,” because it was solely the king’s grace that decided their continued employment or compensation. In response, our Constitution tried to insulate the federal judiciary from outside influence by providing for lifetime appointments.

But fast-forward to the present day, and President Donald Trump has repeatedly demeaned and insulted judges, variously claiming that a judge’s heritage, religion, or political affiliation can compromise their legal judgement. In February, he flagrantly labeled the members of the Supreme Court who had voted to overrule his tariffs as “fools and lapdogs,” claiming they were “swayed by foreign interests,” and attacking Neil Gorsuch and Coney Barrett, two of the justices he himself had appointed, calling them “an embarrassment to their families.”

Even more egregiously, the Trump administration has gone beyond schoolyard insults to taking actions that actually circumvent the rule of law.

For example, Trump’s use of the Justice Department to bring criminal prosecutions against those he thinks wronged him personally is one of his most brazen acts of defiance of established legal norms. The indictments of former FBI director James Comey, whom Trump fired, and Letitia James, the New York attorney general who brought a successful civil fraud case against Trump, his children, and Trump family businesses, were both thrown out of court because Trump’s selection of one of his former personal lawyers as the prosecutor was found illegal. The newest prosecution of Comey, because of a supposedly threatening arrangement of seashells on a beach, is equally unlikely to stand up under prevailing law.

The Ábrego Garcia matter is another instance of abuse, because it dramatizes the disobedience by the Trump administration with respect to immigration court orders. Kilmar Armando Ábrego Garcia was deported to the Salvadorean mega-prison despite being legally present in the US. The government first refused to return him, claiming, without adequate proof, that he was a member of the criminal organization MS-13. However, once the pressure became too much, he was returned to the US. Only then did the Justice Department charge him with human smuggling, claiming he had transported people within the US who were in the country unlawfully. His case was dismissed by the trial judge on the grounds of vindictive and selective prosecution and remains on appeal.

We are, without a doubt, in the midst of a veritable plague of looming dangers aimed squarely at the judiciary. Not only did an armed man attempt to assassinate Justice Brett Kavanaugh at his home in 2022 following a leak of the Dobbs decision, hostile threats directed at judges have more than tripled over the past decade, according to Chief Justice Roberts’s 2024 year-end report. Citing statistics from the US Marshals Service, the report said that in the past five years alone, more than 1,000 serious threats were investigated, and dozens of people were charged with crimes. In 2020, the US Marshals said it responded to over 4,000 threats or inappropriate communications against federal judges. In that same year, a disgruntled lawyer murdered US District Judge Esther Salas’s son and wounded her husband after gaining access to their home by posing as a delivery person. According to NBC News, in 2025, there were 103 unordered pizza deliveries to judges who had ruled against the Trump administration or spoke out about threats against the judiciary, and 20 were sent in Salas’s name.

As novelists, for decades, we have all explored themes of corruption, influence peddling, and pressure and threats against public servants in our fiction.

In Scott’s latest novel, Presumed Guilty, about a murder trial in a rural area in the upper Midwest, the longtime prosecutor, Hiram Jackdorp, and the trial judge, Wendy Carrington, have a contentious relationship. Jackdorp forced her out of his office when she was a young prosecutor, and later unsuccessfully attempted to prevent her election to the bench. But there is no moment during the trial when the novel’s narrator, the defense lawyer Rusty Sabich, sees Judge Carrington’s rulings as based on anything but a fair application of legal principles. She is a good judge whose fidelity to the rule of law prevents her from using her position for personal revenge.

In John’s 2008 novel The Appeal, an ambitious young attorney is unwittingly recruited by some nefarious special interests to seek election to the state supreme court. Their big money pours in and buys enough votes. He wins, unseats a legendary jurist, and takes office. But when the pay-off comes due, he realizes that his judicial independence is far more important than playing politics.

In David’s 1996 novel Absolute Power, an American president presumes himself to be above the rule of law and seeks to force his underlings to commit criminal acts that will benefit him. However, the institutions created to check and prevent just such abuses hold fast against these brazen king-like attempts to be immune from baldly unlawful actions. At the end of the novel the truth is revealed, and the criminal justice system holds the president appropriately accountable for his misdeeds.

The “rule of law” is not simply a slogan the three of us learned in law school, or a plot device we use in our fiction. It is what keeps our life in society from turning into the war of all against all, where laws that allow for a civilized way of life matter little and violence and chaos reign. It’s also what keeps our economy vibrant and growing.

Without the fair enforcement of the laws being sacrosanct, economic decline inevitably follows as investors decide against investing in American businesses, building plants or factories here, or purchasing American corporate or government bonds and other investment vehicles. If there is no certainty that commercial contracts or international trade agreements will be honored, this will also vastly diminish the potential of any economy. And if the environment is one where an unbiased court is not the final arbiter of legal disputes, our allies may well think twice before committing resources and lasting cooperation since the environment they sought to work and invest within could change without regard to legality. Economic decline invariably leads to widespread job losses, a lessening standard of living, a loss of confidence in institutions by the citizens, our allies stampeding away from us, and a dilution of every individual right outlined in the Constitution.

And it’s not just us who are worried. There are many other lawyers and judges who have expressed concern about the trajectory of this country to ignore court rulings if they collide with political expediency or partisan goals. Nonpartisan organizations like Keep Our Republic’s Article III Coalition initiative and the Democracy Rising Collaborative have brought together retired judges and advocates to sound the alarm over a country in peril.

What we are all advocating for is that the courts be given the respect they are due under the founding documents of this country. Article I of the United States Constitution established the legislative branch, the United States Congress. Article II established the executive branch, headed up by the presidency. Article III created the US Supreme Court, and granted the power to Congress to establish lower federal courts.

In the 1803 ruling of Marbury v. Madison, the Supreme Court asserted that the courts had the power of judicial review, and with that power came the ability to declare laws passed by the Congress as being unconstitutional. This one ruling lifted the judicial branch to full equality with the other branches, because their decisions would constitute the final ruling on whether or not something was legal or constitutional and in agreement with our rights protected under the Constitution.

In order to be fair and objective arbiters of the law, federal courts must be free from influence, bias, and manipulation from outside sources. There can be no middle ground here. The courts are either free to do their work or they are not.

Each time a court order is ignored or defied, a sliver of independence is torn from the judicial robe. If the executive branch’s answer to a ruling it does not like is simply to not enforce it, or to encourage disobedience through open disrespect, then the independence of the judiciary evaporates. Not only does the legal system itself suffer from this noncompliance, but every citizen does as well, because if one branch of government can defy and ignore court decisions, that means they can potentially defy and ignore the individual rights of any American citizen.

The rule of law must be respected, and the valid decisions of courts must be upheld by the government, even, and perhaps most importantly, when that ruling goes against the government. Only in that way can a free and independent judiciary continue to deliver the ideals outlined in the founding documents of what is the most durable democracy ever conceived and created. Without that, America can no longer claim to be the shining beacon on the hill, inspiring democracy the world over. We, in fact, will become the opposite of what this country has always stood for. Even with our combined imaginations, we can envision no greater tragedy.

I'm old enough to remember watching Da Ali G Show on HBO back in the early 2000s. Back then, a lot of the comedy Sacha Baron Cohen was doing was beyond outrageous.

Well, just recently, I watched Cohen's new movie, Ali G: Who Iz I? with my Prime subscription, and I have some very, very mixed feelings about it.

On one hand, it feels like we never left the 2000s, which is a good thing when this movie hits. But on the other hand, it feels like we never left the 2000s, which is a terrible thing when this movie falters. I'll explain.

Here's the thing about Sacha Baron Cohen: if he makes a comedy, there's a high probability that I'm going to laugh, A LOT, and Ali G: Who Iz I? is no exception. In fact, one scene in particular had me laughing so hard my stomach hurt.

In the scene, Ali G is making an apology video in which he uses A.I. to splice in the likes of Biggie and 2Pac, which is silly in itself. Then, he splices in Moses, Greta Thunberg, and Adolph Hitler rapping on a microphone, and I had to wipe my eyes. I was crying so hard. Mind you, Ali G showed this to a room full of people with different religious denominations, and one by one, everybody left the room. Pure gold.

There are other funny moments, too. That said, some of the “humor” in this movie is awful. This goes back to my earlier comment about how this movie feels like it comes right out of the early 2000s, as some of these jokes regarding race and sexism feel super dated.

This movie also feels fake at times - even more so than Cohen's other flicks. Even though there's a whole section in the credits showing the people who weren't in on the joke, it still feels too ridiculous to believe any of it, which brings me to my next point.

Sacha Baron Cohen is famous and has even been labeled ‘a thirst trap’ at times. So, I have a hard time believing that so many of the people involved in this story aren't just actors. Because come on now. Are you really going to tell me that people like A$AP Rocky and George Santos never heard of Ali G before?

In fact, that might be why Cohen takes on two new characters in Dr. Nira Cain-N'Degeocello - who's an annoying anti-appropriator - and Colonel Errab Morad - who's an Israeli counter-terrorist expert with nefarious intentions.

That said, a big problem with these characters is that they make the film seem even more scripted than other films in the past, like Bruno and Borat. That’s because there’s much more of a narrative in this one, and seemingly, a lot less spontaneity from those who are the butt of the jokes.

In that way, it's hard to suspend my belief that most of the events in this film are not just scripted, which robs it of the usual Sacha Baron Cohen humor and flair. At least for me, anyway.

So, while this movie did make me laugh at times, next to 2002's Ali G Indahouse, it's my least favorite of the Cohen stable of movies, those being the two Borat films and Bruno. This just reminds me that Ali G is my least favorite of Baron's characters.

In fact, I'm surprised that I laughed as much as I did given that I generally don't find Ali G funny as much as I find the responses he elicits from his interviewees. In that way, the movie is hilarious at times, but cringe at others. So, if you're looking for a good comedy in the current release schedule, then I guess you could do worse.

#3609. 10 Hacks Ever Siri AI User Should Know

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

If you're like me, you've spent years ignoring most of Siri's functionality. Sure, it's great for setting timers, making calls, and sending a text. But that's kind of it—Apple's promise of an "always-on" digital assistant never truly delivered.

But that's finally changed with the recent launch of Siri AI. Fifteen years after debuting the app on the iPhone 4S and four years after the release of ChatGPT, Apple has taken the time to build out its own private Apple Foundation Models (with little help from Google) that work both on-device and on Apple's servers to give quick responses to your queries. Siri AI's answers are short, to the point, and actually useful. However, the conversational side isn't the only new thing about Siri AI. In fact, once you scratch the surface, you'll find Siri AI features embedded across the entire iOS and macOS ecosystem. Here's how to get the most out of Apple's new, enhanced digital assistant.

Siri AI is already tuned for brevity. Compared to Gemini or Claude, its responses are short and to the point. But still, if you ask something with your voice, it responds using voice as well. I personally prefer to quickly read through Siri responses. If you’re like me, you can enable a hidden setting that makes sure that Siri always answers silently, no matter if you’re writing to it or using your voice. Go to Settings > Siri > Responses and switch to the Silent Response option.

On the other hand, if you prefer to listen to Siri's responses, it's worth it to spend some time fine-tuning them. If you have an iPhone that’s under two years old, you have access to a more expressive Siri voice. Siri AI has an Expressive Voice feature that works on iPhone 17 Pro and higher, iPhone Air, and Macs with an M3 processor or higher (at least 12GB RAM).

To find this feature, go to Settings > Siri > Voice. Here, you can change the Pace to make Siri faster or slower. The big feature is the Expressivity slider; you can use it to make Siri sound brighter and more enthusiastic, rather than flat. You also have several voice options at the top (color-coded).

Visual Intelligence is deeply integrated into iOS 27 and macOS 27, and it turns anything on your screen into a source that Siri AI can act upon. It can search anything on your screen, and even take action on things it finds out. You can highlight any text on an iPhone, tap and hold, and choose the Ask Siri option. On the Mac, Ask Siri is the first option in the right-click menu. Choose a file, select text, and get started talking to Siri.

But it goes further. Just pull up Siri AI on your iPhone or Mac and start asking questions about what you’re seeing on screen. If you’re seeing a photo of a cafe on Instagram, ask where it is, or ask Siri to open it in Maps. If you’re watching a scene from a movie or a TV show, ask Siri where it’s from.

Clean Up was part of Apple Intelligence features in iOS 18, but it wasn’t great. It used on-device models to remove objects, and the results were lacking. Now that Apple runs its own Apple Foundation Models in Private Cloud Compute, it can securely process images on its servers, and the Clean Up process is much better. It now removes objects from photos very reliably, and even accounts for shadows. But to use this, you have to make sure to use the High Quality feature (instead of the default Auto mode).

Tap the Edit button in a photo, go to Tools > Clean Up, and from the top, switch to the High Quality option. Now brush over or tap an object you want to remove. Then, tap Clean Up and wait for a while until Apple’s servers complete the process. Tap Done to save the changes.

One of the most tedious parts of using the Calendar app is manually entering multiple events from a complicated schedule—say, for a season's worth of your kid’s soccer practices, or your college course's weekly lecture schedule. With Visual Intelligence in iOS 27, this is now table stakes: You can point your iPhone camera towards a schedule or take a screenshot of one, then tap the Add to Calendar button. Siri will recognize all the events, and you’ll get an option to add them to the calendar individually or all at once.

Siri AI's Mail integration is a hidden gem. Once your iPhone or Mac is done indexing your local data from Mail, you can use Siri AI to triage and manage your Mail without even opening the Mail app. In my testing, it works really well, especially because Siri AI understands the context of an email. This means you don't need to remember the exact details about the sender or the subject. You can just ask something like, "Find all emails about my flights from last week and send them to my accountant." You can also ask it to do things for you. For example, you can say, "Archive all the emails from Walmart from last month," and it will give you a one-button option to do just that.

When you start using the new Siri AI more often, you'll realize that it asks for confirmation way too often. For things like deleting mail, that's useful. But for sending messages, less so. There is a hidden setting that removes the extra step when it comes to sending messages via Siri. Go to Settings > Siri > Responses and enable Automatically Send Messages.

After the Siri AI upgrade in iOS 27, I find myself using the Camera Control often, and you should try it too. Just press and hold the Camera Control button to launch the camera's Siri mode. Point towards anything you want to find out more about and tap the big Siri icon. In a second or two, you will get the Siri response at the top, along with relevant actions based on what you're looking at. This feature is genuinely useful, and if you don't like using the Camera Control (or don't have access to it on your iPhone), you can also add the Siri AI shortcut to the lock screen, Control Center, or the Action button.

While Shortcuts has been one of Apple's most powerful features, it's also one of the hardest to use. Making an automation requires setting up steps, selecting variables, and thinking about chronology, and more. With Siri AI, Apple is trying to reduce that burden. And when it comes to simpler stuff that an everyday iPhone user needs, it works.

For example, you can open Shortcuts, create a new shortcut, and use the Describe a shortcut feature to talk about a Shortcut you want to build in natural language. You can ask Siri to create a daily morning Shortcut that shows you the day's weather, upcoming calendar events, and the to-do list for the day. You can also ask it to create a Shortcut that converts images in batches and creates new notes with a pre-made template.

While Apple is now using its own Apple Foundation Models for the new Siri AI, ChatGPT isn’t technically gone. If you have a complex question, or if Siri AI’s answer isn’t doing the trick, you can still summon ChatGPT from the Siri AI app (no need to go to the ChatGPT app for this). Tap on the text field in the Siri app, choose the Ask option and then switch to the ChatGPT service. Siri AI is quite intelligent at routing, so if ChatGPT can’t answer, it will route you back to Siri AI’s own models.

#3608. Right-Leaning Tech Billionaires Are Prepping for a Blue Wave

It’s election Tuesday, and after years of lying low, the tech left is ready for its big comeback. “We’re gonna wipe the floor pretty aggressively,” one Democratic consultant who works with big tech donors boasted to me late last week. Meanwhile, a DC tech lobbyist I caught up with told me, “For my Republican friends, it’s like the fall of Saigon. Everyone’s trying to get the last chopper out.”

After the votes are all counted, I expect the postmortems coming out of Silicon Valley to start getting spicy. After all, the tech right hardly sat this one out. Elon Musk alone spent a reported $474 million on midterms races. A billionaire coalition including Sergey Brin, Patrick Collison, and Eric Schmidt spent more than $333 million to prevent the so-called billionaire tax in California. A swirling cadre of PACs and dark-money groups were caught using less-than-aboveboard tactics to combat a rising tide of public fury around AI. Spoiler: It didn’t work.

Over the last few weeks, I’ve been reporting on Greg and Anna Brockman, two of the tech mega-donors who’ve thrown the most money at this chaotic election cycle. While OpenAI cofounder and president Greg Brockman’s story has been told pretty extensively, Anna remains one of the last great mysteries on the AI frontier. As The Wall Street Journal put it this spring, “She is intensely private: Almost no information, including her maiden name, is available online.” Until now.

Read on to learn more about their AI-fueled love story, their slow-motion political misfire, and one of the more surprising twists in my journalism career: I went to college with her.

Over the weekend, Citrini threw a Halloween party in the now infamous apartment, where political data scientist David Shor, former OpenAI researcher Will DePue, and Ritual cofounder Niraj Pant stopped by. Dark.

But after learning more about the technology’s progress—and interviewing more than a couple of people he noted seem to “lack the empathy gene”—he became more fearful of what might happen when we unleash “swarms of agents that we allow to get out of our control.”

Buried in The Atlantic’s excellent profile of Donald Trump’s former White House deputy chief of staff and top Republican strategist James Blair was the tidbit that Meta had hired Blair to advise on its data-centers communications strategy. Meta did not respond to a request for comment.

#3607. Report: Apple expected to ship up to 1.5 million OLED touchscreen MacBook Pros in 2027

A new report from TrendForce explores Apple’s impact on the OLED notebook market following the launch of its first touchscreen MacBook Pro, and the company’s own shipment prospects for 2027. Here are the details.

Apple yesterday announced the new touchscreen MacBook Pro, which features the same tandem OLED technology it first introduced with the M4 iPad Pro in 2024.

With two OLED layers stacked on top of each other, the technology delivers higher brightness than conventional single-layer OLED displays, while maintaining the deep blacks, high contrast ratios, and power efficiency that OLED is known for.

And while yesterday’s announcement made it official, Apple’s first touchscreen Mac has long been rumored through leaks, reports, and supply chain analyses.

In September 2025, for instance, The Elec reported that Samsung Display was preparing to begin mass production of 14-inch and 16-inch OLED panels for Apple’s MacBook Pro in the second quarter of 2026, with an estimated annual output of 2–3 million units.

Two months later, TrendForce predicted that OLED notebook market share would reach up to 12% between 2027 and 2028, partly driven by Apple’s expected adoption of the technology.

Then, earlier this year, TrendForce published an OLED roadmap predicting that Apple would introduce OLED displays to the MacBook Pro lineup in 2026, followed by the MacBook Air in 2029 (pushed back from 2027).

Now, TrendForce has published a new report with new shipment forecasts for Apple’s OLED MacBook Pro and the broader OLED notebook market.

According to the firm, Apple is expected to ship between 1.2 million and 1.5 million units of the new MacBook Pro in 2027. Meanwhile, global OLED notebook shipments are projected to “grow nearly 40% YoY in 2026, followed by another increase of more than 40% in 2027.”

Until now, the OLED notebook market has been driven primarily by Windows-based brands such as Lenovo, HP, and ASUS, which have gradually expanded their OLED offerings across different price segments. Apple’s arrival is expected to give the market additional momentum, encouraging brands to prioritize OLED models in their product roadmaps while strengthening consumer acceptance of the technology. This, in turn, could pave the way for broader OLED adoption in notebook displays.

TrendForce also notes that the “new MacBook Pro’s premium starting price of US$2,899 for the 14-inch model, coupled with its initial availability alongside existing Mini-LED models, could temper near-term replacement demand.”

As for Apple’s first OLED MacBook Air, now expected to debut in 2029, TrendForce says LG Display, BOE, and TCL CSOT are currently competing to become display suppliers for the upcoming model, as the companies continue developing their OLED manufacturing capabilities.

Finally, TrendForce projects that global OLED notebook shipments will reach 46.6 million units by 2030, though year-over-year growth will slow to 30.8%, following a peak of 42.8% in 2028.

Scott Pelley found himself at the center of various headlines this past summer following his firing from his longtime post at 60 Minutes. It was reported in June that the veteran journalist had a tense meeting with the series’ then-relatively new executive producer, Nick Bilton. During that conversation, Pelley apparently accused CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss of “murdering” the news magazine show. Pelley was let go days later, and he’s now opening up about what happened in the immediate aftermath of his firing.

For over 25 years, Pelley served as a correspondent for 60 Minutes, reporting on a wide range of topics in that time. His firing, however, marked a rare instance in which he himself was part of the news, and that was a point made during a recent interview. Pelley recently spoke with Illinois State University’s WGLT and discussed his career as well as the state of journalism. When asked about what it was like having his name “in the headline,” Pelley began by discussing what occurred in the lead-up to CBS News cutting ties with him:

Well, it was surprising and it was sudden. We had been fighting a battle at 60 Minutes for more than a year trying to maintain the independence that we had had from our corporate owners, independence that we'd had for decades. The new owners didn't see it that way and they wanted to influence our scripts, influence our reporting.

The corporate details Pelley (which on YouTube) seem to allude to the formation of Paramount Skydance in 2025, which saw David Ellison serve as CEO. Last year, there were reports that various changes were happening at 60 Minutes under the new management and that some employees were unhappy. Pelley said that “for more than a year, the writing was on the wall.” The former CBS Evening News anchor then segued into his actually firing and how it led to an unusual situation for him (and his wife):

When they fired me for standing up for the people who had stood up for me at the broadcast and protected my stories and refused to kill my stories, I was, like I said, very surprised. I suddenly became the center of all of that reporting. And my colleagues in the press were camped out at the end of my driveway, waiting for me to come out and say something. My wife actually took one of the photographers to lunch one day. [laughs] So I appreciate my colleagues in the press. I understand they were just doing their jobs. But it was a crazy time.

Scott Pelley Has Advice For CNN Staffers After Paramount Merger And Issues With CBS And Bari Weiss

Scott Pelley hasn’t held back his thoughts about the state of 60 Minutes and CBS News as a whole. Not long after his firing, he criticized Bari Weiss and the leadership team and argued that the organization needed some “adult supervision." Pelley also didn’t mince words about the staff meeting that was held shortly after May 28, which saw other show alums like Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega were fired.

As indicated by his comments from the WGLT interview, Pelley has also made claims of editorial interference against his former bosses. Vega and others have also made similar claims about supposedly being asked to inject bias into their reporting. Weiss and co. have denied claims of journalistic interference. While Pelley isn’t pleased with the state of his former workplace or how his tenure there ended, he still feels a sense of gratitude:

I have such warmth in my heart for the 27 years that I was allowed to do 60 Minutes in the right way. And I feel that the way it's being done now is just was going to shock my conscience even further. And that if they hadn't have fired me, I probably would have quit by now.

Amid its ongoing 59th season, 60 Minutes has reportedly been experiencing ratings troubles. Bari Weiss recently addressed concerns during a public conversation and asserted that the show had been doing “tremendously well.” As for Scott Pelley, he’s stated on a few recent occasions that he hasn’t watched the show since his firing.

#3605. Everything You Should See Along With ‘You Can See Everything’

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

You Can See Everything, the new documentary about Theranos founder (and accomplished con artist) Elizabeth Holmes from filmmakers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, is breaking records (and brains). Not only is it raking it in at the box office in a way that few documentaries can manage, it’s also dominating the pop culture chat right now thanks to genre-defying techniques; a huge, rule-breaking twist (that I won't spoil); and its unrepentant and inexplicably mesmerizing subject.

While some might argue that you should head into this incredible film experience fresh, if you’re unfamiliar with any of the three major figures involved, you will benefit from a little prep work before you head in—and if you've already seen it, you're no doubt eager to dive even deeper into this truly remarkable (in every sense of the word) story. Here’s what you should watch, read, and listen to before or after You Can See Everything.

To put it simply: There’s a lot going on here. To ensure you can appreciate the film, you should make sure you know at least the basics about three things: Elizabeth Holmes (and why she’s infamous), and the work of both Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. Here’s the crash course.

The 2019 podcast The Dropout is one of the most efficient ways to get the background on Holmes and Theranos. In the style of a true crime podcast, this show from ABC and journalist Rebecca Jarvis offers a deep dive into Holmes and her crimes that will give you all the background you’ll need.

John Carreyrou is the journalist who broke the Holmes story wide open, and his award-winning book Bad Blood offers a more journalistic and less sensational investigation than other accounts, providing a close-up look at Holmes in her CEO persona—an alternately terrifying and charismatic person who comes across as a “character” Holmes is playing. The book will inform your viewing of the documentary in important ways.

While Nathan Fielder is getting most of the attention for You Can See Everything, co-director Lance Oppenheim brings his signature technique to the film—it wouldn’t be nearly as interesting without his visual sensibility and framing.

Oppenheim has helmed several notable films, as he’s made a name for himself as a brilliant documentarian over the last few years, but to get ready for You Can See Everything, check out Spermworld, his 2024 exploration of unregulated sperm donations (you read that right). The doc deals with people who are as reality-challenged, manipulative, and possibly delusional as Holmes, and it will prep you for his visual style of extreme close-ups and excessive coverage that seems almost impossible in a normal documentary setting. You can stream Spermworld on Hulu.

If you’re unfamiliar with Nathan Fielder’s work, you need to strap in, because he’s unlike any other comedian or documentarian you’ve ever encountered.

To get a sense of his style, start with Nathan for You, a comedy-documentary-reality TV hybrid in which Fielder—as a version of himself—tries to use his business experience to help struggling people and small businesses. Presented as totally sincere, Fielder’s ideas are nevertheless increasingly elaborate and, in a word, unhinged. This show will familiarize you with Fielder’s persona and approach, but if you only have time to cram one episode, check out the series finale, “Finding Frances.” It follows Fielder’s attempts to reunite one of his earlier clients with his long-lost love, and it is a nearly perfect encapsulation of his style and approach. You can stream Nathan for You on HBO Max, Hoopla or Paramount Plus, or rent it episode-by-episode on Prime Video.

You should also watch at least some of Fielder’s other series, The Rehearsal. Here, Fielder (again, portraying a version of himself) attempts to help people prepare for difficult conversations utilizing increasingly outlandish techniques and scenarios that spiral into comedic insanity, including building sets, hiring actors, and immersing himself and his subjects in an alternate reality of sorts—an approach that will prepare you for some of You Can See Everything’s swerves. If you don’t have time to watch the whole thing, just check out the first episode, “Orange Juice, No Pulp.” It’s a self-contained chapter and will give you the basics. You can stream The Rehearsal on Apple TV or HBO Max, or rent episodes on Prime Video.

Have more bandwidth before watching You Can See Everything, or want a deeper dive after the documentary has melted your brain? Here’s what else you can check out.

The companion podcast to Carreyrou’s book, Bad Blood: The Final Chapter, is well worth a listen. Hearing the journalist’s perspective about his investigation and work during and after Holmes’ trial offers additional insight into her personality and methods that will really resonate after watching her in Fielder and Oppenheim’s doc.

Once you’ve noodled on You Can See Everything for a moment, there are two more movies you should check out.

For more on Holmes’s specific grift and how she pulled it off, Alex Gibney’s excellent The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley is the way to go, especially if you didn’t follow the Theranos story closely at the time and your main visual guide to Holmes is the new documentary. Gibney’s film is more traditional, but offers a wealth of insight into Holmes and her bubble. You can stream The Inventor on HBO Max or rent it on Prime VIdeo.

If you more from co-director Lance Oppenheim, watch Some Kind of Heaven, his 2020 breakout documentary about The Villages retirement community in Florida. It’s the film that put Oppenheim on the map, and offers hints of the same detached observational style that makes You Can See Everything so arresting. You can stream Some Kind of Heaven on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Speaking of which, if you loved the visual style and “enhanced” reality of You Can See Everything and want to see more of that, catch the Robert Pattinson-starring Primetime, still in theaters. It’s Oppenheim's narrative film directorial debut, and combines his hyperstyled visual flair with thriller pacing and a narrative based on a true story.

The Curse, Fielder’s 2023 TV series, is his first work of fiction, and it offers some fascinating insights. It follows a newly married couple (played by Fielder and Emma Stone) who struggle to get an HGTV-style show off the ground as things get excruciatingly awkward (and, eventually, kind of surreal). After watching You Can See Everything, it will be interesting to see how Fielder views the power of editing, the ethics of reality TV, and working with a name actor to get the results that he wants. Plus, similarly to the film, The Curse swerves into a final act that will melt your brain. You can stream The Curse on Apple TV or rent it on Prime Video.

You should also definitely watch The Dropout, the 2022 Hulu series starring Amanda Seyfried. It’s a well-made film, and Seyfried’s performance was rightly praised for capturing the weirdness of Holmes' public persona. You can stream The Dropout on Hulu.

#3604. Phantom Blade Zero Meets God of War Ragnarök in Upcoming Steam Action Game Hit

There's more God of War here than expected

Right now, the gaming world is obsessed with Phantom Blade Zero. S-Game’s Wuxia-inspired action game landed as one of the highest-rated games of 2026 and immediately tore up the charts on Steam, cracking 800,000 concurrent players on launch weekend. I’m enjoying Phantom Blade Zero, even if it does have a few too many parries for my taste. But it’s primarily made me more excited about a similar, promising game I briefly played earlier this year: Tides of Annihilation.

Tides of Annihilation is a forthcoming contender in a specific subgenre of games largely developed in China that defy easy characterization but have been rapidly growing in popularity, thanks to hits like Phantom Blade Zero and Black Myth: Wukong. Earlier this year, at Gamescom 2026, I played about 45 minutes of what appeared to be an early level. It ruled. (Tides made Polygon’s list of the best games at Gamescom 2026.) It’s a little bit character action game, a little bit Soulslike. But in many ways, it’s more in conversation with God of War (2018) and its sequel, God of War Ragnarök, than with anything out of FromSoftware’s haunted halls.

In fact, here’s a line directly from my notes: “Hot girl god of war???”

There is simply no way around it: Gwendolyn, the main character of Tides of Annihilation, is stunning. This has become some matter of debate among the game’s community.

In July, 2025 Game Awards winner Jennifer English, initially slated to play Gwendolyn, dropped out of the role, citing health concerns. Eclipse Glow Games quickly revealed her replacement as Angela Sant’Albano (best known for her role as Grace Ashcroft in Resident Evil Requiem), and around the same time, redesigned Gwendolyn’s facial features. “Do we all agree that she looks beautiful?” reads one top Reddit post from the time. You’ll never believe this but: No. No they did not all agree.

Hands-on with Tides, I can say that Gwendolyn’s model doesn’t look cheap, rushed, or like “every mmo Korean AI slop model,” to quote one Reddit user. She looks great — like an actual human being rather than an anime figurine tucked into the corner of an IKEA bookshelf. And yes, she happens to be conventionally attractive. But Gwendolyn’s character design isn’t played for sheer objectification, like, say, genre contemporary Stellar Blade treats its main character Eve. The camera never lingers uncomfortably at creep-shot angles, nor are scenes framed like peep shows. That said, because I only played a small portion of Tides, who knows what the full game will be like. But given how much discussion Gwendolyn’s character model has already generated, this will almost certainly be a hot topic upon its release.

Anyway. The game. Tides of Annihilation’s fantasy elements are inspired by Arthurian legend (there’s another God of War nod for you). Set in modern-day London, a mysterious entity called the Fog has wrought apocalyptic destruction, as tree roots a foot wide snake their way through the city. Rage-red crystals pepper the buildings that remain, as do a variety of Gothic-inspired humanoids and fantasy creatures. Gwendolyn appears to be the only person left alive who possesses any way to resist the Fog, and seeks a way to undo its damage.

On a basic level, combat in Tides is a lot like many other flashy, fast-paced character action games: You can perform light attacks, heavy attacks, and various combos that string both together. You can jump, dodge, and parry, and variously colored glints of enemy attacks will indicate which of those defensive moves you should make. Enemies have stagger bars that you whittle down, stunning them when depleted. And finishing moves tend to be stylish as hell; in one, Gwendolyn ripped a 15-foot-long spear out of her enemy’s hand, then leapt into the air before careening it through her foe. But the biggest gimmick in combat is the addition of equippable knights.

Knights are avatars, inspired by the famous Knights of the Round Table, who accompany Gwendolyn at all times. You can use these knights to “enhance” your attacks; though Gwendolyn is always a speedy fighter, knights can alter your moveset to be more defensive, to prioritize staggering, or apparently to even introduce game-changing abilities like a time-stopping mechanic. Though I only was able to use two in my demo, Gwendolyn can unlock up to ten knights in the full game. (Historians disagree about how many knights actually sat at the table.)

These knights are also critical parts of the 3D Metroidvania aspects of Tides. My preview was largely located in a single area, in and around a museum of Egyptian history. To explore the museum fully, I needed to use my knights. Bors had to fire his bow to create ziplines across wide chasms, while Palamedes needed to smash down fractured walls and reposition bookshelves between balconies, creating makeshift bridges. It’s all reminiscent of the ways Kratos and Atreus navigate the nine realms of Norse myth: merrily moving along until you need to tap Triangle to shoot the thing. All the combat prowess in the world, and you still can’t navigate it alone.

That’s not all the God of War on display here. For instance, at one point, my path forward was blocked off by a wall of red crystals. I later earned the ability to pick up an explosive red sphere that looked like a grapefruit; tossing it at the wall of crystals caused them to shatter, a mechanic that’s an almost 1:1 recreation of God of War Ragnarök’s Shatter Crystals.

I say this not as a knock on derivative game design but rather as a compliment to an evolving niche of popular video games. You don’t need to closely follow the industry to see that the Chinese action game scene is popping off in a real way in recent years, with a string of slick projects that each have a distinct feel and style. Tides of Annihilation comes on the heels of Black Myth and Phantom Blade, but is also on most-anticipated lists alongside Blood Message, one of the most promising games out of Summer Game Fest 2026. (This is to say nothing of the behemoth that is miHoYo, which has its own game in this vein with the forthcoming Nodusfall.)

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

These games all neatly fit into what my colleague Oli Welsh has deemed the “outsider AAA” game — highly polished games from well-funded studios that nevertheless outside of the Nintendo-Xbox-PlayStation Bermuda Triangle. These games aren’t quite born from the halls of megawatt funding, but they’re no less excellent — nor held in lower esteem. Black Myth: Wukong nabbed a Game Awards nomination in 2024. Phantom Blade Zero is in the conversation for 2026, though faces a steep uphill climb against the likes of You Know What. For many reasons, least of all that it does not yet have a release year, I would not even begin to wager a formal prediction about Tides of Annihilation, let alone in writing. Then again, you don’t need to see the tides change to know that they will.

Tides of Annihilation will be released for PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X.

A new breed of reactionary studio from outside gaming's traditional heartlands wants a piece of the blockbuster pie

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Am I the only one who is tired of hearing about Phantom Blade? It's not a big deal outside of Asia, and I can't tell if article authors are unaware or chasing what they believe is the next giagantic game because the game China driving the huge numbers and everyone else seems to be rather average on it.
