#3602. Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death Is a Documentary About the Shocking Deaths of Two Biohacking Influencers

If you’re familiar with the term “looksmaxxing,” which refers to an online trend dedicated to optimizing one’s life by way of physical improvement through steroids and peptides made popular in the manosphere, then you’ve inevitably come across Clavicular. The 20-year-old influencer, born Braden Peters, has become the (often bone-smashed) face of this male-dominated internet subculture. Famous for viral stunts that often leave him bruised, battered, or, in at least one instance, hospitalized, Peters has faced a slew of legal battles while documenting his physical transformation for his more than 2 million followers.

“It was actually never a Clavicular thing,” says director Stacey Lee, the filmmaker behind Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death, a three-part docuseries about manosphere biohackers that begins streaming on Hulu November 10. News that the online looksmaxxing influencer Clavicular would appear in a documentary “got picked up and swept into places that weren’t what we were up to,” Lee tells Vanity Fair in her first interview about the project.

“Look, when you’re making a documentary about influencers, it’s very hard for the documentary itself not to become caught up in that [world],” she says, clarifying that Clavicular was never the documentary’s focus. “We were looking to spend time and actually understand these guys—not just as outrageous human beings, but what is driving them? Where are they coming from?” says Lee.

Following influencers like Clavicular may help illuminate what motivates an increasingly popular, exceedingly online idea of modern masculinity. A generation of boys who were socialized behind screens, and sold steroids as a cure-all for their societal woes, came of age in the two years that Lee and her crew spent shadowing various manosphere influencers, starting in 2023. “When we came in, this was niche,” says Lee, “and even after the first [day of] shooting, it was front and center, mainstream cultural conversation—politics, RFK, all these things coming into play as we were making this documentary. Simultaneously, all of the documentary’s main looksmaxxers “escaped to Thailand because America doesn’t offer them enough,” Lee says, shrugging. “So there’s a bit of contradiction in that.”

The resort city of Pattaya, Thailand, is where Lee was introduced to Tony Huge, born Anthony Hughes, an “overstuffed Marvel character,” a biohacking influencer who predated Andrew Tate, Bryan Johnson, and Clavicular, says Lee. “He became famous for taking DNP, which is a fat burner. Essentially you take one pill and lose a bunch of weight, you take two pills and…people [could] die,” she explains. “He was willing to go on camera and do things that a lot of people at the time were not. In the world of bodybuilding and fitness culture, so many men are taking a bunch of drugs but not really talking about it, whereas Tony took a different approach. And that created this brand, maybe an illusion for him, of radical transparency. But when you are like, you can see everything, it actually makes you more on guard like, what are we not seeing?”

Tony Huge, whose online mantra to his 250,000 followers across social media became “a day natty [short for natural] is a day wasted,” became a steroid-injecting pioneer for a group of vulnerable men, such as documentary participant Elon Muscular, a then-suicidal 19-year-old who messaged Hughes on Facebook and received an invite to his hero’s Thailand compound. “Young men were drawn into this world because they were disillusioned with the modern medical kind of environment of being told what not to do,” says Lee. “They were also feeling the statistics of loneliness and depression amongst men that are just becoming increasingly worse.”

Muscular found community in Hughes’s admittedly “cult-like” living situation, one where multiple men manipulated each other’s brain chemistry—and made social media content about it—all in the name of masculinity. “Most men come to Thailand because they’re mentally unstable,” Hughes says in the docuseries. Among his rotating circle of sidekicks was online influencer Leo Longevity, a fellow biohacker and self-described penis-enlargement expert who died in January 2023 inside the home that he shared with Hughes. “Obviously, a penis influencer dying within this manospheric space was already a really absurd story,” says Lee. “But we started to see that this wasn’t just a one-off situation, but a larger reoccurring issue within this world, and certainly people that are part of this specific community. Then it became a little bit more urgent, the story.”

“Why Is Everyone Around Tony Huge Dying?” reads a YouTube comment under one of Hughes’s videos after the death of Longevity, real name Laith Abdallah Algaz, which is included in the documentary. That is a central question that also emerges in Looksmaxxing, as the series uncovers the string of sudden and strange deaths of Hughes’s closest confidants, including Nick Weisser (in 2018) and Josh Brooks (in 2021), and the apparent disappearance of Coach Trevor in 2022. “Throughout the process, I was very straight up with Tony, ‘I’m going to ask you all the things that everyone’s already talking about behind your back. And I think it’s really important that you have to answer them,’” Lee recalls. “He’s never fazed by that, to be honest, which doesn’t feel like a normal response. Tony said in the beginning, ‘I don’t care if I’m a villain or hero. I don’t know which one it is,’” says the director. “He gets censored so much that he’s just willing to put his story out and see.”

Lee’s crew began filming with Hughes following Algaz’s death. “Everyone was presenting a united front on camera, and behind the scenes there was a lot of conversation that we started to become aware of about how they were being portrayed or what they were going to say,” she says, even pitching ideas to the director. “Actually, no, that’s for your channel. Just be yourself and let’s see how that feels,” Lee told them. “These guys don't do therapy. We did offer them mental health services many times. But they exist in this matrix, so to speak. They don’t trust medical professionals, [preferring to rely on] their own best sense of judgment.”

Nevertheless, Lee was welcomed into Hughes’s scarcely female circle of trust. “I was in their life so much, it was like they forgot that I was a woman a lot of times. After we’d wrapped something, Tony would be like, ‘Oh, what did you think of that?’” she says. “It’s almost like he remembered that they were talking about Red Pill philosophy or whatever it was in front of me. I remember a conversation very early on talking about how women can’t be successful in careers and should never be a leader. And yet here I was, sitting here directing a team of mostly men in a documentary.”

Gender dynamics were harder to ignore when documenting the multiple women who live with Hughes in Thailand. “A man should only have as many girlfriends as he can leg press,” Hughes says in one video that’s in the docuseries. “In regards to the women, yeah, that was one of the hardest parts to witness,” says Lee. “That’s where the inherent contradiction of who he is comes in. He proposes freedom, yet he’s got these women that are forced to live with him. Well, they can leave at any point in time. But there’s power dynamics at play, money at play. He genuinely believes he’s helping, improving them. It’s a very complex situation to say the least,” the filmmaker continues. “It was important to give those women, where we could, the voice to speak for themselves, but also to showcase what biohacking looks like for them within that space.”

Lee and her crew also built trust with Hughes’s closest allies, including Connor Murphy, a fitness-influencer-meets-performance artist whose online presence was predicated on pranks and then, while living with Hughes, on being the influencer’s “art project,” Murphy says in the doc. “My parents are extremely worried because a lot of people in the atmosphere around you-know-who seem to be dying,” Murphy tells Lee in the documentary. “At first it frightened me, but now it kind of enlivens me. I almost feel like a wizard. The boy who lived—for now,” he adds, raising his eyebrows in a smirk.

“As we got to know the characters deeper, they weren’t just one lump unit, but their own tectonic plates that were constantly realigning,” says Lee. “And that’s symptomatic of the larger manosphere itself. Everyone’s climbing a totem pole. They were, in a way, competing over who gets to tell the story.”

Things came to a sudden halt on July 7, when Murphy died at the age of 32 in what authorities have ruled an apparent drowning. “Production had finished [four weeks earlier] when he passed. I was on the phone with these guys all the time talking to them about what’s going on and where they’re at,” says Lee, who grows visibly emotional at every mention of Murphy. “His death was absolutely shocking. When you spend two years filming with them and getting to know them just as a regular human being, it affected me deeply.”

Hughes subsequently made a video saying that Murphy drowned in his backyard lake during an erratic drug-induced episode. (Investigators reportedly found two unused syringes and several white pills in a bag inside Murphy’s car.) “His passing reinforced why we were making this documentary. He wasn’t just somebody who died,” says Lee. “Being able to show that complicated side of who he was and not just his death defining his life was really, really important for us.”

As the mother of a nine-year-old son, Lee worries about the dearth of positive male examples in online spaces. “With these influencers—the Tates, the Fuentes, all these guys who are performing masculinity, it was so apparent to me that we are lacking really good male role models, where men have each other’s backs, where they’re looking out for the best in each other, where they’re lifting one another up,” says Lee. The next generation of men are “looking at these guys and seeing it as a blueprint for their life. When you call yourself an influencer, there is a level of responsibility that needs to be taken for what you say and do,” she says. “And in this world, because they want to be anarchist and free and don’t take responsibility for anyone, that is what creates these tragedies.”

While more daring online personalities infiltrate the manosphere, “there is a sense of Tony losing relevancy,” Lee says of Hughes, who is father to three daughters and a son on the way with his live-in girlfriends. “When you lose relevancy,” she adds, “you try and control what’s closest to you. When your identity is built around pushing boundaries, what happens when the next generation’s going further than you? And how do you know when it’s enough?”

As the younger generation turns to new influencers in the biohacking space, Lee says there’s plenty of evidence to suggest looksmaxxers—and the appetite for their content—aren’t going anywhere. “What we are witnessing is nihilism within the next generation where it’s about living for today. I need to look as hot as I can today,” she tells VF. “We are being trained to find the easy, quick solution and those solutions are never going to fix these emotionally complex layers of confidence and purpose and true connection. Those aren’t going to be found online.”

#3601. The Best Apple Watch for Most People Is Over $100 Off

The Apple Watch Series 10 was released in September 2024, and it's one of the best ways to get into the Apple Watch in 2026 without breaking the bank. Right now, the titanium 46 mm case model with cellular capabilities is $112 off, bringing the price down to $637 (originally $749). That's the lowest price after Apple raised prices this summer due to the RAM shortage, according to price-tracking tools. The same model in gold titanium is also over $100 off, reaching $679 (originally $799), saving you the same amount compared to the latest Series 12 going for $799.

The Apple Watch Series 10 was considered the best Apple Watch for most people last fall and is a great replacement if you're still wearing the more budget SE. There are also some key upgrades from the Apple Watch 9, although they're less noticeable than previous Apple Watch upgrades. If you're curious to know how it compares to other flagship smartwatches from its time, you can check out our head-to-head comparison.

Some of the first things you'll notice on the Series 10 are a thin case and a big OLED screen (either 1.6 inches or 1.8 inches, depending on which model you get). The Series 10 has audio playback, meaning you can listen to podcasts, take calls, or listen to Spotify on its speakers. The sleep features allow notifications for signs of sleep apnea. What you're giving up by saving on this version over the latest Series 12 is a faster S11 chip, a newer Health Sensing System and the Readiness app (tracks daily insights, vitals, and other metrics), a longer battery life (from 18 to 24 hours), 5G RedCap support (it helps save on battery life and has better network coverage compared to 5G), and audio intelligence features like Live Rewind, Siri Recap, and Sound Recognition.

If those extra features don't matter to you, the Series 10 is a great Apple Watch to get in 2026 at a discount, when many are still suffering from their price hikes.

Warning! The following contains spoilers for the Dancing With The Stars episode "Disney Night." Stream the episode with a Disney+ subscription, and read at your own risk!

Dancing With The Stars' Disney Night made me realize I'm ready to share some thoughts about frontrunner Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson that I've sat on for a while. As they continue their run on the 2026 TV schedule, I have a separate issue with both dancers that is making me root against them.

Harry and Jenna received another perfect dance score, and Julia Stiles was sent home as I expected. They're still the favorites to win it all, but honestly, they're losing my support down the stretch for two major reasons.

Jenna and Harry's Disney Night dance was a tribute to Mary Poppins, and one that seemed strangely centered on Jenna. It was odd the judges gave a perfect score to a dance in which Harry was essentially relegated to a backup dancer in the final thirty seconds of the routine, while the camera focused in on her at center stage.

Judges are usually quick to point out when a pro dancer is highlighting themselves more than their celebrity companion, as it's often done to mask the weak dancing of the competitor. Of course, we all know Harry is talented, so they wouldn't say that, but I'm shocked no one on the Dancing With The Stars panel at least mentioned how little the dance revolved around him. We need to see more of what Harry can do, not Jenna.

Harry Shum Jr. is also annoying me, because I feel his shock each and every week at the judges' scores is so performative. He is one of the few competitors with professional dancing experience in Dancing With The Stars, and yet I feel he's constantly going out of his way to appear shocked when he gets a 10 or talk about how unexpected all the praise he's getting is.

Shirley Ballas' DWTS Scores Were A Real Jump Scare, But I Think They Were Needed

It's giving me the same vibe as when Jenna Johnson performed with JoJo Siwa, and it has made me want to root against him. Harry is the odds-on favorite to win Dancing With The Stars Season 35, and the less he acts like it, the angrier I get.

I get that Harry Shum Jr. is working just as hard as everyone else on Dancing With The Stars. I think there's a way for both him and Jenna to acknowledge the work they've done, while admitting they can also do more elaborate routines because she doesn't have to teach him the basics. I'd be much more supportive if they took that route, but acting like the 10s are a surprise is making me want to give my vote to someone else.

Dancing With The Stars continues on ABC on Tuesdays at 8:00 p.m. ET, and with just three weeks to go, it's almost time to crown a winner! Is this going to have another predictable ending, or will we be crowning a dark horse winner on finale night?

#3598. Hasan Piker’s Lawyer Says Suing Scott Jennings is Just the Beginning

The clash between left-wing political commentator Hasan Piker and his media detractors is moving from the chatroom to the courtroom. One week after Piker filed a $72.5 million defamation suit against conservative commentator and CNN personality Scott Jennings, his attorney, defamation lawyer Daniel Watkins, tells Vanity Fair Piker is “just getting started.”

“There are other people and other entities that will likely receive outreach from my law firm in the coming days,” says Watkins. “They know they have a reckoning coming.”

The Jennings lawsuit, which accuses the former Republican strategist of falsely telling listeners of his Salem Media podcast that Piker advocated for lynchings, comes at the end of a busy, and tumultuous election cycle for Piker, who—after years of online politicking—became a popular surrogate for far-left insurgents, and a popular boogeyman for virtually everyone else. It’s an apparent payback for the mainstream media, whose obsession with villainizing Piker has meant guilt-by-association for everyone Piker champions (and has far outpaced Piker’s actual name-recognition and influence).

On the podcast, which aired on August 11, Jennings shared a spliced montage of the Twitch streamer appearing to make racist and incendiary remarks, some of them about lynching. It’s packaged as an attempt to dissuade Michigan voters from voting for Senatorial candidate Abdul El-Sayed, Piker’s “best pal and campaign partner,” Jennings said.

I watched the October 2024 stream from which the most inflammatory snippets in Jennings’s sizzle reel were spliced together. On the stream, Piker is live-reacting to a YouTube video from the popular channel Jubilee, in which a Black conservative debates a Black liberal.

At one point, an incredulous Piker pauses the video and very clearly mocks the Black conservative by saying, “Can we go back to a better time when lynchings were happening?” At another point, after a commenter asks why he’s “always doing too much with black people” Piker responds sarcastically, “Yes dude, it’s because I’m racist, that’s why. It’s because I’m fucking racist dude.” Both of these clips are included in the Jennings segment without context.

At the end of August Watkins sent a retraction demand and spoke to Christopher Henderson, Salem Media’s chief legal officer. Absent a reply, they proceeded with a lawsuit. (At the time of publication Henderson and Jennings have not responded to a request for comment.)

Piker’s suit against Jennings is seeking $27.5 million in compensatory damages, and $45 million in punitive damages. Piker says he left it to the lawyers to crunch the numbers. “I don't know what I'm worth, if we're being real,” Piker told Vanity Fair in an interview this week.

“I have been very deliberately anti-litigation for a very long time,” Piker said, “but something shifted that’s been bubbling up where…people like Scott Jennings, and there are others as well,” he claims, “started trafficking in outright lies, defamation, and slander.”

“It is particularly pernicious to misattribute a quote to someone,” Watkins said. He explained that for Piker, “who has built a career at a platform based on advocating for marginalized people and taking stances that are not necessarily popular,” such misattributions are “disgusting and vile and dangerous.”

For Piker, the turn to legal action is partly a pro-truth crusade against “pundits who’ve gotten far too comfortable thinking that they can just get away with making ridiculous claims about people.” He pointed out what he claims is a pattern where outlets circulate clips that omit key words, fundamentally transforming the sentiments of their subjects. “I’ve observed this with the likes of James Talarico, for example. He’ll say something and then they’ll cut it right before you can associate with the full context of the statement,” Piker said.

He also admitted that it’s personal. “First and foremost, [the lawsuit is] for me.” He cited what he alleges is “reputational harm,” “emotional harm,” and “financial damages,” sharing that the lynching comment had spurred someone to “stalk a public event [he] was at.”

“When is the last time you experienced eight consistent months of [mainstream media] having one primary villain?” Piker asked. “It’s not fun at all. It sucks.”

Discussing the Michigan race where the controversy with Jennings began, Piker noted El-Sayed’s primary opponent Haley Stevens’s surprising Sunday endorsement of Republican nominee Mike Rogers. Explaining her party defection, Stevens made specific reference to Piker, criticizing El-Sayed for associating with him.

Piker believes Stevens’s statements will backfire in El-Sayed’s favor as the votes are tallied in Michigan.

“Okay, a Twitch streamer is the reason why you’re endorsing ICE raids in every city?” Piker said, referencing Rogers’s platform. “That’s ridiculous.”

Piker maintains, as he has since July, that his political interventions do more good than harm—for everyone except him. In the case of his surrogacy for El-Sayed, he said, “The only person who got attacked in the process was me. I was the one who had his reputation destroyed in the process.”

As for Piker’s own relationship with El-Sayed, he admits it’s not quite as buddy-buddy as Jennings suggested. Piker stumped for the Michigander in the primaries before receding somewhat. “My relationship with him has always been one of…a transactional nature,” he said.

Piker will spend election night streaming live from his home in LA and checking in periodically with candidates. When the midterms are over, he seems prepared to continue delivering comeuppance to those he feels have unfairly represented him during this election cycle.

So who else can expect to get hit with a lawsuit?

Piker didn’t say, exactly, but he did note that Ronna McDaniel, the former chair of the RNC, who, on C-Span last week, repeated the claim that Piker supports reinstating lynchings. He also pointed to Sen. Ted Cruz, who re-shared the clip from Jennings on X. Last week, Piker responded to the X post with a link to the news of his lawsuit against Jennings and wrote, “hey ted you seen this ?” (Cruz and McDaniel did not respond to a request for comment.)

When asked if Piker’s post on X was a clue as to a future lawsuit against Cruz, Watkins answered: “Buckle up.”

Piker did not disclose other specifics regarding future litigation, saying only this: “if you felt as though you could outright fabricate quotes and make up totally ridiculous claims about me, you should probably work on your retractions immediately.”

I wish all of late night were this hopeful.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Late night has been a heavy topic of conversation ever since CBS announced The Late Show with Stephen Colbert was canceled months in advance last TV season. The fall 2026 schedule still has a reasonable number of late night shows airing, with NBC and ABC still participating and hosts like John Oliver filling some of the gaps left by CBS. However, for completely valid reasons, some late night fans have been concerned about the future of the genre, particularly when it comes to Jimmy Kimmel's future.

The good news? NBC doesn’t really seem to be on the same page.

If you’ve been browsing the interwebs at all over the last couple of years, you probably know the relationship between Jimmy Kimmel and the White House is strained at best and hostile at worst. Jimmy Kimmel Live! (and other series The View) have faced pressure from the FCC and Kimmel was famously suspended following comments made on the air about the assassination of Charlie Kirk.

Since he’s been back, his monologues have been heavily political and targeted at Donald Trump. The President of the United States has called Kimmel a “loser” and more choice words.

Meanwhile, people have been tuning in to hear what Jimmy Kimmel has to say in larger volume, particularly in the wake of the loss of Stephen Colbert. Things are seemingly good, or are they?

We’re nearing Christmas, and there’s a lot coming down the pipeline at ABC. Of note, it’s worth pointing out that Kimmel’s contract is up at the end of the TV season next spring. I would have assumed with Colbert out of the picture and ratings up, a renewal would have been considered a sure thing, but then ABC’s Dana Walden said the financial picture CBS painted around Colbert was not inaccurate. The head honcho called Kimmel “phenomenal,” but said ad dollars on YouTube and other social media sites are not as lucrative as Live+7 viewers are, noting the late night audience is increasingly becoming more and more segmented.

Some insiders aren’t bullish about the future for the “unmanageable” late night host, either. Meanwhile, Jimmy Kimmel actually wanted to retire from late night at one point, so Jimmy Kimmel Live! ending probably wouldn’t be a personal disaster for the man. For the genre, however? Well, it’s a whole lot more worrying.

Meanwhile, over at the Peacock Network, head honchos seem pleased as punch with Jimmy Fallon and The Tonight Show. This is despite the fact Fallon is losing in total viewership to Jimmy Kimmel. (Though it’s worth noting ratings are up for both the Jimmys, with Fallon getting a 5% total viewer lift and 16% lift in the 18-49 demo.) While I’m sitting here on pins and needles worrying about the future of Live, NBC’s own Chris Miller, the showrunner on The Tonight Show, is already looking ahead to 2029.

That’s the year The Tonight Show will hit its 75th anniversary, a huge milestone number, and one Miller believes NBC is excited about. Miller told Variety:

We’re absolutely talking about it. We are sort of next in line for a big tentpole type of anniversary. Yes, we are actively thinking about it and talking about it and hope we will have fun news for that soon.

It’s not unusual for late night shows to look ahead. Miller mentioned in the same interview The Tonight Show is already booking out well into March of next year. The show in general seems to be thinking about the future of the show, but also non-linear programming. While Walden mentioned the lost ad revenue, Jimmy Fallon is looking at the bright side:

We are being seen by more people than, I think, in the history of The Tonight Show. People are watching in different ways.

Fallon sometimes takes flak for his blandly positive attitude, general fun tone, and avoidance of politics, but in this landscape, I think a little bit of positivity can go a long way. The future is uncertain, but the two Jimmys do have one thing in common. They are both showing up in the face of uncertainty and doing the job in their own ways and as well as they can.

#3595. Magic: The Gathering Is Reprinting a Powerful $30 Sword With Perfect Pixel Art

Magic: The Gathering is reaching into its inventory of powerful artifacts to reprint a sword worth nearly $30, complete with gloriously nostalgic video game artwork. Sword of Truth and Justice, a popular Equipment first released in 2019, is returning in a new Secret Lair collection that draws inspiration from the blocky, polygonal graphics of the Nintendo 64 and original PlayStation era.

Announced by Wizards of the Coast on November 3, the Rise of the Polygons | Extra Life 2026 drop features four reprinted cards and an Elemental token, with half of the purchase price benefiting children's hospitals. The $39.99 non-foil collection also includes another valuable reprint in Balefire Dragon, making this a potentially enticing proposition for Commander players, collectors, and anyone who still gets misty-eyed thinking about Ocarina of Time (or its remake).

Originally released in 2019's Modern Horizons, Sword of Truth and Justice belongs to Magic's illustrious cycle of “swords,” many of which command considerable sums on the secondary market. According to recent market prices, the original non-foil printing hovers around $29, while certain premium versions fetch even more.

The three-mana artifact gives its equipped creature +2/+2 and protection from both white and blue, already a formidable combination. However, its combat damage ability is where things get particularly nasty. Whenever the equipped creature damages an opponent, its controller places a +1/+1 counter on a creature they control, then proliferates, adding another counter of each existing kind to any number of eligible permanents or players.

For decks revolving around +1/+1 counters, proliferate, or even planeswalkers, that represents an abundance of value from a single successful attack. And since the Equipment costs just two mana to attach, it's easy to keep the sword swinging away.

The artwork is arguably just as appealing as the card's impressive abilities. Whereas 2024's Extra Life collection, Pixel Perfect, embraced the 16-bit era, this year's installment advances a console generation with chunky, low-polygon character models and distinctly late-'90s RPG aesthetics. The result looks like something that might have occupied a treasured memory card back in 1998.

Given how collectible Magic's more unusual Secret Lair treatments have become, this particular sword seems destined to attract attention.

Sword of Truth and Justice might be the proverbial final boss of this collection, but Balefire Dragon is hardly a pushover. Originally printed in 2011's Innistrad, this seven-mana, 6/6 flying Dragon has become a beloved Commander menace, with ordinary non-foil copies generally commanding between $15 and $20.

Its ability is delightfully straightforward: Whenever Balefire Dragon deals combat damage to a player, it deals that much damage to every creature that player controls. One successful attack from an unmodified Balefire Dragon can leave an opponent staring at six damage across their entire army. Ouch.

Together, Sword of Truth and Justice and Balefire Dragon represent roughly $45 or more in existing card value, depending on the printings being compared. That already exceeds the $39.99 asking price of the non-foil drop, before accounting for the remaining cards.

Those include Young Pyromancer, the popular two-mana "spells-matter" creature that produces Elemental tokens whenever its controller casts an instant or sorcery, and Big Score, a useful red instant that converts discarded cards into fresh draws and Treasure tokens. Neither is particularly expensive, but both are eminently playable.

It's another welcome round of reprints from Wizards, which recently announced the long-overdue return of the roughly $18 Soul Spike after two decades without another printing.

Rise of the Polygons | Extra Life 2026 goes on sale November 16 through Magic's official Secret Lair storefront, with the sale ending November 30 at 1 a.m. PT. Non-foil copies cost $39.99, while traditional foil versions retail for $49.99.

Collectors attending MagicCon: Atlanta from November 13–15 will also have an opportunity to purchase the collection early, although quantities will be limited.

The charitable component deserves attention, too. Half of the online sales price, minus third-party transaction fees, will support Extra Life and Seattle Children's Hospital. At MagicCon, Wizards says all proceeds from its Extra Life merchandise and the Rise of the Polygons drop will go toward the cause.

It's an admirable initiative with some genuinely desirable reprints, especially for Commander enthusiasts. And for anyone who spent their childhood battling suspiciously angular dragons with impossibly oversized swords, the artwork is a rather charming bonus.

At least this time, beating the dragon won't require blowing into a cartridge.

#3594. Apple’s best MacBook Pro decision this week had nothing to do with touch

Apple’s new touchscreen MacBook Pro brings plenty of welcome upgrades, but one of the best things about this week’s launch is what the company decided not to change.

Was I aching for a touchscreen Mac? Not particularly. But I can see how useful it might be for a great deal of users, and I’m happy that their day has finally come. Or will come, starting November 6.

But I’ve been aching for a new Mac. Though my 2023 M2 Pro 16-inch MacBook Pro is still a great machine, its 16GB of RAM is starting to feel a bit cramped. Past me knew this was a mistake.

With the prospect of a revamped MacBook Pro just around the corner, I spent the past few weeks excited about the possibility of biting the bullet and splurging for a new one, even though there had been very conflicting rumors about which chips it would pack.

Although in my heart of hearts I had acquiesced to the idea that the new touchscreen MacBook Pro would get the same chips as the current non-touchscreen line, I was also holding on to the hope that Apple would throw in some performance gains to sweeten the rumored $400 premium deal it would carry.

Performance-wise, the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is identical to the non-touchscreen models, though there is a case to be made that its redesigned thermal system could make it run faster despite using the same chip, though the changes appear to be aimed more at keeping the display cool than improving heat dissipation. Time, and reviews, will tell.

Which makes Apple’s decision to keep the non-touchscreen M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro for sale all that more welcome and unexpected.

Even when Apple introduced the Touch Bar back in 2016, the only non-Touch Bar option left was the entry-level 13-inch MacBook Pro. If you wanted a more powerful Mac or a 15-inch model, you had to get with the program and pony up the extra $300 for the 13-inch model with Touch Bar, or $400 for the redesigned 15-inch model.

Yes, there is plenty new with the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. Tandem OLED display, improved thermal performance, thinner, lighter design, slimmer bezels, redesigned audio system, Dynamic Island (debatable for some, I know), and even the return of the glowing Apple logo (woo!) on the lid are all welcome additions. Oh yeah, and “it has touch as well.”

Put all of that together, and the $400 premium is arguably not that unreasonable.

But if, like me, these improvements feel secondary to the performance boost you’re prioritizing for this particular upgrade, getting those same specs for effectively $400 less (or using those $400 for better specs!) feels like a pretty great deal for all parties involved, future me included.

Will future me have preferred that I wait for the M7 generation? Possibly. But then again, waiting for the perfect moment to upgrade is what got me into this situation in the first place, recent price hikes and all.

#3593. This Ultra-Wide Samsung Gaming Monitor Is $600 Off

An ultra-wide curved gaming monitor with ridiculous specs is every gamer's dream, but they (usually) don't come cheap. The 57-inch Samsung Odyssey Neo G9, one of the best ultra-wide gaming monitors on the market, is currently on sale for $1,499.99 (originally $2,499.99 at launch)—that's its second-best discount, according to price-checking tools.

The Samsung Odyssey Neo G9 Series is not a regular ultra-wide gaming monitor. It has impressive specs, but you'll need a top-notch gaming computer with specific outputs to take full advantage of its 240Hz refresh rate potential.

This monitor came out in 2023 with an "excellent" review from PCMag, mainly due to its impressive 7,680 by 2,160 4K native resolution, the ridiculous 57-inch screen size, its great color range and accuracy, the 240Hz refresh rate, and its design. The VA panel also means you get a bright 1,000-nit screen. To make full use of its powerful 240Hz refresh rate, you'll need to use a DisplayPort 2.1, or you'll be limited to 120Hz. You'll also need a powerful modern graphics card that is able to push the frames at a native resolution to max out the monitor's potential.

Although it is pricey, this monitor is a great value for the right gamer. You'll need plenty of space to fit a 57-inch screen, as well as a powerful computer to justify using the monitor—if you're not a competitive gamer with a powerful computer, it's probably not worth the price tag. Instead, consider this Asus gaming monitor going for $329.99 (originally $499) right now.

#3592. Annie Andrews Flips South Carolina In Senate Race Against Lindsey Graham's Sister

Few people outside South Carolina knew who Annie Andrews was just six months ago. But in the 2026 midterms, she has made history as the first Democrat to win a statewide Senate election in the deeply red state since 1998, according to CNN.

Andrews was poised to take on longtime senator Lindsey Graham when she won the Democratic primary in June. When Graham died unexpectedly in July, it threw “us for a loop,” Andrews told Vanity Fair's Aidan McLaughlin. Andrews pivoted to campaign against Darline Graham, the late senator's sister, who was appointed by Governor Henry McMaster to fill his seat through January 2027.

With the blessing of President Donald Trump, Darline Graham opted to run for a full term, facing off against Andrews three weeks ago in a tense debate, during which the Democrat physician faced off against the political neophyte. “Why would we hand Darline Graham a full term in the US Senate? She is unserious and unqualified,” Andrews—who previously ran against Republican Nancy Mace in the 2022 race for South Carolina’s First Congressional District—said.

“In order for a Democrat to win in South Carolina, you need three things,” Charleston political operative Tyler Jones told Vanity Fair in July. “You need a popular Democrat, you need an unpopular Republican, and you need a favorable national environment." With Trump's support eroding across the US, Andrews has at least one of those—and if the most recent polling numbers are accurate, Andrews' popularity has just continued to grow.

Now, she must make good on her promise to “go to Washington and solve problems.” If Lindsey Graham had remained “a John McCain–style center-right Republican,” Andrews told McLaughlin, “I probably wouldn’t have gotten in this race.”

The Avengers haven't even assembled in theaters yet, and the numbers are already getting awkward for DC.

I've been watching the early numbers for Avengers: Doomsday with some curiosity, especially after all the continued talk of superhero fatigue (honestly, at this point, I have "superhero fatigue talk" fatigue). The Marvel movie doesn't arrive on the 2026 movie schedule until December, but it's already putting up numbers that would make plenty of released films jealous. According to a new report, it's collected $125 million in worldwide advance ticket sales. Compared with how DC's Supergirl performed this summer, things get pretty uncomfortable for the Girl of Steel.

Forbes reported the $125 million figure on Oct. 31, with roughly seven weeks still separating the movie from its Dec. 18 theatrical release. That's a huge amount of money for tickets to a movie that hasn't even opened yet. It's also strikingly close to the $126.5 million Supergirl earned during its entire worldwide theatrical run, according to Box Office Mojo. That's about a difference of about $1.5 million. Yikes.

Now, before anyone declares Marvel the winner of the latest comic-book movie showdown, there's an important distinction. Doomsday's number reflects tickets sold in advance for future screenings, not the final gross of a movie that's finished playing. The $125 million worldwide figure is also a reported estimate, not a total Disney has publicly confirmed. Still, having that many people commit to seats well before opening weekend is encouraging.

This isn't the first time the movie's advance sales have drawn attention. In September, according to The Wrap, Disney Chief Financial Officer Hugh Johnston revealed that Doomsday had already passed $50 million in domestic pre-sales three months before release. The latest worldwide figure covers additional markets, but both milestones show how early the rush began. I've covered the unusually early ticket rollout before, and there were already signs of serious demand when general sales opened in August.

Meanwhile, Supergirl's numbers paint a much rougher picture. Craig Gillespie's film, starring Milly Alcock as Kara Zor-El, opened in June and ultimately earned about $72.4 million domestically and $54.1 million internationally. It's a disappointing result for a major new DC release, even if box office numbers don't tell you whether it's worth watching. I know some fans enjoyed it, and they aren't suddenly wrong just because Marvel fans bought a bunch of tickets.

Of course, Doomsday has some advantages that Supergirl never had. Robert Downey Jr. is back in the MCU, this time playing Doctor Doom, and Anthony and Joe Russo are returning to direct an Avengers crossover packed with familiar faces. The combination of returning heroes and the promise of a major multiverse showdown was always going to attract attention. It's also following a massive year for Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which gave Marvel another enormous theatrical hit.

There's another interesting wrinkle: Doomsday opens opposite Dune: Part Three on Dec. 18. I've already written about the so-called "Dunesday" clash and the fight for premium screens, and advance demand for both movies suggests moviegoers could have a very busy holiday weekend. Those early tickets don't tell us which film will ultimately have the longer legs.

For now, I wouldn't call $125 million a guaranteed blockbuster, but it's hard not to be impressed. Supergirl spent its whole theatrical run reaching roughly the same number. Doomsday still has more than six weeks left before it opens. That's one heck of a head start.

Avengers: Doomsday opens in theaters on Dec 18. As for Supergirl, if you haven't had a chance to see it yet, it's streaming with an HBO Max subscription.

Throughout the Dick Wolf CBS procedural’s run, there have been a handful of exits. In the last couple of years, FBI has seen three big departures. It seemed like the curse could be done after Juliana Aidén Martinez’s addition at the beginning of Season 8, but alas, another could be coming.

In this week’s episode, “Atonement,” Scola (John Boyd) told the team that Nina (Shantel VanSanten) was offered to run her own task force. It was great news, but Scola didn’t seem too sure about it. He later tells Eva (Aidén Martinez) that the job is in San Diego. While at first he told Nina not to take it, he eventually calls her to say that she should after his conversation with Eva.

Scola was scared about uprooting their life and moving across the country, which is why he told Nina not to take it in the first place. His hesitation is understandable. Whether Boyd is actually leaving FBI remains unknown. Scola and Nina have gone through a lot over the last several seasons, between breakups, makeups, near-deaths, and welcoming their son. While I would absolutely hate to say goodbye to Scola, it would only make sense for him to follow Nina to San Diego so they can stay together and raise their son in the same proximity and not 2,800 miles apart.

Nothing is confirmed, and it’s not even clear if Nina will end up taking the job. It’s likely we’ll get more information during VanSanten’s return on November 16, but fans may have to brace themselves. Boyd has been on FBI since Season 2. It’s hard to imagine the show without him, but at this point, unfortunately, anything is possible. For now, we’ll just have to wait and see. #3586. iPadOS 27.2: Two new features just upgraded your iPad

iPadOS 27.2 arrived this week as the latest noteworthy iPad software update, here are two new features it includes.

Siri AI is a major improvement over the old Siri, and I’m using it all the time on my iPad—often with a CMD + Space keyboard shortcut since Siri and Spotlight are now integrated.

In iPadOS 27.2, Apple added another convenient way to interact with Siri that first debuted on the Mac in macOS Golden Gate.

When you select text in iPadOS 27.2 via a trackpad or mouse, there’s a new Siri contextual popup that appears to the left of your selection. If you hover over the Siri icon with your cursor, it instantly expands to offer an ‘Ask Siri’ text field.

This makes it quick and easy to ask Siri about whatever you’ve highlighted. And if you’re in the writing process, the Siri popup even has suggestions like ‘Proofread,’ ‘Rewrite,’ and ‘How does this sound?’ so you can get help with just a click.

Siri AI also includes several new upgrades that make it more capable. Per Apple’s release notes:

iPads make great video devices whether you’re an adult or a kid. And if you share an iPad with a partner or child, the Apple TV app has a welcome new addition: user profiles.

iPadOS 27.2 brings over the same profiles feature that tvOS already offered on Apple TV 4K.

When you open the Apple TV app on iPad, you’ll see a new profile selection screen at startup. From here, you can choose who’s watching and the TV app will automatically update its queue, playback history, and content recommendations based on your selection.

If you’re a parent, profiles will take content restrictions into account. So when your child’s profile is active, they’ll only see films and TV shows that match the age settings you’ve previously set.

And if you don’t want to use profiles, it’s easy to disable them from showing on startup with a quick tap.

#3584. WoW: Forever's Beta Was Pure Magic. No One Knows What Happens Next

Blizzard's retro MMO is about to sail into uncharted waters, but right now, it's clearly something special

The first thing I did in the World of Warcraft: Forever beta was roll a Troll. It was an instinctive response; my original WoW character, all the way back in 2005, was a Troll, and the sun-baked plains and dustbowls of Durotar and The Barrens will always be my Azerothian homeland. Naturally, the first thing I wanted to see in WoW: Forever's reimagining of classic WoW was how these environs look in the game's gorgeous new rendering.

I only took the character to level 6, however. I realized that this was the character I'd want to play and the path I'd want to follow in the live game when it launches this week, on Nov. 4, and I didn't want to spoil that experience. At the same time, I felt a professional obligation to check out Forever's brand-new race, the Skyborne elves, and their flying-island starting zone, Zephras Isle. So I started again, with a Skyborne Druid.

I had a nice time. I experimented with the official gamepad support and found it very useful, if not a natural fit for every facet of WoW's complex interface. I marveled at the developers' ability to write quests and build landscapes in the classic WoW style, effectively unlearning two decades' worth of evolving game design.

Here is an MMO that is simultaneously tougher and more relaxing than the modern game. It's less directed and has a much slower pace. It's dangerous to battle more than two everyday monsters at a time, and you will sometimes dip below 80% health while questing (unthinkable in modern WoW). This is a game that forces you to take your time, sweat the details, cover ground slowly, and live in the moment.

But still, something felt off. I didn't quite buy the Skyborne, and their free-floating home felt like a cop-out to me. It's an illustration of the difficulty Blizzard will have finding ways to expand this old world without stepping on its iconic status, or on the 20 years of accumulated lore that follows it. (WoW: Forever does not exist in a parallel universe; it's set in the main WoW timeline during the same period as original WoW, and therefore can't contradict anything that happened later.) Also, while I was enjoying the game, I found it easy to set aside; I wasn't as gripped by it as I was in 2005, or during the Wrath of the Lich King or Legion expansions.

Then I departed Zephras Isle and sailed down to Azeroth proper, and everything clicked into place. I was, suddenly, as enveloped as I had ever been by WoW, which is as enveloped as I have ever been by any game ever made.

One cause of this delayed reaction is baked into the design of classic WoW. Below level 10, it's a simple grind that just gets you situated in the world. It's between levels 10 and 20 that the game really comes alive and sinks its teeth into you. The vistas expand; the opportunities for adventure branch and multiply in every direction. You enter the hubbub of capital cities and start participating in the world's economy. You unlock air taxis (fast travel is extremely restricted in WoW) that unfurl the massive continents beneath you. You choose a class specialization and start to develop more involved combat routines. You enter your first dungeons alongside other players. You begin to get an inkling of the staggering scale of the world Blizzard built back in the early 2000s.

It's still one of the most thrilling gear-changes I've ever experienced in a game. WoW: Forever's development team has captured the experience perfectly and smoothed out its bumps expertly — without sacrificing the original game's spirit, which is what is attracting so many nostalgic lapsed players (and a good proportion of new players) to Forever. The classes feel distinctive yet tuned, the leveling is well-paced and devoid of ugly troughs, there's always more than enough to do. The game is absolutely humming. This is WoW, not as it was, but as it was meant to be.

In the beta, I ran a few dungeons: Ragefire Chasm, Wailing Caverns, the new Ruins of Lordaeron. There's a new looking-for-group system that's something like an organized want-ad board; it seems clumsy compared to modern WoW's instant matchmaking, but in reality I found groups pretty quickly. You can flag your playstyle as "learning," "relaxed," or "competitive." The point of the system is to encourage communication between players, and it works. Every "relaxed" group I entered was just that: polite, friendly, willing to talk and be flexible, and not in the wordless, impatient rush that characterizes dungeon-running in modern WoW. There was real camaraderie between players who didn't know each other. I realized how sorely I'd missed this.

WoW: Forever is also unexpectedly, heart-stoppingly beautiful. I've never seen a remaster quite like this. The original textures and art assets (though you can opt to use more detailed "HD" character models), in all their chunky, rough-hewn charm, are bathed in cutting-edge lighting, with dramatic fog and weather effects and beautiful water. These work with WoW's real-time, 24-hour diurnal cycle to create an incredibly strong sense of place, stronger than so many more graphically rich game worlds.

It is not shallow to say this is, perhaps, the best reason to play WoW: Forever — certainly if, like me, you have a longstanding affection for Azeroth. The first of the development teams' four guiding principles is "the world is the main character," and Forever revives one of the all-time great game worlds in a way that's simultaneously dazzling and 100% authentic.

Exploring this world, you can sense the passion of the Forever development team. They have set themselves the task of expanding on classic WoW without ever raising the level cap past 60 and turning it into the content treadmill it became. This sounds difficult; I'm not sure if it's even possible. But, in the short term, and based on my experience of the beta, they've created something truly magical, with a reason to exist that goes beyond pure nostalgia. WoW: Forever cracks one of the most influential and brilliant games of all time out of the amber that WoW Classic preserves it in, along with everything that made it special, and gives it room to live and breathe.

#3583. In Ohio, Amy Acton Defeats Vivek Ramaswamy for Governor

Ohio was home to one of the nation’s most competitive races for governor in the 2026 midterm elections, as entrepreneur and former Republican presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and Democrat physician Amy Acton battled to replace term-limited GOP governor Mike DeWine. But on Tuesday, Acton defeated Ramaswamy, according to the AP.

The Buckeye State, which is also home to Vice President JD Vance, hasn’t elected a Democrat to its highest office since 2006. But rising concerns regarding affordability and data centers boosted the campaign of Acton and running mate David Pepper, the former chair of the Ohio Democratic Party. Ramaswamy’s running mate, Rob McColley, is currently the Ohio Senate president.

A $4 million ad campaign from Ramaswamy had also split Republicans. The commercial featured Acton’s mother, from whom Acton has been estranged since her stepfather was reportedly arrested and charged with raping Acton when she was 12 years old. (According to The New York Times, the stepfather, who died in 2004, pleaded not guilty to the charges and then fled the state before trial.) In the ad, Acton’s 82-year-old mother, Donna Arthur, says, “Don’t let her become your governor,” prompting GOP members, including DeWine, to repudiate the commercial.

Meanwhile, Ohio’s US Senate race also went to the Democrats, further cementing their grip on the House. Over $500 million has been spent in the battle for the seat currently held by Republican senator Jon Husted, who was appointed to the role by DeWine in 2025 to replace JD Vance. Husted has been singled out for praise by President Donald Trump in recent weeks, especially when it comes to his physique, but trailed in the polls behind Democrat Sherrod Brown, who lost his previous seat in the US Senate to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024. The Associated Press and CNN have projected Brown as the winner, giving his party a major win in one of the country's most closely watched Senate contests.

#3582. You Should Enable This Chrome Feature That Flags Suspicious Websites

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you use Google Chrome, you can turn on a new safety feature that will warn you if you navigate to a suspicious website that looks like others already known for malicious behavior. The alerts are part of Enhanced Protection mode in Chrome's Safe Browsing, which checks your activity against potentially harmful sites and warns you if you're at risk of encountering malware, phishing, intrusive ads, or social engineering attacks.

Most internet users are familiar with the full-page alerts that appear if you navigate to a site that's known to be malicious. These red "dangerous site" warnings indicate a high risk of harm to the user and can't really be ignored since they take up the entire screen and urge you to go back to safety.

The new "suspicious site" alerts indicate possible risk of harm based on patterns consistent with other known malicious sites. This means that Google isn't as confident that the website is actually dangerous, but it looks a lot like others that are spreading malware or running phishing scams. These suspicious site warnings are smaller pop-ups with the text "This site doesn't seem right" and two button options: Mark as safe or Back to safety. The different colors, text, and formatting make it easy for users to distinguish between what Google deems dangerous versus suspicious.

Safe Browsing in Chrome has three options: standard protection, enhanced protection, and no protection at all (which isn't recommended). Standard protection checks your browsing activity, extensions, and downloads against Google's list of unsafe sites, which is updated periodically. By contrast, enhanced protection works in real time and uses AI analysis. Note that enhanced protection does require you to share more information about your activity to Google, and the data are linked to your Google Account.

#3581. iOS 27.2 adds new Find My feature at just the right time

iOS 27.2 is here, and alongside new features for Apple Photos, Messages, and Siri AI, the update also has a welcome addition for Find My: support for Apple TV 4K remotes.

Find My has long been the iPhone’s go-to hub for locating people as well as your Apple devices.

Except until now, there’s been one Apple device not included in the app.

The Siri Remote for Apple TV 4K has historically been absent from Find My. There was another way to locate it using the Remote app via Control Center, but most users probably didn’t realize that feature existed.

But with iOS 27.2, Apple TV remotes have now been added to the Find My app for location tracking. Open Find My in iOS 27.2 and go to the Devices tab, and compatible Siri Remotes (2nd gen and later) will now appear there.

It’s nice that Apple finally addressed this oversight, but the timing is no coincidence. That’s because the new Siri Remote (4th gen) is going to make finding a lost remote way easier.

That's great but I just discovered that my Apple Watch series 10 does not have the ability to notify me if I leave my iPhone behind. I can use Find My to see where the phone is, but it doesn't give me a notification alert. My series 7 watch had that ability and I'm shocked that the series 10 does not. This was confirmed to me by an Apple tech support technician this morning.

The new remote features Precision Finding support and a built-in speaker. So the next time it’s lost somewhere in your house, your iPhone can direct you step-by-step to its location and trigger a noise to help.

The new Siri Remote is included with the 4th generation Apple TV 4K. But you can also buy it separately for $59 and get the same new features.

The upgraded remote is compatible with all Apple TV 4K and Apple TV HD models. To benefit from Precision Finding though, you’ll need an iPhone 17 or newer.

Did you know the Remote app offered support for finding a lost remote? Will you use the new feature in Find My? Let us know in the comments.

Mckenna Grace has been working since she was a little kid, and at 20 years old, it feels like she’s done a bit of everything. She’s done drama, action, horror, romance and more, and in her next project, the book-to-screen adaptation of Sunrise on the Reaping, she’ll play out a deeply intense tragedy that also features massive action. However, while it’s clear she’s open to many kinds of projects and work, there is one thing she says no to: nudity. Surprisingly, her reasoning has to do with Disney.

As I said, when it comes to Grace's career, she's explored lots of different genres, which have put her in many different situations. I mean, in the last year alone, she’s worked on Regretting You, Five Nights at Freddy’s 2, Scream 7, PAW Patrol: The Dino Movie, The Last Kiss, Nimrods and Sunrise on the Reaping. Those are all very different movies, and during an interview with Cosmopolitan, she was asked if there are any kinds of roles she’d say no to. Here’s how she responded, and how nudity and Disney came into the conversation:

At this point, I definitely don’t do nudity or very hypersexual things. I respect anybody who can, but it’s terrifying to me. I don’t know if that’ll ever change. It’s not like I only do wholesome things—my character literally gets gutted by Ghostface in Scream—but my dream is to try and be a Disney princess someday.

See, it’s obvious from her explanation that she has nothing against intimacy or nudity. And it seems like she has a lot of respect for actors who do work on projects that require it or very sexual sequences, like Off Campus, for example. However, it’s not her cup of tea, and I do see why.

As she said, she wants to be a Disney princess someday. If you’ve seen the best Disney movies, you know there’s a certain level of wholesomeness involved. That’s not to say an actor who participates in a project that involves sex scenes or nudity wouldn’t get a role as a Disney princess or prince. However, it’s clear Grace is trying to create an image for herself that makes her an unquestionable fit for one of these very wholesome roles.

I think she’s doing a good job at that too. I mean, before Teagan Croft and Milo Manheim were cast as Rapunzel and Flynn Rider for the live-action Tangled, Mckenna Grace and Mason Thames were popular fan casts for the parts. She legitimately looks like a princess, and her bubbly and bright personality fits right in with that kind of character too.

Now, getting back to what she said, she made it clear she’s not only going to do wholesome roles, and her work on the 2026 movie schedule clearly showcases that. I mean, Scream 7 is a horror movie, and as she said, she gets brutally murdered in it. Also, Sunrise on the Reaping is not for the faint of heart. As a fan of the book, I know how brutal the story is, and I know we’ll see Grace acting out some truly violent and intense moments.

However, while she’s willing to do work like that, she does have boundaries she does not want to cross. That means she’ll say no to projects that are hypersexual or involve nudity, which is totally respectable.

With that said, hopefully someday she’ll get her wish of being a Disney princess. While we wait for that to happen (because I do feel like it’s inevitable), you can catch Mckenna Grace in Sunrise on the Reaping on November 20.

#3579. James Talarico Flips Senate Seat In Texas, While Gina Hinojosa Takes Governor's Race

The polls closed in Texas at 7 p.m. local time (the state is split between Central Time and Mountain Time) Tuesday, and within hours, one of the state's most contentious battles in the 2026 midterm elections was over, with Democrat James Talarico prevailing over Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, giving Democrats their first statewide victory in Texas since 1994.

As part of a campaign in the state's most closely watched race, Paxton embarked on a whirlwind tour across Texas, joined by President Donald Trump along the way. Given Trump's slumping approval, combined with popular discomfort around Paxton's scandal-plagued career, Talarico's lead continued to grow even as Elon Musk pumped cash into the Republican side.

In June, political advisor Mark McKinnon described Talarico in a piece for Vanity Fair as “a rare talent.” “He’s an eighth-generation Texan, a former middle school teacher, and a Presbyterian seminarian. In a state where the Scriptures amount to a kind of civic fixture, Talarico out-Bibles many Republicans,” McKinnon wrote. "What’s more, he is preaching a new kind of message that is not along partisan lines. Here’s a sample: ‘The biggest divide in this country is not left vs. right. It’s top vs. bottom. Billionaires want us looking left and right at each other instead of looking up at them.’”

Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Greg Abbott in Texas's governor's race, becoming the state's first Latina governor, as well as the first Democrat to hold the office in more than 30 years. The last one was also a woman: Democrat Ann Richards, who served from 1991-1995. Richards was the mother of Cecile Richards, the longtime president of Planned Parenthood.

#3578. What to Wear When Exercising Outdoors, Based on How Cold It Is

I fell in love with cold weather running while I was training for a spring marathon. It wasn’t a choice at first: Some weeks, the weather was bad for days on end, and if I stayed home, I would fall behind in my training. Everybody else in my training group was braving the elements, so I did too—with no regrets.

I got to run on quiet mornings while snow was softly falling. I signed up for a winter race that herded finishers into a heated barn for hot chocolate and soup. I set a personal record at a spring race, during which I pushed myself hard without breaking a sweat. I now find it sad when somebody tells me they’re afraid of running in the cold, or that they would run in the winter but don’t know what to wear.

No, cold weather doesn’t have to stop you from running, but getting dressed can be a puzzle: How do you keep from freezing your butt off at first and avoid overheating once you start to sweat? Fortunately, it isn’t as tough as it looks. With the right gear, your fingers and ears can stay toasty while you jog through a winter wonderland. Below, I’ll give you a temperature-by-temperature running cheat sheet, and then dive into the specifics on how to buy the best socks, shirts, and more.

When I get dressed to run in winter, I take a look at the “feels like” temperature, not the actual high or low. I also make sure to check the weather for the time I’ll go running, not for the whole day. It doesn’t matter how warm it will be at 2 p.m. if my run will be happening at 6 a.m., before the sun is up. I use the Carrot Weather app, but any app that gives you hourly feels-like temps will work just fine.

Next, use the 20-degree rule. Imagine that the temperature is 20 degrees (Fahrenheit) warmer than it really is. What would you wear then? Here's an example: if it’s 50 degrees out, you should dress as if it were 70: in a T-shirt and shorts, most likely. If it’s 30 degrees, you’d dress as if it were 50: long pants and maybe a light jacket. Get the idea?

Everybody has their own preferences. Some people wear shorts even when it’s snowing, while others will pop a beanie on as soon as there’s a detectable chill in the air. I’m a pretty middle-of-the-road runner when it comes to keeping warm, so here’s what I wear at each “feels like” temperature, starting with warmer weather and working our way colder. I'll give a guide to each type of garment or accessory at the end.

At 50+ degrees Fahrenheit, I’m wearing basically the same things I would for a summer run.

Head and hands: Nothing special. No gloves and no hat, unless it’s a baseball cap to shade my eyes from the sun.

We’re starting to feel the first bit of a chill. This is where I may start bringing gloves, although they’ll probably get stuffed into a pocket by the end of the run. Remember, with the 20-degree rule, it will feel like 60 degrees by the time you're warmed up.

Bottoms: Leggings, lightweight long pants, or shorts.

Top: Something with long sleeves, but ideally made of thin material (think long-sleeved T-shirt, not a full-on sweatshirt or jacket). If you wore a sun shirt in the summer, that's a good layering option for these cool temps. I like my REI Sahara Shade hoodie here, but any long sleeve will do. If you run fall and winter races, you'll probably be handed a free long-sleeved version at some point.

Hands: I usually just pull my shirt's sleeves over my hands, but you could wear knit gloves if you want. Consider something like Flipmits for an intermediate option (they can be folded down into a wrist cuff when your hands warm up).

Head: A headband if you need protection for your ears.

You may see a few snowflakes drifting down, but don’t bundle up in a snowsuit. Once you’re warmed up, it will only feel like 50 degrees—so go for something in “light jacket” territory.

Bottoms: Leggings or running tights. The fleece-lined kind can be nice. (I have these.)

Top: You’ll want some kind of jacket or sweatshirt. A lightweight, reflective rain jacket is great here, or just throw on a regular hoodie over your T-shirt. (I go with cotton sweats in dry weather or light snow, but I'd go for synthetics or wool if there's rain or sleet.)

Hands: Definitely wear gloves. The cheap knit ones are usually good enough, but consider treating yourself to a nice pair of running gloves.

Head: Your choice of hat or headband; I’d stick with the headband.

Feet: This is around the temperature you may start to want warmer socks. That goes double if snow is in play: snow that falls onto your shoes will work its way through the mesh, melt, and make your feet wet. Wool is a good material here, so consider something like these from Smartwool.

This is where I’ll officially say it’s “cold.” Whatever warm-weather gear you were getting away with at warmer temps, you’ll probably have to swap it out now. Shorts people will break out their long pants. Headband people will wear a real hat.

Bottoms: Leggings and shorts. I don’t care if you think it looks goofy to wear both; this is an A+ hack. Or try a puffer skirt.

Top: It’s definitely jacket weather. Rather than getting a warmer jacket, I like to wear the same light jacket as I did at 30 degrees, but this time with a long-sleeved fleece or wool base layer underneath.

Hands: Real gloves, please. You can keep wearing your little knit gloves if you’re able to tuck your hands inside your jacket sleeves, or if you have a pair of mittens to wear over top; otherwise, get windproof gloves.

Head: A hat, and maybe also a buff for your nose and mouth. (If you have any cloth masks still hanging around from the early COVID days, they’re perfect for cold weather runs.)

Feet: Warm socks for sure. If you’ll be doing a lot of running in these temperatures, you may want shoes that are specialized for the elements. Look for ones with Gore-Tex uppers, like the Brooks Ghost GTX.

This is where I tap out. If a run is just barely in the teens, I’ll make do with the 20-degree items I mentioned above, adding an extra layer wherever needed. But if that isn't enough, I opt for the treadmill. You certainly can run in this weather if you are determined. You’ll want windproof everything, some kind of face covering, and you may need eye protection such as goggles.

Whenever the weather gets to your own personal “too cold” temperature, remember that you still have options. The early afternoon is often the warmest part of the day, so a run may be tolerable then. There’s also no shame in using a treadmill (even if you have to join a cheap gym for this reason alone).

Everybody has different preferences, and with practice you’ll figure out if you’re the kind of person who wears three shirts before it hits freezing or the type to run through the snow in shorts. But this should give you a starting point when you head out for your first (or next) cold weather run.

As you continue on your cold-weather running journey, you may need to buy some new gear or repurpose things from elsewhere in your closet. And yes, the first few minutes of your run will feel chilly. But if you’re wearing the right shoes and clothes (and planning routes with a few extra factors in mind, which I’ll discuss below), winter running is not just feasible; it’s actually fun. So here are the items you may want to consider.

Your feet need to be warm and, if possible, dry. Warm socks go without saying, but there are some extra considerations when you’re picking socks to run in. Wool socks are ideal because they keep your feet warm even when they get wet. You may not think of winter as a wet time, but any snow that meets up with your body heat will turn into water. If you don’t have wool socks, synthetic wicking fabrics are a good second choice. Cotton is a no-no

First, the socks have to be able to fit into your shoes. If you’ve been running in super thin cotton or synthetic socks all summer, thick socks may not fit. Smartwool run socks are available in a thin version that can fit no problem—but in colder weather you’ll want some thickness for extra warmth. That thickness, in turn, may mean that your winter running shoes need to be roomier than the shoes you wear in summer. If you’re buying a new pair, make sure to try them on with the type of socks you intend to run in.

If your warm socks fit, you can make do with the same shoes you wore in the summer. Your feet will stay dry if the weather is dry and you stay out of puddles. If you encounter snow and slush, though, your feet will have to endure warm-but-wet conditions for the rest of your run. That can be okay for short runs, but for serious winter running, consider upgrading your shoes.

Some running shoes are available with water-resistant uppers. This level of water resistance will keep stray snowflakes out of your socks, but it isn’t reliable if you’ll be stepping in slush puddles. In that case, you’ll want something more waterproof, like Gore-Tex shoes, many of which are made for running trails.

If you expect to run on a lot of ice or packed snow, especially on trails, spikes can give you a little extra grip.

Yaktrax makes a rubber harness that stretches to fit your shoe, with steel coils and small spikes, for about $40.

Microspikes are a notch up from there, costing around $90 for what look like a miniature version of the chains you’d put on car tires.

And if you’re really dedicated—and are seeking a purpose-built pair of snow shoes—you can attach individual spikes: either these traction spikes from IceSpike, or via a DIY approach using sheet metal screws. (There’s a tutorial here.)

The versions that include rubber, like Yaktrax, can wear out quickly on pavement, so it’s best to save these for runs on trails or on unplowed paths. You’ll also want to be careful about the fit. I tried a pair that were similar to Yaktrax, but they were a tad too big. Shortly into my run, I found that the rubber stretched enough to pull the front set of spikes up over the top of my shoe. I've since gotten better-fitting ones, and they work great.

Spikes and specialized shoes help you go more places, in worse weather—but remember that they’re not required to just head out on a chilly day. Regular shoes are fine if the weather is cold but dry, or if you’re willing to put up with a little moisture.

I actually love when the weather gets cold enough that I need a jacket, because then I get to wear something that gives me extra pockets! Stick with thin jackets that have some room inside. By the time temps dip into the 20s or below, you’ll be doing some serious layering: for example, an undershirt, a long-sleeved warm layer, and a jacket. A great option for that warm layer is a wool base layer like this one. (Don’t worry, it’s not itchy.) If you can’t wear wool, a synthetic fleece is a good alternative.

Before you run out to buy all new clothes, experiment with what’s in your closet. Try repurposing a thin sweater, for example. Some people would never wear cotton for running (it can be cold when wet), but I wear it as my undershirt layer and have lived to tell the tale. Just make sure to shower or change after your run, so you aren't sitting around in cold, wet clothes.

The jacket is the most important layer. You can grab a sweatshirt in a pinch, but to be really well-equipped for nasty weather, you’ll want a jacket that is windproof and water-resistant. Jackets made for running are lightweight, for layering. Consider ones that are visible at night, with bright colors and reflective areas, and that come with zippered pockets.

Once it’s too cold for shorts, you’ll want to start layering your bottoms, too. Loose pants let cold air in, which is why leggings or “running tights” like these are standard winter wear for all genders. Running tights come in different thicknesses; go for something fleece-lined for your coldest runs, or layer two pairs.

You need to keep your ears warm, but don’t reach for a winter hat right away: an ear warmer or headband can cover your ears while still letting heat escape from the top of your head. And if anything is falling from the sky (say, snow), a baseball cap will keep it out of your eyes.

Fleece or knit hats are great for cold enough days, of course. The dividing line between earwarmer weather and hat weather is a personal one, and depends on whether you’re overheating. If you’re wearing a hat but sweating into your base layers, the hat is probably overkill.

Gloves, however, are essential. I keep a pair of cheap knit gloves in my jacket pockets, but windy or very cold days call for something stronger. You can layer gloves; I find gloves under mittens work well. You can also get windproof insulated gloves, which are warmer than any number of layers of holey knit gloves.

Your face will freeze on windy or very cold days, so this is where your old stash of pandemic face masks really shines. Consider a balaclava or even a fleece-lined bandana. A neck gaiter stays on better than a scarf if your neck is cold. At this point, every inch of you is covered but your eyes. Sunglasses can take care of that.

iPhone Duo has a lot of software features that are widely praised, but one area commonly seen as an issue is Safari web browsing. Here are two tips for improving the Safari experience on your iPhone Duo.

If you want to make the most of your iPhone Duo screen size when browsing, and your eyesight isn’t a problem, Dylan McDonald recently posted a couple tips he’s found helpful.

iPhone Duo has always been a game changer for me and productivity, something about it is just so dang goodPro tip, set your text size to 90% for a little extra space, and set default website zoom to 85% to enable wide layouts on most sites! https://t.co/xqziFwrYH5

He adds in a follow-up that setting your default website zoom to 85%, in his opinion, makes the size of sites look more natural. And of course, the chief benefit is enabling a wide/desktop-class layout in many cases on the folding display.

You can change these settings via the following:

I don’t have my iPhone Duo yet, but getting a wider layout for websites has definitely been on my wishlist for the Duo, so I look forward to trying these settings out.

The outer display Safari layout has been an especially big issue for some iPhone Duo users. That’s because the right-aligned controls take up a lot of space, making websites feel cramped.

Apple has even publicly acknowledged it’s investigating ways to improve the outer display Safari experience.
