Liberty Mutual has gone too far with its latest ad campaign, and people are taking to the streets to protest it. While the general public often rallies behind commercials featuring popular actors or funny mascots, dozens gathered outside the headquarters of the insurance company to protest the existence of "Liberty Biberty." I'm sad I missed this protest, but I'm totally down to show up for the next one.

Led by YouTuber DimesAreTasty, people recently gathered in Boston in front of the Liberty Mutual headquarters to protest Liberty Biberty. Looks like the heat is officially off Limu Emu and Doug, because consumers decided they have bigger fish to fry.

In the words of the protest organizer himself, Liberty Biberty is a "nasty little pest" that was created by Liberty Mutual to "make the world worse." While his original video was directed specifically at how the new creature is a disgrace to all corporate mascots, the protest itself seemed to consist of people who were annoyed by seeing ads for the company while they watched sports or streamed shows with a Prime subscription.

The protest was only one day and only attracted dozens of people, and legitimate outlets like ABC News and others came out to cover the event. Unfortunately, I think the negative attention will only give Liberty Mutual more incentive to use the character, and maybe this all builds to a wild Super Bowl halftime ad. We shall see!

Liberty Biberty originally started as a joke in an older Liberty Mutual commercial, which featured an actor trying to say "Liberty Mutual" and instead saying "Liberty Biberty" instead. That character went on to do more commercials, with a running gag that he couldn't correctly say Liberty Mutual.

32 A-List Celebrities Who Have Appeared In TV Commercials

This gag evolved into a creature, which Liberty Mutual officially rolled out in July. The yellow fur ball was a puppet created in collaboration with the Jim Henson Workshop, so yes, I think that makes it a muppet. It's unlikely it'll be remembered as one of the best Muppets, but possibly the first to have a protest against it.

There is a part of me that suspects that Liberty Biberty was made in part to be annoying. The more people are making videos and content online about how much they hate the Liberty Mutual mascot, the more the company gets its name out there. It's not like having an annoying mascot is going to do much to impact the company's legacy and how it sells insurance. Heck, this might be the most I've talked about insurance all year, so if that was the play by the marketing team, kudos to them for pulling it off.

The Liberty Biberty ads will continue as the 2026 TV schedule rolls on. I'll be interested to see if any future ads address the backlash to the mascot, or if they'll phase out the mascot entirely after this negative attention.

#3550. HomeKit Weekly: SwitchBot’s K11+ Pro packs strong suction and Apple Home support into a tiny robo vacuum

The robot vacuums designed for large open floor plans often have big batteries but take up a ton of space. The SwitchBot K11+ Pro goes the other direction: a tiny vacuum, a small dock, and Matter support so it works with Apple Home.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

The SwitchBot K11+ Pro is 9.76 inches across and 3.62 inches tall, and weighs about 5 pounds. That size is the whole point. It can work its way between chair legs, get closer to corners and walls, and slide under beds, couches, and cabinets that larger robots bump into and give up on. If you have a couch that sits lower to the ground, you know what this means

Navigation for the SwitchBot K11+ Pro is done by LiDAR for mapping and route planning, plus a close-range sensor for spotting furniture legs and following wall edges. It stores up to five maps, so you can carry it upstairs and it’ll know where it is, too. Inside the SwitchBot app, you get room and zone cleaning, schedules, no-go zones, and virtual walls. I use the SwitchBot app almost daily and really like it a lot. It’s super easy to use and navigate.

To me, the small dock is more critical than a small vacuum. Self-emptying docks are great until you realize most of them are the size of a small trash can. The Switch K11+ Pro’s station is around 9.4 by 7.1 inches. It also has a wood-patterned lid, so it looks less like an appliance sitting in your living room or laundry room. Inside the dock is a disposable dust bag that should last up to 3 months, depending on usage.

SwitchBot rates the K11+ Pro at up to 12,000Pa of suction, which is double the original K11+. I’ve got the original K11+, and while it’s great, it’s better suited to a bedroom than to a main living area. One thing to keep in mind: that’s a peak number from Max mode. Day-to-day, the Quiet, Standard, and Strong modes run much lower, and the robot automatically bumps up to Max when it hits carpet. On the other end of the power spectrum, Quiet Mode runs at about 45dB, which makes it a lot more realistic to run while you’re working from home or after the kids are in bed. My wife prefers quiet mode at all times, where I want more power at all times. With my other SwitchBot vacuums, the difference between Max and Quiet mode is that the latter can run while watching TV, whereas the former cannot.

For pet owners, it uses an all-rubber main brush and a two-arm side brush, both designed to keep hair from wrapping around them. If you’ve ever had to sit on the floor with scissors cutting dog or cat hair out of a roller, you’ll appreciate this feature.

The K11+ Pro supports Matter over Wi-Fi, so it pairs directly with Apple Home, and you can start a cleaning with Siri. SwitchBot lists Apple Home support for section cleaning, so you’re not stuck with an all-or-nothing on/off switch. Once it’s in Apple Home, it’s also available to your automations. Start cleaning when everyone leaves the house, and finish it before anyone gets back, etc. One thing to keep in mind is that the mapping and advanced functionality are managed in the SwitchBot app. So you’ll need to do a lot of your initial setup in it, but then you can rely on Apple Home day-to-day.

Big robots are built for big houses, but smaller homes will fit perfectly with it. The K11+ Pro is small enough to reach under the furniture, the dock is small enough to hide, and Matter means it works well with Apple Home. We have a larger unit in the main part of my house, but I am considering swapping to this one simply for its smaller footprint and manageable power. If you vacuum while no one is at home, you won’t mind that it has to recharge and empty itself a few times.

The SwitchBot K11+ Pro is available now in Black and White on Amazon and SwitchBot’s website.

#3549. Liam Neeson's New 2026 Action Movie Flopped At The Box Office

Another year, another Liam Neeson action movie. What else is new? This time, it's a police chase flick in the form of "The Mongoose." Ever since "Taken" became a box office hit that led to Neeson's unexpected action star makeover, the Oscar-nominated actor has been churning these pieces of genre fare out with regularity. His latest effort, however, failed to drum up much business.

"The Mongoose" opened to just $464,421 on 1,014 screens over the weekend, making for a terrible $458 per-screen average. It was duking it out with the badly reviewed horror comedy "Christmas at the Kringles," which bombed with just $710,526 on just over 1,800 screens. Because Halloween fell on a Saturday, it was a lousy weekend for new releases, so Samuel Goldwyn Films decided to throw this one at the wall to see if it would stick. It didn't.

Directed by Mark Vanselow, Neeson's new actioner centers on Ryan "Fang" Flanagan (Neeson), a man who, having been accused of a crime he didn't commit, leads law enforcement on a cross-country car chase with the help of his brothers in arms, all while the public roots for his getaway. The film's cast also includes Marissa Tomei ("Spider-Man: No Way Home"), Ving Rhames ("Mission: Impossible — The Final Reckoning"), and Michael Chiklis ("The Shield").

This is actually Leeson's second action flick to come and go while hardly registering with the moviegoing public this fall, as "The Fix" also opened in theaters in September, making roughly $1.2 million domestically in total. The days of the "Taken" trilogy are indeed very far behind us, it seems.

Like many of Liam Neeson's late career action movies, "The Mongoose" isn't exactly a critical darling, having only earned a 30% approval rating among critics on Rotten Tomatoes at the time of writing. That being said, this one was undoubtedly financed with the understanding that if it can be made at a certain price point, it'll find its audience on VOD/streaming.

Case in point, Neeson's "Blacklight" somewhat inexplicably took over Prime Video's streaming charts earlier this year, despite being considered one of the actor's worst films in recent memory. Similarly, in late 2024, Netflix breathed new life into Neeson's 2015 crime thriller "Run All Night." This sort of thing happens pretty regularly. People really enjoy these movies, even if it's more about enjoying them from the comfort of home. They may not be cinematic events, but they're good library titles that generate streaming revenue.

It's honestly been some time since one of Neeson's action movies was an out-and-out hit. 2018's "The Commuter" was like "Non-Stop" on a train and pulled in $120 million at the global box office. Ever since then, though, his films have tended to perform more like "The Mongoose." Setting aside the Neeson vehicles that were hampered by the pandemic, "The Marksman," "Blacklight," "Memory," "Marlowe," "Retribution," and "Absolution" are all real movies, yet each of them either disappointed or outright flopped at the box office.

We're arguably far removed from Neeson's best action movie "The Grey" or hidden gems like "A Walk Among the Tombstones." His recent efforts have tended to follow a very basic formula, and while it may not sell tickets in theaters, it clearly makes money elsewhere within the Hollywood ecosystem.

In a new interview with Collider, Safran confirmed Thames casting, which has been rumored for awhile. Here's what he said about the 19-year-old from How To Train Your Dragon and The Black Phone movies earning the role.

We always talk about wanting volunteers and not recruits to be part of the DCU, to be part of DC Studios, and Mason always wanted to be Dick Grayson. He just did. When Mason Thames stopped by San Diego Comic-Con's suite back in July, he gushed with us about his deep love for the character. As he shared with us at the time:

I'm a big comic book nerd... Spider-Man's always been No. 1, but I love Robin, specifically Dick Grayson's Robin. I've loved his comic books. I have about a million of them. It's just fun to see his journey from him being first Robin to becoming Nightwing, to becoming kind of the symbol of what Batman wishes Batman was. And, he's always kind of been the best of him.

DC's Dynamic Duo movie is set to have Thames' Dick Grayson working together with another Robin iteration, Jason Todd. Grayson grew up in a family of circus performers, but had to watch his parents fall to their deaths while trying to be complete one trick (after the act was sabotaged). He becomes Batman's first sidekick. Jason Todd, on the other hand, is a character who grew up on the streets of Gotham to a petty thief and a drug addict for parents before being taken in by Batman.

When the movie was announced it on X in October 2024, Gunn revealed it'd be "a mix of animation, puppetry, and CGI," making it a rather unique take on the characters. While Thames is presumably just taking on the voice role for Robin in this movie, Gunn has previously said this in 2023, per IGN:

#3545. Security Bite: This iOS 27.2 camera bug still isn’t enough to make me buy a camera cover

9to5Mac Security Bite is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Making Apple devices work-ready and enterprise-safe is all we do. Our unique integrated approach to management and security combines state-of-the-art Apple-specific security solutions for fully automated Hardening & Compliance, Next Generation EDR, AI-powered Zero Trust, and exclusive Privilege Management with the most powerful and modern Apple MDM on the market. The result is a totally automated Apple Unified Platform currently trusted by over 45,000 organizations to make millions of Apple devices work-ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

On Security Bite, it’s one of my favorite pastimes to explain why camera covers are virtually useless today. I’ve been called out plenty of times for it. So when Apple patches a bug that lets a malicious app get access to the camera without permission, I find myself in a rather precarious situation.

This week, Apple released iOS 27.2 to the public, and with it, over 160 different vulnerability patches. One of them fixes a bug that could let a malicious app access an iPhone’s or Mac’s camera without the user’s permission. Rest assured, this is not a hardware issue. Apple’s post-2008 change that put the camera module and the green LED indicator on the same circuit is not at fault here.

The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-86990 and credited to researcher Mustafa Calap, lives in CoreMedia, the framework apps use for audio and video. Apple’s notes only say “an access issue was addressed with improved access restrictions.”

That means the permission prompt, the one that asks whether an app can use your camera, could effectively be skipped entirely. On the Mac, that prompt comes from a system called TCC (Transparency, Consent, and Control), the gatekeeper that’s supposed to keep apps away from your camera until you say yes.

So, am I ordering a camera cover now? No. The green light would still come on (for iPhones that’s the green dot in the status bar rather than a physical LED), because the bug went after the permission, not the indicator. The problem is that the indicator only helps if someone’s there to see it. If you happened to be away from your desk, or your iPhone was face down on the table, there’d be nothing standing between that app and a live feed of the surrounding area.

It’s the exact scenario where tools like Patrick Wardle’s OverSight can come in handy. It’s free, open source application, that alerts you every time the camera or mic turns on and which app triggered it. I use it to log activity on all my Macs. Plastic over the camera can’t do that, huh?

There’s no indication from Apple that this one was exploited in the wild, which is good news here. Still, it’s important to update to iOS 27.2 and macOS Golden Gate 27.2, or iOS 26.7.2 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.2 if you’re holding off on the new OS. Older iPhones like the XS and XR get it in iOS 18.7.11.
